entry.title: AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization
entry.content:
Reference

  • Paper: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
  • Code: mit-han-lab/llm-awq

I read the arXiv v6 version. The core of AWQ is not “one more 4-bit quantizer”. The useful observation is more specific: the importance of a weight cannot be decided from the weight value alone. It also depends on the activation channel multiplied by that weight.

That observation has a direct deployment consequence. If we preserve an explicit FP16 outlier path, as in mixed-precision outlier handling, the runtime kernel has to handle both a regular low-bit dense path and an exceptional high-precision path. AWQ takes a more conservative route: keep a regular dense low-bit weight format, and only use activation statistics offline to decide how to scale input channels before quantization.

The paper also ships TinyChat, which is important. AWQ is not presented only as a compression recipe; the authors also show how the resulting W4A16 models run on desktop GPUs, mobile GPUs, ARM CPUs, and edge platforms. The algorithm and the system design are coupled: AWQ is useful for deployment because it preserves a hardware-friendly dense 4-bit weight layout.

One Sentence

AWQ is activation-aware weight-only quantization:

  • activations stay in FP16/BF16 at runtime, not INT4;
  • weights are quantized group-wise to INT3/INT4;
  • calibration activations are used only offline to identify important input channels and search per-channel scales;
  • those scales are folded through equivalent transformations, so the final runtime format remains close to a regular dense W4A16 format.

What I like about the paper is that it does not overcomplicate the problem. There is no training loop, no Hessian solver, and no long layer reconstruction process. AWQ mainly trusts one robust statistic: some activation channels have much larger magnitudes, and the weight columns connected to those channels contribute more to the layer output.

Motivation: Salient Weights Depend on Activations

Figure 2 is the center of the paper. Direct RTN quantization makes OPT-6.7B INT3-g128 perplexity very poor. If 1% salient weights are kept in FP16, perplexity recovers dramatically. The problem is that a mixed FP16/INT3 format is inconvenient for hardware, because the kernel now needs to combine a regular dense low-bit path with an irregular high-precision path.

AWQ’s alternative is not to keep actual FP16 outliers. Instead, it scales up salient channels before quantization. After scaling, the weights on those channels occupy a larger range on the quantization grid, so their relative rounding error becomes smaller. The activation is scaled in the opposite direction, so the floating-point computation remains equivalent.

The key question becomes: which weights are salient?

Table 1 gives the first strong clue:

  • randomly keeping a small fraction of FP16 weights is unstable;
  • selecting weights by weight magnitude or weight norm is not enough;
  • selecting channels by activation magnitude is much more effective, and even 0.1%-1% salient channels can reduce perplexity significantly.

This means “important weights” are not simply large values in the static weight tensor. Importance is input-dependent. A weight column may not look extreme by itself, but if its corresponding activation channel is often large, its quantization error is amplified in the output.

Formula 0: Fixing the Linear Layer Notation

To stay close to the paper, I write a linear layer as:

Here is the linear layer weight and is the input activation. Many deep learning frameworks write the same computation as ; that is only a layout convention. AWQ scales the input channel direction. Under the notation, that corresponds to the columns of .

If we insert a diagonal scale matrix , the floating-point computation satisfies:

This is the equivalent transformation used by both AWQ and SmoothQuant. The goal is different. SmoothQuant mainly uses the transform to smooth activation outliers for W8A8 quantization. AWQ uses the transform to protect selected weight channels in W4A16 weight-only quantization.

The important point is that the transform is exactly equivalent only before quantization. Once is applied to , the quantizer sees a different weight distribution, and the quantization error changes.

Formula 1: Uniform Weight Quantizer

The paper first defines a standard weight-only quantizer:

Here denotes the weights inside a group or block, is the bit-width, and is the scale for that group. My reading of the formula is:

  1. divide the floating-point weight by to map it to an integer grid;
  2. round the mapped value to the nearest grid point;
  3. multiply by again to dequantize it back to the floating-point domain.

The error comes from . If the maximum absolute value in a group is large, then becomes large, and ordinary weights in the same group get a coarser effective grid. This is the central tradeoff in group-wise quantization. A larger group size reduces metadata overhead and often gives better kernels, but it also makes unrelated channels share the same quantization scale.

This screenshot contains Equations 1-3 from the paper. I unpack them below because the whole AWQ idea is hidden inside these few lines.

Formula 2: Scale Up Salient Weights, Scale Down Activations

Suppose a salient weight belongs to a channel scaled by . The corresponding activation is multiplied by . Without quantization, the product is unchanged. With quantization, however, the quantizer is applied to the scaled weight:

Here is the new quantization scale after the group has been scaled.

There are three pieces to understand:

  1. becomes , so it is represented by a larger coordinate on the integer grid. Small details are less likely to be rounded away.
  2. The output is multiplied by , so the floating-point function would remain unchanged if quantization were absent.
  3. The risk is that may also grow. If scaling changes the group maximum, the whole group gets a coarser quantization grid, and non-salient weights in the same group can be hurt.

So AWQ is not saying “larger scale is always better”. It is searching for a balance: protect activation-salient channels while not making the group scale too coarse for the rest of the weights.

Formula 3: Why the Relative Error Can Drop

The paper writes the original quantization error and the scaled quantization error as:

This derivation relies on a few practical approximations:

  • the expected rounding error is roughly similar before and after scaling;
  • when only a small fraction of salient elements are scaled, the group maximum often does not change much, so ;
  • and are still represented in high precision, so the main new error source is weight rounding.

Under these approximations, the scaled salient weight gets about a reduction in output error:

This is the mathematical intuition of AWQ. Scale up an important channel before quantization, then scale it back at runtime; the floating-point function is preserved, but the relative quantization error on that channel can decrease.

The same derivation also explains the failure mode. If is too large, is no longer close to 1. Then the group scale becomes too coarse, and the extra error on non-salient weights can outweigh the benefit on salient weights.

Table 2 verifies this behavior. On OPT-6.7B with 1% salient channels, gives the best perplexity. Increasing the scale to keeps reducing the relative error of salient weights, but it changes more group scales and damages non-salient weights, so total perplexity gets worse.

Table 3 shows a related point. A fixed already works, but searching the scale is more stable and can match or exceed the mixed-precision “1% FP16 salient weights” baseline while keeping a regular dense low-bit format.

Formula 4: The Real Objective Is Layer Output Error

The previous error analysis explains why scaling can help. The actual AWQ search is layer-wise: find an input-channel scale such that the quantized layer output stays close to the FP16 layer output:

Here is the cached activation from a calibration set. I interpret the objective as:

  1. scale the input-channel direction of by ;
  2. scale the corresponding channels of by ;
  3. quantize the scaled weight;
  4. compare the quantized output against the original FP16 output.

If were removed, the loss would be exactly zero because . Therefore the whole loss comes from quantization. AWQ is not changing the model function in floating point; it is changing the distribution seen by the quantizer.

This objective looks like reconstruction, but it is different from GPTQ in spirit. GPTQ uses calibration activations to build an approximate second-order problem, then quantizes weights sequentially with error compensation. AWQ does not run backpropagation and does not invert a Hessian. It searches over a small activation-aware scale family.

Formula 5: The Search Space Is Parameterized by Activation Magnitude

Optimizing an independent scale for every channel would be difficult because rounding is non-differentiable and the search space is high-dimensional. AWQ reduces the problem to a one-dimensional hyperparameter:

is the average activation magnitude for each input channel, computed from calibration data. The exponent controls how strongly AWQ trusts the activation statistic:

  • : , so the method degenerates to RTN/group quantization with no scaling;
  • larger : high-activation channels receive stronger protection;
  • : the scale fully follows the activation magnitude.

The paper performs a fast grid search over . This design is important because it turns a high-dimensional, non-differentiable, and potentially unstable problem into the offline evaluation of a small number of candidate scales.

My mental model is: “activation-aware” does not mean AWQ dynamically reacts to activations at runtime. It means calibration activations are compressed into fixed channel scales. Once deployed, each layer already has its chosen scales, and the runtime can still follow a regular W4A16 path.

AWQ Pipeline

Putting the formulas together, the offline quantization pipeline is roughly:

  1. collect a small number of calibration sequences and run the FP16 model;
  2. cache the input activations for each linear layer;
  3. compute the average activation magnitude per input channel to obtain ;
  4. grid search and form candidate scales ;
  5. for each candidate, evaluate the output gap between and ;
  6. choose the scale with the smallest loss, then apply weight clipping to further reduce group-wise quantization MSE;
  7. store the final weights as group-wise INT3/INT4 and run W4A16 dequantization plus matrix multiplication at inference time.

The easy implementation bug is the channel axis. AWQ scales the input channel of a linear layer, which corresponds to the columns of under the notation. If the framework stores weights as [out_features, in_features], the scale is applied along the in_features dimension.

Why Weight-Only Quantization Works Well for On-Device Decode

Figure 3 is the system motivation. Autoregressive generation at batch size 1 is often memory-bound rather than compute-bound. For every new token, the model reads a large amount of weight data, while the activation footprint is much smaller. W4A16 does not quantize activations, but it can reduce weight bandwidth to about one quarter of FP16, so it is especially useful in the decode stage.

This also explains why AWQ and SmoothQuant target different deployment regimes:

  • SmoothQuant targets W8A8 so both activations and weights can enter INT8 GEMM;
  • AWQ targets W4A16 so memory-bound decode reads much less weight data;
  • if the workload is large-batch prefill, W8A8 or FP8 can be more attractive;
  • if the workload is interactive edge decoding, weight bandwidth reduction is more direct.

TinyChat: Format and Kernels Matter

W4A16 is not automatically fast because most hardware does not expose a direct INT4 x FP16 matrix instruction. A real kernel has to read packed 4-bit weights, unpack and dequantize them, and multiply them with FP16 activations.

TinyChat handles several engineering details:

  • on-the-fly dequantization: do not write dequantized FP16 weights back to DRAM; unpack and dequantize inside the matmul loop;
  • platform-aware packing: reorder 4-bit weights for ARM NEON, CUDA, and other backends so unpacking uses fewer SIMD or bitwise instructions;
  • kernel fusion: reduce launches and intermediate memory traffic for operations such as LayerNorm, QKV projection, positional embedding, and KV cache update.

This part is a useful reminder: reporting a compression ratio is not the same as reporting speed. Low-bit formats only accelerate inference if the decode path accounts for unpacking, scaling, metadata loads, and memory traffic.

Language Modeling Results

Table 4 is one of the main language-modeling results. It compares RTN, GPTQ, GPTQ-R, and AWQ across LLaMA/Llama-2 model sizes. My takeaways:

  • INT4-g128 RTN is not catastrophically bad, but AWQ is consistently better;
  • INT3-g128 creates a larger gap, which means AWQ matters more when the bit-width becomes aggressive;
  • GPTQ-R’s reordering trick can help on some models, but AWQ does not depend on reordering;
  • AWQ remains close to FP16 even on 70B models, so the method is not a small-model artifact.

I see AWQ as complementary to GPTQ. GPTQ behaves more like a local second-order reconstruction solver. AWQ behaves more like an activation-statistics-guided equivalent transform. Both use calibration data, but they use it in very different ways.

Instruction-Tuned Models

Instruction-tuned models test generalization. A quantization method that reconstructs a calibration set very well does not necessarily preserve chat or instruction-following behavior. The paper uses GPT-4 pairwise evaluation on Vicuna and shows that AWQ has more quantized wins and fewer quantized losses than RTN/GPTQ under INT3-g128.

This should not be overinterpreted as “GPT-4 evaluation is the final answer”. The useful signal is narrower: AWQ avoids heavy fitting to a small calibration set, so it appears less likely to damage instruction behavior under distribution shift.

Multi-Modal Models

The OpenFlamingo result is useful because VLMs are not pure text-only language models. AWQ quantizes only the language component, yet it clearly outperforms RTN/GPTQ on COCO captioning across few-shot settings. In INT4-g128 32-shot evaluation, the degradation shrinks from RTN’s -4.57 to AWQ’s -1.17.

The VILA table is even more direct: INT4-g128 is nearly lossless across multiple visual-language benchmarks. The point is not only that the numbers are good. It suggests that activation-aware scaling is not tightly bound to one text calibration distribution; it captures a lower-level channel magnitude statistic that transfers across model families and tasks.

Code, Math, and Extreme Low-Bit Settings

The MBPP and GSM8K results show that AWQ is not merely reducing WikiText perplexity. Code and math tasks are sensitive to generation quality. Under INT4-g128, AWQ stays close to FP16, and some numbers are even slightly higher than FP16. I would not read that as “quantization makes the model smarter”; it is more likely evaluation noise, sampling variance, or a mild regularization effect. The important point is that AWQ does not visibly destroy complex generation behavior.

Table 9 is also important. AWQ can be combined with GPTQ under an extreme INT2-g64 setting and further reduce the gap. This supports a clean division of labor: AWQ is an equivalent-transform or preprocessing step, while GPTQ is a quantization solver.

Calibration Robustness

Figure 8 best shows the character of AWQ.

The left plot shows that AWQ can work with fewer calibration sequences. This makes sense because it mainly estimates average activation scale rather than fitting a complex reconstruction solution.

The right plot shows that AWQ is less sensitive to calibration distribution mismatch. When calibration and evaluation domains are swapped between PubMed and Enron, GPTQ has a much larger perplexity gap. AWQ’s degradation is only about 0.5-0.6. This matches the paper’s claim: avoiding backpropagation and heavy reconstruction reduces the chance of overfitting the calibration set.

This does not mean AWQ can ignore calibration. Activation magnitude still comes from calibration data. If the target deployment domain has unusual activation patterns, it is still better to recalibrate with representative prompts.

Speed Results

TinyChat’s speed plot connects the algorithm to actual tokens per second. Compared with HuggingFace FP16, AWQ W4A16 improves throughput on RTX 4090, Jetson Orin, and RTX 4070 laptop GPUs. Some models that run out of memory in FP16 also become runnable in W4A16.

The VILA throughput table shows the same benefit for multi-modal models. VILA-13B is OOM in FP16 on RTX 4090, while AWQ W4A16 runs with a throughput of 99.0.

Figure 10 compares AutoGPTQ, llama.cpp, exllama, and TinyChat. The comparison is not perfectly apples-to-apples because these systems support different model families, packing formats, and kernel backends. The useful message is that TinyChat is not optimized only for a single LLaMA path. It covers StarCoder, StableCode, Mistral, Falcon, and other models, and it runs on edge devices such as Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi.

AWQ vs. GPTQ / SmoothQuant / LLM.int8 / SpQR

These methods address related LLM quantization problems, but their runtime formats are quite different:

  • LLM.int8() targets mostly INT8 computation with an FP16 outlier path. It demonstrates that LLM activation outliers are real and that naive INT8 quantization is not enough.
  • SmoothQuant targets dense W8A8 INT8. Its key signal is the activation/weight max scale, and its main idea is to migrate activation quantization difficulty into the weights.
  • GPTQ targets dense W3/W4A16 weight-only quantization. Its core signal is calibration-based Hessian/reconstruction, so it behaves like a local second-order rounding solver.
  • AWQ also targets dense W3/W4A16 weight-only quantization, but the key signal is activation magnitude plus scale search. My interpretation is that AWQ protects activation-salient weight channels through an equivalent transform while preserving a kernel-friendly dense layout.
  • SpQR targets low-bit weights plus sparse correction. It stores some sensitive/outlier weights in a sparse path, which is closer to a near-lossless compression format but gives the runtime a more complex format.

AWQ and SmoothQuant look similar at the formula level because both use diagonal scaling as an equivalent transformation. The objective is different:

  • SmoothQuant mainly wants activations to be representable in INT8;
  • AWQ wants salient weights to have lower error under INT3/INT4 group quantization;
  • SmoothQuant moves difficulty from activations into weights;
  • AWQ uses activation statistics to decide which weight columns deserve protection.

The difference between AWQ and GPTQ is more engineering-oriented:

  • GPTQ’s strength is precise local reconstruction, especially at low bit-widths;
  • AWQ’s strength is simplicity, speed, and lower risk of calibration overfitting;
  • under extremely low bit-widths, AWQ scaling can be used before GPTQ, which is exactly what Table 9 explores.

Implementation Notes

If I were implementing AWQ from scratch, I would check these details first:

  1. Attach the calibration activation hook to the right tensor. AWQ uses per-input-channel scales, so the axis for linear, attention, and MLP layers must not be flipped.
  2. Verify the floating-point equivalent transform. Before quantization, should match up to numerical error.
  3. Watch group scale inflation. If many groups have much larger than 1, the scale is too aggressive and non-salient channels will be damaged.
  4. Do not judge only by a single-layer MSE. The final model should still be checked by perplexity or task metrics because local layer error is not always aligned with full-model behavior.
  5. Account for metadata. INT4 weights still need scales, zero points, and packing padding. The real memory footprint is not just the raw bit-width.
  6. Profile the kernel path. W4A16 will not be fast if unpacking/dequantization is slow or if dequantized weights are written back to DRAM.

A practical debug plot is: for each layer, draw channel activation magnitude, selected scale , and per-channel output error before and after quantization. When AWQ works correctly, high-activation channels should receive stronger protection, while ordinary channels should not see a global error increase.

Limitations

AWQ is not a universal low-bit quantization answer.

First, it mainly reduces weight memory and weight bandwidth. It does not solve KV cache memory. In long-context serving, KV cache can become the larger bottleneck, where KIVI, KV quantization, PagedAttention-style memory management, and related methods belong to a different line of work.

Second, AWQ still uses FP16/BF16 activations at runtime, so it does not get all the benefits of W8A8 integer GEMM. Choosing AWQ depends on whether the workload is decode memory-bound or prefill compute-bound.

Third, activation magnitude is a calibration statistic. The paper shows that AWQ is less sensitive to calibration distribution mismatch than GPTQ-style reconstruction, but a very unusual deployment input distribution can still require recalibration.

Finally, AWQ depends on kernel quality. A smaller model file does not imply faster end-to-end inference unless the W4A16 kernels are actually optimized.

Takeaway

AWQ’s core contribution can be compressed into one sentence: use activation statistics to identify important weight channels, then protect those channels through equivalent scaling while keeping the final model in a regular dense low-bit weight-only format.

This paper is best read between GPTQ and SmoothQuant. GPTQ teaches that calibration activations can guide weight rounding. SmoothQuant teaches that diagonal scaling can move quantization difficulty between activations and weights. AWQ combines both ideas into a lightweight W4A16 recipe and follows the system path all the way to TinyChat.

For me, the most valuable part of AWQ is not one particular perplexity number. It is the deployment principle: if protecting outliers would make the kernel irregular, first ask whether an equivalent transform can fold that protection back into a regular dense format.

entry.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable NAS
entry.content:
Paper : AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search.

AdaBERT is an early attempt to connect two lines of work: BERT compression and differentiable NAS. The paper’s core claim is not simply “make BERT smaller”. It argues that a single compressed architecture is wasteful because downstream tasks use BERT differently. Sentiment classification, sentence-pair equivalence, and entailment recognition should not necessarily share the same student network.

The method searches a small task-specific architecture under three signals:

Here, L_CE is the supervised task loss, L_KD distills task-oriented knowledge from a fine-tuned BERT teacher, and L_E penalizes inefficient structures. In the experiments, the searched students are about 6.4M to 9.5M parameters, compared with 109M parameters for BERT-base.

Motivation

Most classical BERT compression methods pick one student shape and reuse it across tasks. That is convenient, but it hides an assumption: the best compressed architecture for SST-2 should also be good for MRPC, QQP, MNLI, QNLI, and RTE.

AdaBERT challenges this assumption. Prior probing work had already shown that different BERT layers and attention heads carry different linguistic signals. If each downstream task only needs part of that information, then compression can be task-adaptive: keep the behavior useful for the target task and remove structure that is redundant for that task.

The framework is easy to read from the figure. A fine-tuned BERT teacher gives task-oriented signals, the labeled target dataset gives supervised loss, and the efficiency term pushes the search toward smaller models. The output is not a pruned BERT block. It is a searched small model.

Search Space

The searched student is CNN-style rather than a shallow Transformer. This choice is important. AdaBERT is not trying to preserve the original Transformer computation graph; it treats the teacher as a source of task behavior and searches a cheaper network that can mimic that behavior.

The architecture has two levels:

Component What is searched Why it matters
Stacked layers K in [1, K_max] Controls depth, capacity, and latency.
Cell structure Operations on directed edges Controls how local/contextual features are encoded.

The cell is a directed acyclic graph. Candidate operations include:

  • standard 1D convolution with kernel sizes 3, 5, and 7;
  • dilated 1D convolution with kernel sizes 3, 5, and 7;
  • average pooling and max pooling with kernel size 3;
  • skip connection;
  • zero operation.

For single-sentence tasks, the two input nodes can receive the same input sequence. For sentence-pair tasks, the two input nodes correspond to the two texts. This gives the search space a way to express either self-interaction or pairwise interaction.

The paper sets K_max = 8, the number of inner nodes N = 3, gamma = 0.8, beta = 4, and searches the architecture distribution for 80 epochs.

Distillation As A Search Signal

The distillation design is more specific than ordinary logit matching. AdaBERT freezes a fine-tuned BERT teacher and trains probe classifiers on the hidden layers. These probes turn intermediate teacher states into task-related logits. The student then learns from a hierarchy of teacher signals, not only the final output.

This matters because NAS needs a useful search signal early. If the student only sees labels, small GLUE datasets such as MRPC and RTE may not provide enough information to distinguish candidate architectures. The paper’s task-oriented distillation gives the search process a smoother target:

  • final task labels keep the student grounded;
  • probe-based intermediate logits expose which teacher layers are useful for the task;
  • data augmentation enriches the distillation set;
  • attentive weighting emphasizes teacher probes that predict the sample better.

The differentiable part uses Gumbel-Softmax relaxation for both layer count and operation choices. During forward computation the method uses one-hot sampled choices; during backward propagation it uses continuous relaxed variables through a straight-through estimator. After search, taking argmax over the learned architecture distribution gives the final child model.

Efficiency-Aware Loss

AdaBERT adds an explicit architecture cost:

The exact form in the paper normalizes operation size and FLOPs, then uses FLOPs as a proxy for inference time. This is a simple cost model, but it forces NAS to care about deployment. Without this term, the search can choose larger structures that look slightly better in accuracy but lose the point of compression.

Compression Results

The main result is that AdaBERT trades a small accuracy drop for much smaller and faster models.

The headline numbers:

Model Params Inference speedup Average score
BERT-base teacher implementation 109M 1x 82.4
TinyBERT4 14.5M 9.4x 80.6
AdaBERT 6.4M-9.5M 12.7x-29.3x 80.1

AdaBERT is not the most accurate row in the table. TinyBERT4 and BERT6-PKD have slightly better average scores. The point is the speed/size tradeoff: AdaBERT is much smaller and faster, while keeping the average GLUE score close enough to make the compression credible.

The per-task architecture sizes are also useful.

SST-2 gets the smallest model: 3 layers, 6.4M parameters, and 29.3x speedup. MNLI gets the largest searched model: 7 layers, 9.5M parameters, and 12.7x speedup. This matches intuition. Binary sentiment classification is easier than entailment over diverse premise-hypothesis pairs.

Task Adaptiveness

The strongest evidence for task-adaptiveness is Table 3. The authors take the structure searched for one task, reinitialize it, train it on another task, and compare performance. If one architecture were universally good, cross-task transfer would work well. It does not.

The diagonal entries are the best in every column. That means the SST-2-searched structure works best on SST-2, the MRPC-searched structure works best on MRPC, and so on. Transfer within related sentence-pair tasks is less harmful than transfer across task types, but the overall pattern supports the paper’s claim: the searched structures are task-specific.

The visualized cells make the same point from another angle.

SST-2 uses more aggregation-style operations such as max pooling and smaller convolution filters. MRPC, a sentence-pair equivalence task, has more direct interactions between the two input nodes. QNLI uses a more diverse mix, including skip connections and average pooling, which fits the paper’s explanation that entailment needs more complex interactions.

This is the part I find most convincing. The paper is not only reporting a better average number; it shows that the architecture shape changes in a way that roughly matches task structure.

Ablation

The knowledge-loss ablation explains why AdaBERT is more than a plain DARTS-style search over small CNNs.

Adding probe models improves every task over base KD. Adding data augmentation improves again, especially on smaller datasets such as MRPC and RTE. Adding the supervised cross-entropy term gives the best row. The lesson is that task-oriented compression needs both teacher behavior and target labels.

The efficiency-loss ablation is also clean.

With beta = 0, the model becomes larger. With beta = 8, the model becomes smaller but accuracy drops because the search overuses cheap operations such as skip and zero. The middle setting, beta = 4, is the best tradeoff in this experiment.

Reading Notes

I would read AdaBERT as a compression framework, not as a pure NAS benchmark. Its interesting idea is that the teacher defines task relevance, while NAS decides how much student structure is needed to reproduce that relevance.

What I would keep from this paper:

  • do not assume one compressed BERT architecture fits every task;
  • include an explicit efficiency term in the search objective;
  • use intermediate teacher signals when labels are too weak for architecture search;
  • evaluate whether searched structures transfer across tasks, not only final accuracy.

There are also limitations.

  • The student search space is CNN-based. This gives speed, but it means the student is no longer a Transformer-like model.
  • The method needs a fine-tuned BERT teacher and a search run per task.
  • The experiments are on six GLUE tasks and BERT-base; the conclusions do not automatically transfer to modern LLM compression.
  • FLOPs and batch-size inference speed are useful proxies, but real deployment still depends on kernels, sequence length, hardware, and batching.

Overall, AdaBERT is useful because it makes task-specific compression concrete. The paper’s numbers are not the final word on BERT compression, but the design principle still holds: if different tasks use different parts of a teacher, the compressed student should be allowed to have different architecture too.

entry.title: AdaRound: Adaptive Rounding for PTQ
Regularized Evolution for Image Classifier Architecture Search
entry.content:
Real E, Aggarwal A, Huang Y, Le Q V. Regularized Evolution for Image Classifier Architecture Search. AAAI 2019.

Paper / Colab

AmoebaNet is a useful paper because it separates two things that were often mixed together in early NAS papers:

  1. the search space, which was already made strong by NASNet;
  2. the search algorithm, where the paper compares evolution, RL, and random search under similar conditions.

The key algorithmic change is aging evolution. Tournament selection still chooses a good parent from a sampled subset of the population, but the algorithm removes the oldest individual instead of removing the worst one. That sounds like a small queue-management rule, but it changes the failure mode: a model that got lucky early cannot sit in the population forever.

The result is AmoebaNet-A, an evolved NASNet-style cell architecture. The paper reports that evolution reaches good candidates faster than the reproduced RL baseline in the early part of the search, and the final AmoebaNet-A transfer result is competitive on ImageNet.

Motivation

Before this paper, the strongest automated image classifiers were mostly RL-based NAS results, especially NASNet. That makes the comparison tricky: if an RL controller finds a good model, is the controller the important part, or did the NASNet cell search space already do most of the work?

AmoebaNet keeps the NASNet-style search space and changes the optimizer. This is the clean part of the paper. It is not trying to invent a new convolution operator or a new macro skeleton. It asks whether a simpler evolutionary process can compete with an RL controller when both search over the same kind of cells.

The historical point also matters. Evolution had been used for neural topology search for a long time, but earlier evolved image classifiers did not clearly beat hand-designed networks. This paper argues that, with a modern cell space and enough compute, evolution is not just a toy baseline.

Contribution

The main contributions are:

  1. It proposes aging evolution, also called regularized evolution, for NAS.
  2. It compares evolution, RL, and random search in the same NASNet-style search space.
  3. It gives a concrete mutation-only implementation: mutate hidden-state inputs or operation labels inside cells.
  4. It discovers AmoebaNet-A and reports competitive CIFAR-10 and ImageNet results.
  5. It studies aging versus non-aging tournament selection and argues that aging helps under noisy architecture evaluation.

The contribution is not “evolution always beats RL.” The stronger reading is narrower: in this controlled setup, regularized evolution is a very strong and simple NAS baseline.

Methodology

NASNet search space

All main experiments use the NASNet search space. A model is a stack of two searched cell types:

  • normal cell: preserves feature-map resolution;
  • reduction cell: reduces spatial resolution, usually by stride-2 operations.

The outer skeleton is fixed. The search only decides the internal wiring and operations of the normal and reduction cells. After the cell topology is selected, two manual scale knobs still exist:

  • (N): number of normal cells per stack;
  • (F): number of output filters for convolution operations.

Each cell is built from five pairwise combinations. A pairwise combination selects two earlier hidden states, applies two operations, and adds their outputs to create a new hidden state. Unused hidden states are concatenated at the end of the cell.

The operation set includes identity, separable convolutions with several kernel sizes, average pooling, max pooling, dilated separable convolution, and a 1x7 then 7x1 convolution. This is a rich enough space for interesting cell topologies, but it is still strongly hand-shaped.

Aging evolution

The search maintains a population of already-trained candidate architectures. In the main setup, the paper uses population size (P=100) and tournament sample size (S=25).

The loop is:

  1. Initialize a population with random architectures.
  2. Randomly sample (S) candidates from the current population.
  3. Choose the highest-validation-accuracy candidate in that sample as the parent.
  4. Mutate the parent architecture to produce a child.
  5. Train and evaluate the child.
  6. Push the child into the population.
  7. Remove the oldest individual from the population.

The last line is the whole regularization mechanism. Standard tournament selection often removes the worst individual. Aging evolution removes by age, so survival requires repeatedly producing descendants that train well. A model that only looked good once because of training noise eventually leaves the queue.

This distinction matters because NAS candidate evaluation is noisy. The paper’s interpretation is that non-aging evolution can overfit to lucky trained models, while aging evolution pays more attention to architectures that can reproduce good performance across generations.

Mutations

A child is produced by applying a random mutation to the parent’s architecture. The paper mainly uses two mutation types:

  • hidden-state mutation: choose one pairwise combination and replace one of its input hidden states with another valid previous state.
  • operation mutation: choose one pairwise combination and replace one operation label.

There is also an identity mutation with small probability. That is useful in a noisy evaluation setup because sometimes the same architecture deserves another training/evaluation sample.

Search and augmentation

The search itself is done on relatively small CIFAR-10 models. The paper withholds 5k CIFAR-10 examples for validation, trains each candidate for 25 epochs during search, and stops after evaluating 20k models. The reported large-scale experiment uses 450 K40 GPUs for about 7 days.

After search, the best architectures are augmented by increasing (N) and (F), then trained longer for CIFAR-10 or ImageNet. This is the same basic recipe as NASNet: search a cell cheaply, then scale the discovered cell for the final model.

Results

Search dynamics

The first result is the side-by-side search comparison. The paper runs five repeats for evolution, RL, and random search.

Evolution reaches high pre-augmentation CIFAR-10 accuracy earlier than RL in these runs, while both are clearly above random search. This is the part of the result I find most useful: if the search has to stop early because compute is limited, the trajectory matters more than only the final point.

There is one caveat. Figure 3 plots accuracy over wall-clock search time, not the compute cost of each discovered model. The paper handles that in the next comparison.

After augmentation, evolved models have better accuracy than random search at similar cost, and lower FLOPs than RL at similar accuracy. Within this case study, evolution lands in the better corner of the accuracy-cost plot.

AmoebaNet-A on CIFAR-10

The best evolved architecture is named AmoebaNet-A.

The architecture is still recognizably NASNet-style: a repeated normal cell and reduction cell, not a fully free-form model. The found cells use separable convolutions, pooling, identity/none choices, and several skip-like edges.

On CIFAR-10, AmoebaNet-A is compared against the published NASNet-A baseline:

Model Params Test error
NASNet-A baseline 3.3M 3.41
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=32) 2.6M 3.40 +/- 0.08
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=36) 3.2M 3.34 +/- 0.06

This table should be read carefully. The paper notes that the NASNet-A comparison is not perfectly controlled because the exact final training code and number of experiments may differ. The cleaner comparison is still the evolution/RL/random-search study above.

ImageNet transfer

The ImageNet result is where AmoebaNet-A became visible as more than an algorithm toy.

Model Params Multiply-adds Top-1 / Top-5
NASNet-A 88.9M 23.8B 82.7 / 96.2
PNASNet-5 86.1M 25.0B 82.9 / 96.2
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=190) 86.7M 23.1B 82.8 / 96.1
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=448) 469M 104B 83.9 / 96.6

At comparable size, AmoebaNet-A is around the same level as NASNet-A and PNASNet-5. At the very large setting, it reports 83.9% top-1 / 96.6% top-5, but that model is huge: 469M parameters and 104B multiply-adds. This is an accuracy result, not an efficient-deployment result.

Aging versus non-aging

The most interesting ablation is aging evolution versus non-aging tournament selection.

Most points are above the (y=x) line, which means aging evolution beats the non-aging variant in these small-compute experiments. The proposed explanation is practical:

  • non-aging evolution can keep a lucky model alive for a long time;
  • aging evolution removes old models, so useful architectures must keep reappearing through descendants;
  • this acts like regularization against noisy architecture evaluation.

This is why the paper’s title says regularized evolution. The regularization is not a loss term. It is an algorithmic constraint on population lifetime.

Reproduction Notes

A faithful reproduction should separate three stages:

  1. Search phase: small CIFAR-10 models, 25 epochs per candidate, validation on a 5k holdout split, fixed (P) and (S).
  2. Selection phase: choose the best architecture from search history, not just the current population.
  3. Augmentation phase: scale (N) and (F), then train the final model from scratch with the full recipe.

I would report at least four things:

  • validation accuracy during search;
  • final CIFAR/ImageNet accuracy after augmentation;
  • final model cost in FLOPs or multiply-adds;
  • number of evaluated models and actual hardware time.

The hardware number matters here. The search still trains child models independently. This is not an efficient-NAS method in the ENAS/DARTS sense. It is a strong full-training search baseline.

Takeaway

AmoebaNet’s lesson is that evolutionary NAS should not be dismissed as an older alternative to RL. In the NASNet cell space, a simple tournament-selection loop with age-based removal is enough to compete with a more complex controller.

The limitation is also clear. AmoebaNet spends a lot of compute, searches for accuracy rather than latency, and relies on a manually designed cell-based macro skeleton. Later work such as ENAS, DARTS, MnasNet, FBNet, and ProxylessNAS attacks different parts of that cost/deployment problem.

I read this paper as a baseline-setting result: if a new NAS method claims better search intelligence, it should beat regularized evolution under a fair search space, budget, and final training recipe.

entry.title: Attention Is All You Need
AutoFormer: Searching Transformers for Visual Recognition
BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training
entry.content:
Paper : BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training for Natural Language Generation, Translation, and Comprehension

BART is easiest to place as a denoising sequence-to-sequence model. It puts a BERT-style bidirectional encoder and a GPT-style autoregressive decoder into a standard Transformer encoder-decoder, then pre-trains the model by corrupting a document and reconstructing the original one.

Given a document and a noising function , the pre-training target is:

This objective gives BART a useful middle ground. If the downstream output is a label, the model still has a bidirectional encoder for understanding. If the output is text, the decoder is already trained to generate a sequence left-to-right. The paper’s experiments are mostly a stress test of that design choice.

Motivation

Figure 1 is the most useful mental model for the paper.

BERT encodes the whole context bidirectionally, but masked tokens are predicted independently, which makes full-sequence generation awkward. GPT is naturally generative, but every position only conditions on the left context. BART encodes a corrupted document bidirectionally and reconstructs the clean document with an autoregressive decoder.

The key detail is that encoder input and decoder output do not have to align. That makes it possible to delete tokens, replace variable-length spans, shuffle sentences, or rotate a document. The decoder only needs to recover the original sequence.

Noising Functions

The paper compares several input corruptions:

  • Token Masking: randomly replace tokens with [MASK], close to BERT’s MLM setup.
  • Token Deletion: remove tokens entirely, so the model must infer where content is missing.
  • Text Infilling: sample spans and replace each span with a single [MASK]; span lengths are drawn from a Poisson distribution with .
  • Sentence Permutation: split a document into sentences and shuffle their order.
  • Document Rotation: choose a random token as the new beginning of the document.

Text infilling is more generative than ordinary token masking. The model has to recover both the missing content and the missing span length. Based on the ablation results, the large model uses text infilling + sentence permutation, masking 30% of tokens and permuting all sentences.

Fine-tuning

BART’s fine-tuning recipes mostly follow from the encoder-decoder shape.

For sequence classification, the same input is fed to both the encoder and decoder. The hidden state of the final decoder token is used for classification, roughly playing the role that [CLS] plays in BERT, except that it comes from the decoder and can attend to the complete input.

For generation tasks, the setup is direct: summarization, abstractive QA, and dialogue response generation are all standard sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning problems.

Machine translation is a special case in the paper. To translate into English, the authors add a randomly initialized source encoder that maps the foreign-language input into a space that the pretrained BART model can denoise into English. Training first freezes most BART parameters and updates the new encoder plus a small set of related parameters, then briefly fine-tunes the full model.

Objective Ablation

Table 1 is the most informative result in the paper. The models are kept at comparable size, trained for 1M steps on books and Wikipedia, and then evaluated across both understanding and generation tasks.

The important readings:

  • Text Infilling is the most consistently strong single corruption: SQuAD 1.1 F1 reaches 90.8, XSum PPL is 6.61, and ConvAI2 PPL is 11.05.
  • Text Infilling + Sentence Shuffling is best on CNN/DailyMail, with PPL 5.41.
  • Document Rotation and Sentence Shuffling perform poorly in isolation. Shuffling structure alone is not a strong enough signal.
  • A pure Language Model is best on ELI5 PPL, but it is weak on SQuAD. That fits the task shape: ELI5 has long, loosely constrained answers, while SQuAD needs bidirectional context.

The point is not that one noising function is universally optimal. The point is that BART’s architecture makes these noising schemes comparable under one framework, and text infilling turns out to be the most robust choice.

Large-scale Results

The large model uses a 12-layer encoder, a 12-layer decoder, and hidden size 1024. It is trained at a similar scale to RoBERTa for 500k steps. Table 2 answers a practical question: does adding an autoregressive decoder hurt discriminative tasks?

The answer is mostly no. On SQuAD 1.1, BART reports 88.8/94.6 while RoBERTa reports 88.9/94.6. MNLI, QQP, QNLI, and RTE are also in the same range. BART keeps generation ability without obviously giving up language-understanding performance.

Summarization is where BART looks most natural. CNN/DailyMail is relatively extractive and the Lead-3 baseline is already strong, but BART still reaches 44.16 / 21.28 / 40.90. XSum is more abstractive, and extractive systems are much weaker there; BART reaches 45.14 / 22.27 / 37.25, roughly six ROUGE points above the previous BERTSUM-style results.

This is the cleanest use case for encoder-decoder pre-training: the input is a document, and the output is a new piece of text rather than a label or a copied span.

Generation And Translation

ELI5 is long-form abstractive QA, and the output is less tightly constrained by the input than in summarization. BART still reports the best ROUGE in Table 5: 30.6 / 6.2 / 24.3. This does not contradict Table 1, where the pure language model had the best ELI5 PPL. PPL and ROUGE measure different things, and the large-scale setup is also different from the base-model ablation.

The translation experiment is more of a probe for BART’s English generation prior. On WMT16 RO-EN with back-translation data, the baseline is 36.80 BLEU. Fixed BART is slightly worse at 36.29, while tuned BART reaches 37.96. The gain is modest, but it shows that the pretrained English denoising model can be attached to a translation system in a useful way.

Reading Notes

BART is often discussed next to T5 because both models push NLP tasks toward a text-to-text or sequence-to-sequence interface. The emphasis is different, though. BART is mainly about what kind of corruption works well for encoder-decoder denoising.

Text infilling is the core design for me. It forces the model to infer content and length, so it is closer to downstream generation than single-token masking. Sentence permutation then adds a document-level ordering signal, which is why the large model keeps it as an auxiliary corruption.

BART’s contribution is not a complicated new block. It is a clean composition of ideas that already had evidence behind them:

  • the encoder handles bidirectional understanding of corrupted input;
  • the decoder handles left-to-right reconstruction;
  • the noising function can be more flexible than MLM;
  • the same model can be fine-tuned for classification, summarization, QA, dialogue, and translation.

The limitations are also visible. If the task is only classification, an encoder-only model such as RoBERTa is cheaper. If the output is only loosely grounded in the input, a pure language model can be competitive. BART is strongest when the input provides real constraints and the output is still natural language.

Takeaway

BART is not just “BERT + GPT”. The important move is to put a denoising objective inside a sequence-to-sequence architecture. Pre-training teaches the model to recover full documents from damaged ones, and fine-tuning can reuse the same interface for text-in, text-out tasks.

My summary after reading the paper:

  • text infilling is the most important noising function;
  • the bidirectional encoder keeps understanding tasks strong;
  • the autoregressive decoder makes summarization and generation natural;
  • BART is not the lightest classifier, but it is a strong default when the output is text.

The broader lesson is still useful: if the downstream workload is generative, pre-training should look generative too. Recovering damaged text is a better match than predicting isolated masked tokens.

entry.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
BRECQ: Pushing the Limit of PTQ by Block Reconstruction
entry.content:
Paper / Code

BRECQ is a useful CNN PTQ paper to read before looking at later LLM quantization work. The paper is not only about collecting activation ranges. It frames PTQ as a local reconstruction problem: given a small calibration set, optimize the quantized model so its internal computation stays close to the full-precision model.

The key design choice is the reconstruction unit. Layer-wise reconstruction is too local for modern residual networks. Whole-network reconstruction is too large and easy to overfit when only a small calibration set is available. BRECQ argues that a block is the practical middle point.

Reconstruction Granularity

Figure cropped from the paper PDF: network, stage, block, and layer granularities, together with the corresponding Hessian/Fisher block structure.

The figure explains why the paper prefers block reconstruction. In a residual CNN, a layer does not act alone. Convolutions, nonlinearities, batch norm, and skip connections form a functional block. If PTQ optimizes one layer at a time, it ignores error compensation inside the block.

BRECQ compares four granularities:

Granularity What it optimizes Practical issue
Layer-wise one layer output at a time misses cross-layer dependency
Block-wise one residual/building block balances dependency and overfitting
Stage-wise a group of blocks at the same resolution larger search space and harder calibration
Net-wise final network output overfits easily with limited calibration

The Hessian diagram is the paper’s intuition: layer-wise PTQ keeps only the layer-diagonal part, while full-network reconstruction tries to use the full matrix. Block reconstruction keeps the stronger intra-block interactions and drops weaker inter-block terms.

Optimization Loop

BRECQ optimizes block by block, using calibration inputs, full-precision block outputs, gradients, and optional activation step-size updates.

The procedure is still post-training quantization. Labels are not required, and the model is not trained end to end. For each block, BRECQ records calibration input, the full-precision output, and gradient information. It then optimizes the quantized block output to match the full-precision block output.

At a high level, the objective is:

This is the same practical spirit as AdaRound, but the reconstruction target is a block rather than a single layer. The block gives internal layers room to absorb each other’s quantization errors.

Why Block, Not Layer

The block granularity is the best point in this ablation, especially for MobileNetV2.

The ablation is small but important. With 2-bit weight quantization, block reconstruction beats layer, stage, and net reconstruction on both ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2. The MobileNetV2 gap is especially clear: block reconstruction reaches 59.67, while layer-wise reconstruction reaches 52.13 and net-wise reconstruction collapses to 40.76.

This also explains why “larger reconstruction unit” is not automatically better. Network-wise optimization has the most dependency information, but with only a small calibration set it can fit the calibration examples instead of improving generalization.

Low-bit Results

Weight-only ImageNet results. BRECQ remains usable even at 2-bit weights with 32-bit activations.

For weight-only quantization, BRECQ is much stronger than range-only or layer-only PTQ baselines. On ResNet-18, the 2/32 result is 66.30 compared with 71.08 full precision. On MobileNetV2, 2/32 reaches 59.67 compared with 72.49 full precision, which is a meaningful result for such an aggressive setting.

Fully quantized ImageNet results. Activations are quantized too, which makes the setting much harder.

The fully quantized table is the more deployment-relevant one. At 4/4, BRECQ gives strong results across ResNet, MobileNetV2, RegNet, and MNasNet-style models. At 2/4, most previous PTQ methods fail badly, while BRECQ still produces usable accuracy.

Two details are worth keeping in mind when reading the table:

  • The first and last layers are usually treated more conservatively in low-bit CNN PTQ.
  • The method uses calibration data, but not the full training process required by QAT.

QAT Comparison

BRECQ is a PTQ method, but the paper compares it with QAT-style methods to show the cost/accuracy tradeoff.

The QAT comparison is the deployment argument. For ResNet-18 at 4/4, BRECQ reports 69.60 top-1 with 1024 calibration images and 0.4 GPU hours. QAT baselines use about 1.2M training images and roughly 100 GPU hours in this table.

For MobileNetV2, BRECQ reports 66.57 at 4/4 and 70.74 with mixed precision/8-bit activations. HAQ is still slightly higher in the mixed setting, but at a much higher training/search cost.

Mixed Precision

Mixed precision uses per-layer sensitivity to spend more bits where they matter most.

BRECQ also computes layer sensitivity and uses it for mixed precision. The curve is the useful part: under the same model-size or latency budget, mixed precision sits above uniform precision. That means the method is not only choosing better rounding; it is also learning where low-bit quantization hurts most.

This is the same lesson that later becomes common in deployment work: a single bit-width is easy to implement, but it is rarely the best accuracy-cost point.

Reading Notes

BRECQ’s main idea is modest but durable: choose the reconstruction unit that matches the model’s functional structure. For residual CNNs, that unit is usually a block.

The paper also separates two PTQ questions that are often mixed together:

  • How do we choose quantization parameters for a fixed bit-width?
  • How do we allocate bit-widths under a size or latency budget?

For LLM quantization, BRECQ is not a direct recipe, but it is useful background. GPTQ-style methods target different modules and use different solvers, yet they share the same philosophy: use calibration activations and sensitivity-aware reconstruction instead of minimizing a naive tensor error.

entry.title: BANANAS: Bayesian Optimization with Neural Architectures for NAS
entry.content:
White C, Neiswanger W, Savani Y. BANANAS: Bayesian Optimization with Neural Architectures for Neural Architecture Search. AAAI 2021.

Paper / Code

BANANAS is a predictor-based NAS method. It does not build a differentiable supernet like DARTS, and it does not train a controller like early RL-based NAS. The loop is closer to black-box Bayesian optimization: evaluate a small set of architectures, train a predictor from those observations, use an acquisition function to choose the next candidates, and repeat.

The useful part of this paper is that it does not treat “neural predictor for NAS” as one vague block. It studies five design choices separately:

Component BANANAS choice
Architecture encoding path encoding
Predictor feedforward neural network ensemble
Uncertainty ensemble variance
Acquisition independent Thompson sampling
Acquisition optimization mutation around strong evaluated architectures

The paper is therefore more valuable as an analysis of the BO + neural predictor framework than as a single named algorithm.

BO + Neural Predictor Setup

The search space is a set of architectures. Training an architecture gives its validation error, but this evaluation is expensive. BO tries to spend evaluations where they are likely to improve the best architecture found so far.

The practical loop is:

  1. randomly sample and evaluate several initial architectures;
  2. encode all evaluated architectures;
  3. train an ensemble of neural predictors on architecture/error observations;
  4. generate candidate architectures;
  5. score candidates with an acquisition function;
  6. evaluate the best candidates and update the dataset.

This is attractive because the expensive operation is still actual architecture training, while the predictor is cheap. But the predictor is only useful if the encoding makes architecture similarity visible. That is where path encoding becomes the main idea.

Path Encoding

Most NAS predictors before this paper used an adjacency matrix plus operation labels. That representation is faithful, but it gives the predictor an awkward feature space: node indices are arbitrary, edges are highly dependent, and an edge can be meaningless if it does not belong to an input-output path.

BANANAS instead encodes paths. Each binary feature means that a specific input-to-output operation path exists in the cell.

The left side of the figure is the key intuition. Instead of asking the predictor to infer useful computation from raw adjacency entries, path encoding directly records possible data-flow routes such as:

The full path encoding can be long. On NASBench-101, the paper gives the full length as:

But the right side of the figure is important: truncating the encoding can work well. For NASBench-101, the paper reports that the path encoding can be reduced to about 20 bits without hurting the 150-evaluation BANANAS result. Their explanation is practical: many long or rare paths almost never appear under the random graph sampling procedure, so including them can make the predictor overfit noise.

This is the reusable idea from the paper. The representation is not only smaller than it first looks; it also matches the structure that determines architecture behavior.

Predictor And Uncertainty

BANANAS compares several predictor families on NASBench-101: feedforward networks with adjacency encoding, feedforward networks with path encoding, truncated path encoding, Bayesian neural networks, GCNs, and VAEs.

There are three different measurements in this figure:

Plot What it checks What I read from it
left predictor MAE on held-out architectures path encoding and GCN are the strongest predictors
middle RMSCE calibration error ensembles give better uncertainty estimates than the BNN setup used here
right full BO performance predictor quality must still translate into better search

The right plot matters most. A predictor can have low average error but still rank the best candidates poorly. NAS cares about the top of the ranking, not only global regression quality. In the paper’s full BO setting, the path-encoding feedforward ensemble slightly edges the GCN ensemble, while being simpler and less sensitive to GCN hyperparameters.

The uncertainty story is also pragmatic. The authors use an ensemble of predictors, not because it is theoretically perfect, but because it gives a simple mean and standard deviation for each candidate architecture. That is enough to drive acquisition functions such as expected improvement, UCB, Thompson sampling, and independent Thompson sampling.

BANANAS Pipeline

The final predictor is simple: encode architectures with paths, feed the vectors into an ensemble of feedforward networks, then use the ensemble outputs as performance estimates and uncertainty estimates.

The actual search algorithm adds one more strong engineering choice: do not optimize the acquisition function by sampling candidates uniformly from the whole search space. Generate candidates by mutating architectures that already look good.

The mutation step is doing a lot of work. A neural predictor trained on limited observations is usually more reliable near architectures related to what it has already seen. Mutating good architectures keeps the candidate set in that local neighborhood. This also makes the acquisition function easier to optimize than searching the entire discrete architecture space.

The final BANANAS recipe in the paper is:

Part Choice
predictor input path encoding
predictor model feedforward neural network ensemble
predictor loss MAPE-style loss that emphasizes low validation error
acquisition independent Thompson sampling
candidate generation mutation from the best evaluated architectures

The name sounds broad, but the algorithm is a specific combination of these components.

Results

The main experimental result is on NASBench-101, where the paper can run many controlled trials because architecture accuracies are precomputed. The setup uses about 150 architecture evaluations, reported as 47 TPU hours in the NASBench-101 accounting.

The three panels give useful ablations:

  1. acquisition functions are close, but independent Thompson sampling is a strong default;
  2. mutation beats random, local search, and evolution as the candidate-generation strategy in this setting;
  3. the final BANANAS curve is among the strongest baselines under the same evaluation budget.

The paper also evaluates the DARTS search space. This is less clean than NASBench-101 because it is not a precomputed tabular benchmark, but the comparison is still useful because it checks whether the method can leave a small tabular cell benchmark.

The reported DARTS-space result is:

Method Avg. test error Runtime Note
DARTS, paper 2.76 5 GPU-days gradient-based
DARTS, authors’ rerun 2.68 5 GPU-days same evaluation pipeline
BANANAS 2.64 11.8 GPU-days BO + neural predictor

I would not overread the small difference between 2.68 and 2.64. The more important point is that predictor-based BO remains competitive outside the exact NASBench-101 table, at a cost that is still far below early full-training NAS methods.

Reading Notes

What I would keep from BANANAS:

  • Architecture representation is not a detail. Path encoding changes the predictor’s job from graph interpretation to data-flow feature learning.
  • Predictor accuracy and uncertainty calibration should be checked together. A calibrated but inaccurate predictor is not useful for NAS.
  • Candidate generation matters as much as acquisition scoring. The mutation strategy makes BO practical in a huge discrete search space.
  • Truncating path encodings is not just a memory trick. It can remove rare-path noise and improve predictor behavior.
  • NASBench-style experiments are good for controlled optimizer comparisons, but DARTS-space or real training checks are still needed before treating a method as generally strong.

My main caveat is that BANANAS still relies on a search-space-specific encoding and mutation operator. That is fine for cell-based NAS, but it means the method is not plug-and-play for every architecture family. For a new space, I would first ask: what is the equivalent of an input-output path, and can mutation stay near architectures where the predictor has support?

Overall, BANANAS is a clean paper because it separates the NAS problem into pieces that can be tested: encoding, predictor, uncertainty, acquisition, and candidate generation. The final algorithm works because all five choices are aligned, not because Bayesian optimization alone solves NAS.

entry.title: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences
BigNAS: Scaling Up Neural Architecture Search with Big Single-Stage Models
entry.content:
Yu J, Jin P, Liu H, et al. BigNAS: Scaling Up Neural Architecture Search with Big Single-Stage Models. ECCV 2020.

Paper

BigNAS is a one-shot NAS paper about making the supernet itself good enough for deployment. The claim is stronger than “use a supernet to rank candidates”: after training one single-stage model on ImageNet, child models from about 200 MFLOPs to 1 GFLOP can be sliced out and used directly, without retraining, finetuning, or other post-processing.

That is the part worth reading carefully. In many weight-sharing NAS methods, inherited accuracy is only a rough ranking signal and the final architecture still needs stand-alone training. BigNAS tries to remove that last step. The paper is therefore less about a new search algorithm and more about a training recipe that makes shared weights behave like a family of pretrained models.

Motivation

The workflow difference is simple:

Traditional one-shot methods train a supernet, search a path, then retrain or finetune the selected child model. OFA-style progressive methods make this more reusable, but still train the elastic model in stages. BigNAS asks whether all child models can be trained simultaneously in one stage and then deployed as-is.

The practical reason is deployment cost. If every target latency, FLOP budget, or device class requires another finetuning or retraining pass, the “cheap” NAS loop still leaves a long tail of engineering work. BigNAS wants the output to be a model family, not just an architecture list.

Search Space

BigNAS uses a MobileNetV2-style MBConv search space. The searchable dimensions are input resolution, channel width, depth, and kernel size; expansion ratio is mostly fixed by the MBConv type in the table.

The important details:

  • Training samples input resolutions from {192, 224, 288, 320}.
  • The supernet contains stage-wise choices for channel count, number of layers, and kernel size.
  • The reported BigNASModels are selected from roughly 200M to 1000M FLOPs, while the single-stage model covers a wider range during training.
  • The paper also notes that after batch-norm calibration, the trained model can generalize to input resolutions not used during training, such as 208, 240, 256, 272, 304, or 336.

This is not a cell-level NAS search space. It is closer to an elastic mobile network family: same backbone grammar, many possible widths/depths/kernels/resolutions.

Single-Stage Training

Sandwich Rule And Inplace Distillation

BigNAS inherits two useful ideas from Once-for-All:

  1. Sandwich rule: in each step, train the largest child, the smallest child, and sampled intermediate children.
  2. Inplace distillation: use the largest child model as the teacher for smaller child models in the same supernet.

This makes sense for the BigNAS goal. The largest child receives normal supervised training, while smaller children learn from a teacher that shares the same weights. The risky part is optimization: small and large child models do not converge at the same speed.

The left plot shows the core dilemma. The big child peaks earlier; the small child keeps improving later. If training stops early, small children are undertrained. If training continues with a decaying learning rate all the way down, the big child can overfit while the small child catches up.

Their fix is deliberately small: exponential decay with a constant ending. Once the learning rate reaches a floor, it stays there until the end. In the main ImageNet setting, the paper uses a 5% floor of the initial learning rate.

The appendix sweep is also useful:

LR floor Smallest model Biggest model Average
3% 76.5 80.8 78.7
5% 76.4 81.1 78.8
8% 76.3 81.3 78.8
10% 76.3 81.3 78.8

The exact floor is not the whole story, but keeping a non-zero ending learning rate is part of making both ends of the supernet usable.

Initialization And Skip Transitions

The paper spends real space on initialization because the single-stage model changes channel counts and fan-in across child models. A fixed-network initialization rule is not enough when the same residual block can be evaluated under many widths.

The BigNAS modification sets the learnable scaling coefficient in the last batch-norm layer of each residual block. This makes the residual branch initially output zeros before the skip connection, so the block starts close to an identity mapping. The paper says this initialization gives around +0.2% in the fixed-network setting, but is much more critical here, with roughly +1.0% improvement in their single-stage setting.

The early-training plot explains why. Naive initialization at the full learning rate can collapse; reducing the learning rate helps but slows training. Modified initialization lets the model keep the original learning rate and still learn quickly.

They also add explicit skip connections at stage transitions. When resolution or channel dimensions differ, the skip path uses 2x2 average pooling and/or 1x1 convolution. This keeps the identity path meaningful even when child models choose different stage configurations.

After the modifications, the small child improves more steadily and the large child avoids the earlier degradation. This figure is more convincing than just reporting the final architecture search result, because it shows the recipe improving the shared-weight training dynamics directly.

Regularization Only On The Full Model

BigNAS also changes where regularization is applied. A naive recipe applies dropout and weight decay to every sampled child model. BigNAS instead applies regularization only when training the largest/full network.

The reason is capacity mismatch. Small child models are already constrained; regularizing them like the largest model can underfit them. In the paper’s ablation, this modified rule improves the small child by about +0.5 top-1 and the big child by about +0.2.

The ImageNet training setup is still heavy: RMSProp, batch size 4096 on TPUs, AutoAugment, Swish, batch-norm post-calibration, weight decay , dropout 0.2 on the full model, and roughly 36 hours of training in the authors’ setup.

Architecture Selection

After training the single-stage model, BigNAS does not run a complicated controller. It uses a coarse-to-fine selection procedure:

First it evaluates coarse skeletons across resolution, depth, width, and kernel choices. Then it picks promising skeletons and mutates them with a finer grid under the target resource budget. The paper uses FLOPs for the reported selection because FLOPs are easier to reproduce than device-specific latency, but it notes that the evaluation metric could also be latency, memory footprint, or predictive accuracy on a target device.

One detail I like: since ImageNet validation is treated as the public “test set” in this community, they use predictive accuracy on the training set for selection after supernet training. That is not a perfect deployment protocol, but it avoids repeatedly tuning on the validation set.

Main Results

The headline result is the Pareto curve and comparison table:

Compactly, the BigNAS family looks like this:

Model Params FLOPs Top-1
BigNASModel-S 4.5M 242M 76.5
BigNASModel-M 5.5M 418M 78.9
BigNASModel-L 6.4M 586M 79.5
BigNASModel-XL 9.5M 1040M 80.9

The comparisons that matter most are compact enough to write directly:

  • Around 200M FLOPs, BigNASModel-S reaches 76.5 top-1 at 242M FLOPs, slightly above Once-for-All finetuned at 76.4 top-1 with 230M FLOPs.
  • Around 400M FLOPs, BigNASModel-M reaches 78.9 top-1 at 418M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B0 at 77.3 top-1 with 390M FLOPs.
  • Around 600M FLOPs, BigNASModel-L reaches 79.5 top-1 at 586M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B1 at 79.2 top-1 with 734M FLOPs.
  • Around 1000M FLOPs, BigNASModel-XL reaches 80.9 top-1 at 1040M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B2 at 80.3 top-1 with 1050M FLOPs.

This table should not be read as a perfectly fair training recipe comparison. The paper itself notes that MNasNet and MobileNetV3 are mainly optimized for on-device latency instead of FLOPs, and different model families use different training hyperparameters. Still, the result is strong for the paper’s central claim: directly sliced child models are competitive without an extra training pass.

Does Finetuning Help?

For me, this is the most important evidence in the paper.

Table 2 tries to finetune selected child models for another 25 epochs with constant learning rates. A too-large finetuning LR hurts badly. A smaller LR mostly changes nothing. For example:

Model Direct slice Finetune LR 0.001 Finetune LR 0.0001
BigNASModel-S 76.5 76.4 76.5
BigNASModel-M 78.9 78.8 78.8
BigNASModel-L 79.5 79.6 79.7
BigNASModel-XL 80.9 80.6 80.8

Table 3 trains the selected architectures from scratch. Even with the better distillation variant, training from scratch remains slightly behind the directly sliced model:

Model Direct slice From scratch From scratch + distill B
BigNASModel-S 76.5 75.3 76.3
BigNASModel-M 78.9 77.4 78.6
BigNASModel-L 79.5 78.2 79.2
BigNASModel-XL 80.9 79.3 80.4

This is the key point. BigNAS is not only saying “our search found good architectures”. It is saying the weight-sharing model has already trained those architectures well enough that the inherited weights beat or match the usual post-processing baselines.

Relation To OFA

BigNAS is close to Once-for-All in spirit: both want one trained network to provide many deployable subnets. The difference is how much staging the training pipeline needs.

Method Training style Deployment claim
Once-for-All Progressive shrinking over elastic dimensions Subnets can be specialized and selected after elastic training
BigNAS Simultaneous single-stage training with a stronger recipe Sliced child models are directly deployable without retraining or finetuning

BigNAS still borrows OFA’s sandwich rule and inplace distillation. The new claim is that progressive shrinking is not strictly necessary if initialization, skip transitions, learning-rate schedule, and regularization are tuned for a very large single-stage model.

Limitations

The result is useful, but it is not a generic proof that all one-shot NAS supernets are deployable.

  • The search space is manually designed around MBConv mobile CNNs. It does not automatically cover arbitrary operators, attention blocks, or hardware-specific kernels.
  • The recipe is expensive: ImageNet-scale supernet training with batch size 4096 on TPUs is still a serious compute budget.
  • The final comparison is mostly FLOP-based. Real deployment often cares about latency, memory bandwidth, activation size, kernel availability, and device-specific scheduling.
  • The method depends on a carefully tuned training recipe. The paper’s strongest message is that supernet training quality matters; it does not make weight sharing automatically reliable.
  • Batch-norm calibration is still needed when slicing and evaluating child models, especially across different input resolutions.

Takeaway

BigNAS is valuable because it changes the question from “which architecture should NAS pick?” to “can a single trained supernet already be the pretrained model family?” The paper’s strongest evidence is Table 2 and Table 3: finetuning and retraining do not meaningfully improve the selected child models.

My main takeaway is that one-shot NAS fails or succeeds mostly at the supernet-training level. Search over a weak shared-weight model is ranking noise; search over a well-trained elastic model can produce deployable subnets directly. BigNAS is one of the cleaner demonstrations of that idea for mobile CNNs.

entry.title: BinaryBERT: 1-bit BERT Compression
CLIP: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
entry.content:
Paper / Code

CLIP is the paper that made “classification by text prompt” feel practical at scale. The idea is simple to state: train an image encoder and a text encoder on internet image-text pairs, then use text descriptions as classifiers at test time.

The important shift is the label space. Instead of predicting one fixed set of dataset labels, CLIP learns a shared embedding space where images and natural-language descriptions can be compared directly. That makes zero-shot classification, retrieval, and open-vocabulary use cases much more natural.

Training And Zero-shot Use

Figure cropped from the paper PDF: CLIP pre-trains with paired image-text examples, then builds a zero-shot classifier from label text.

The training batch contains aligned image-text pairs. The image encoder maps images into a normalized embedding, and the text encoder maps captions into the same embedding space. The model computes all image-text similarities in the batch and uses the matching diagonal as positives.

The zero-shot classifier is just the same mechanism reused at inference time:

  1. Convert each class name into a prompt, such as a photo of a {label}.
  2. Encode all class prompts with the text encoder.
  3. Encode the image with the image encoder.
  4. Choose the prompt embedding with the highest similarity.

That means a new label set does not require training a new linear head. It only requires writing label text.

Why Contrastive Learning

Contrastive training is more data efficient than the caption-prediction baselines in this comparison.

The paper compares three objectives on zero-shot ImageNet accuracy as training compute increases. The contrastive bag-of-words variant learns much faster than the caption-prediction alternatives. The result is not only that more data helps. It is that the objective matters.

The core implementation is short:

The paper’s numpy-like pseudocode: normalized image/text embeddings, scaled cosine similarities, and symmetric cross entropy.

The symmetric loss is worth noting. CLIP trains both image-to-text and text-to-image matching. In a batch of N pairs, each image should match its paired text better than the other N - 1 texts, and each text should match its paired image better than the other N - 1 images.

Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering and prompt ensembling improve zero-shot classification without retraining the image model.

The paper found that bare class names are often a poor interface to the text encoder. A prompt such as a photo of a {label} gives useful context, and task-specific prompts can help even more.
