12 What This Tiny Llama Leaves Out

Takeaways

The tiny repo is not an inference framework. It is a map. It makes the core forward path small enough to hold in working memory:

Once that map is stable, the larger serving stack becomes a series of implementation choices rather than a black box.

Previous: A Token-by-Token KV Cache Trace.

entry.title: LLM.int8(): Outlier-Aware INT8 Matmul
entry.content:
Dettmers T, Lewis M, Belkada Y, et al. LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale. NeurIPS 2022.

  • Paper: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
  • Code: TimDettmers/bitsandbytes

LLM.int8() is best read as the paper that made a specific LLM quantization failure mode concrete. Standard INT8 recipes can look fine on small or medium transformers, then break when the model reaches the scale where activation outlier dimensions become systematic.

The paper’s answer is not “clip the outliers” and not “fine-tune the quantized model.” It keeps most matrix multiplication in INT8, but detects rare outlier feature dimensions and computes those dimensions in FP16. That makes it a mixed-precision matmul design, not a pure INT8 design.

The Scaling Failure

Figure 1 shows the main empirical story. The ordinary 8-bit baseline tracks the 16-bit baseline up to a point, then collapses around the 6.7B OPT scale. LLM.int8() keeps following the 16-bit curve up to OPT-175B.

This matters because a quantization method can pass small-model tests and still be the wrong method for LLM deployment. The failure is scale-dependent. The paper argues that large-magnitude feature dimensions emerge across layers, and those dimensions dominate both attention behavior and quantization error.

What Is Being Quantized

LLM.int8() targets the parameter-heavy linear layers in transformer inference: feed-forward layers and attention projection layers. The paper does not quantize the attention softmax itself, and it does not focus on training.

For a linear layer, write the activation matrix as X with shape s x h, and the weight matrix as W with shape h x o:

The hard part is that the bad values are not random individual elements. They appear in specific hidden dimensions. In other words, the outlier direction is along h, the same dimension that connects activation columns to weight rows.

Vector-Wise Quantization

The first component is vector-wise quantization. Instead of using one scale for the whole tensor, LLM.int8() treats matrix multiplication as many row-column inner products:

It stores one scale per activation row and one scale per weight column. The INT8 matmul accumulates into INT32, then the output is dequantized by the outer product of those row and column scales.

Compared with a single tensor-wide scale, this gives much better precision. Compared with very fine-grained group quantization, it is still simple enough to map onto ordinary INT8 matmul paths.

But vector-wise quantization alone is not enough once the model has systematic outlier feature dimensions. If a few hidden dimensions are much larger than the rest, per-row activation scales still have to cover them, and ordinary dimensions lose resolution.

Mixed-Precision Decomposition

Figure 2 is the method in one picture. LLM.int8() splits the hidden dimension into two sets:

The normal path uses vector-wise INT8 matmul. The outlier path is extracted and computed in FP16, then both outputs are accumulated back into FP16.

The paper uses a threshold of alpha = 6.0 for identifying outlier features. The key engineering claim is that the outlier set is tiny. For transformers up to 13B parameters, the paper reports at most 7 outlier feature dimensions, roughly 0.1% of the feature dimensions. That is small enough that the FP16 side path can preserve accuracy without giving up the memory benefit of INT8 weights for the main matrix.

This is why the method is practical: it keeps more than 99.9% of values on the low-precision path but refuses to quantize the dimensions that actually break the model.

Perplexity Results

Table 1 is the most useful accuracy table. On C4 validation perplexity, simple INT8 methods degrade as the model scales. At 13B parameters:

Method 13B C4 perplexity
32-bit float 12.45
INT8 absmax vector-wise 16.48
INT8 zeropoint vector-wise 13.47
Absmax LLM.int8() 12.45
Zeropoint LLM.int8() 12.45

Two details are worth keeping:

  • Zeropoint quantization helps because the outliers are often one-sided, but it still fails at 13B.
  • Once the outlier dimensions are moved to the FP16 path, zeropoint no longer has much advantage over absmax.

That second point supports the paper’s interpretation: after removing the pathological outlier dimensions from the INT8 path, the remaining distribution is much easier to quantize.

Outliers As A Phase Shift

The paper defines an outlier feature as a hidden dimension with magnitude at least 6, appearing in at least 25% of layers and at least 6% of sequence dimensions. Figure 3 shows how those features spread with model scale and perplexity.

The parameter-scale plot looks like a sharp phase shift around 6B-6.7B parameters. The perplexity plot looks smoother: as C4 perplexity improves, more layers and sequence positions become affected by these large-magnitude features.

The interpretation I find useful is: model size is a visible proxy, but not the only cause. Data, training quality, and model family can move the threshold. The real deployment lesson is to check activation statistics on the actual model, not to assume a fixed parameter-count cutoff.

Figure 4 adds another piece: once outliers become systematic, their magnitude grows quickly. This is why normal INT8 quantization breaks. A few very large dimensions stretch the quantization range, leaving too little resolution for ordinary values.

Why The Outliers Matter

The outlier statistics table is a good sanity check. For the 6.7B fairseq model, outliers affect 100% of layers and 75% of sequence dimensions. For the 13B fairseq model, the table reports 7 outlier dimensions, 100% of layers, and 73% of sequence dimensions.

The important line from the paper is not only “outliers exist.” It is that removing them is catastrophic:

  • at 6.7B scale, the paper reports about 150k outlier values per 2048-token sequence;
  • those values are concentrated in only about 6 feature dimensions;
  • setting the outlier dimensions to zero can reduce mean top-1 attention softmax probability from about 40% to about 20%;
  • validation perplexity can increase by 600%-1000%;
  • removing the same number of random non-outlier dimensions barely changes the result.

That explains why clipping is the wrong mental model. These dimensions are not noise. They are rare in count but central to the model’s computation.

Hardware Access

The paper’s main deployment win is memory. INT8 storage nearly halves the parameter footprint, while the FP16 side path is tiny. The authors report a 1.96x memory-footprint reduction for BLOOM-176B.

Table 2 makes the consequence concrete. With 8-bit inference, an 8x RTX 3090 24GB server can run OPT-175B/BLOOM, while the 16-bit setup listed there only reaches OPT-66B. A 4x RTX 3090 desktop moves from OPT-30B in 16-bit to OPT-66B in 8-bit.

This is why LLM.int8() became practically important through bitsandbytes. The method changed which model sizes were loadable on available hardware.

Speed Is Not The Main Promise

The speed table is easy to misread. Raw INT8 matmul can be faster, but LLM.int8() also pays for quantization, dequantization, outlier extraction, and the FP16 side path.

The paper reports that LLM.int8() is slower than FP16 for small GPT-3-sized matrices. In the table, LLM.int8() is 0.64x at the 2.7B shape and 0.86x at the 6.7B shape. It becomes faster at larger shapes: 1.22x at 13B and 1.81x at the 175B shape.

The practical reading is:

  • use LLM.int8() for memory first;
  • expect speedup only when the matmul is large enough and the kernels are good;
  • treat outlier decomposition overhead as a real systems cost, not a free side branch.

The BLOOM-176B end-to-end table reinforces that point. INT8 inference is close to the native per-token latency and can use fewer GPUs, but it is not a universal latency win. For batch size 32, the table reports 9.94 ms/token for the bfloat16 8xA100 baseline, 10.44 ms/token for LLM.int8() on 8xA100, 9.40 ms/token on 4xA100, and 9.11 ms/token on 3xA100.

The win is capacity and accessibility. Latency depends on communication, batch size, model sharding, and kernel implementation.

Relation To Later Quantization Work

LLM.int8() is a useful reference point for later LLM quantization methods:

Method Main target How it handles activation difficulty
LLM.int8() W8A8-style inference matmul route outlier feature dimensions to FP16
SmoothQuant W8A8 dense inference migrate activation scale into weights before quantization
GPTQ weight-only PTQ keep activations high precision and compensate weight rounding error
AWQ activation-aware weight-only PTQ use activation statistics offline to protect salient weight channels
KIVI KV cache choose different quantization granularity for key and value cache

SmoothQuant can be read as a direct answer to LLM.int8()’s runtime irregularity. Instead of keeping a separate FP16 outlier path, SmoothQuant tries to smooth the activation outliers offline so the final runtime can use a dense W8A8 path. AWQ and GPTQ avoid activation quantization entirely at runtime by staying weight-only.

Reproduction Notes

If I were reproducing this paper, I would separate the checks into statistics, accuracy, and systems measurements.

For statistics:

  • plot activation max by hidden dimension across model sizes;
  • count how many feature dimensions exceed the threshold alpha = 6.0;
  • verify whether the same dimensions appear across layers and sequence positions;
  • measure the effect of zeroing outlier dimensions versus random dimensions.

For accuracy:

  • compare tensor-wise, row-wise, vector-wise, zeropoint, and LLM.int8() variants;
  • report C4 perplexity by model scale, not only one model;
  • run zero-shot tasks at small, medium, and 175B scale if possible;
  • sweep the outlier threshold and report the FP16 side-path size.

For systems:

  • measure model memory including scales and outlier metadata;
  • report time spent in quantization, INT8 matmul, FP16 outlier matmul, and dequantization separately;
  • benchmark small and large matrix shapes, because the overhead flips the speed conclusion;
  • test end-to-end decoding, not only standalone GEMM.

Takeaway

LLM.int8() is important because it names the LLM activation-outlier problem and gives a practical deployment workaround. Vector-wise quantization gives better INT8 precision for normal values, and mixed-precision decomposition protects the tiny set of hidden dimensions that the model cannot afford to quantize.

The tradeoff is runtime irregularity. The method is excellent for loading large models with much lower memory, but the FP16 outlier path complicates kernels and does not guarantee latency improvement. That tradeoff explains why later methods either smooth the outliers away, as in SmoothQuant, or avoid activation quantization, as in GPTQ and AWQ.

entry.title: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts Before Inference
entry.content:
Paper: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models

Code: https://aka.ms/LLMLingua

LLMLingua is an inference acceleration paper, but it does not start from kernels, KV-cache layout, or batching. It starts one layer earlier: if a long prompt can be compressed before it is sent to the target LLM, then prefill latency, KV-cache memory, and API token cost all shrink together.

That makes the paper interesting for RAG and agent systems. Those prompts often contain long retrieved passages, many demonstrations, or repeated instructions. A serving stack can optimize the attention kernels perfectly and still waste most of its work on prompt tokens that are not needed for the final answer.

Motivation

The method assumes a black-box target LLM and a smaller local language model. The smaller model estimates which prompt tokens or demonstrations are more important, and the compressed prompt is then sent to the target model.

The central idea is not summarization. Summarization asks a model to rewrite the prompt into natural text. LLMLingua treats the prompt as an information source and tries to preserve the parts that keep the target model’s answer distribution close to the answer distribution under the original prompt.

The paper defines the compression rate as:

where is the original prompt length and is the compressed prompt length. The compression ratio is . A smaller reduces inference cost, but it also increases the chance of deleting evidence, constraints, or reasoning steps.

Coarse-to-Fine Compression

LLMLingua splits a prompt into instruction, demonstrations, and question. These parts do not tolerate compression equally. The instruction and question usually carry task constraints, while multiple demonstrations may contain redundancy. The paper therefore uses a budget controller before token-level compression.

The budget controller first allocates different compression rates to prompt components. For demonstrations, it computes perplexity with the small LM and keeps the higher-perplexity demonstrations first. The paper’s assumption is that these examples are more informative for the target task than low-perplexity or redundant ones.

After this coarse filtering, LLMLingua applies iterative token-level prompt compression.

The iterative part matters because one-shot token removal ignores dependency between retained tokens. If a token is removed, the conditional probability of later tokens changes. LLMLingua processes segments iteratively, recomputes conditional probabilities, and selects tokens under an adjusted compression threshold. This is slower than a single scoring pass, but the ablation shows that the extra dependency modeling is not cosmetic.

The third piece is distribution alignment. The small LM is only a proxy for the target black-box model. LLMLingua tries to reduce the mismatch between the small LM distribution and the target LLM distribution, because a token that looks unimportant to a small model may still matter to GPT-style or Claude-style models.

Main Results

The first result table covers ShareGPT conversation and Arxiv-March23 summarization. Both are context-heavy settings where removing prompt tokens should help serving cost, but deleting the wrong context can damage answer quality.

On ShareGPT, LLMLingua keeps stronger ROUGE/BERTScore numbers than the baselines under the reported token budgets. On Arxiv-March23, the paper reports similar behavior: the method reaches higher compression while preserving more of the summarization quality than sentence selection and Selective-Context.

The more interesting table for me is GSM8K and BBH, because these tasks punish missing intermediate reasoning details.

On GSM8K, LLMLingua reports 79.08 EM with a 5x compression ratio under the 1-shot constraint, compared with 78.85 for the full-shot prompt. Under heavier compression, it still reports 77.41 EM at 14x and 77.33 EM at 20x. BBH drops more sharply, which is expected: it contains tasks where one deleted condition can change the answer.

This is the right way to read the paper. The method is not saying that prompts are always 20x redundant. It is showing that some prompt formats, especially demonstration-heavy ones, contain enough redundancy for aggressive compression to be useful.

Ablation

The ablation table is the part that makes the method easier to trust. It separates the effects of iterative token compression, budget control, dynamic compression ratio, perplexity-based selection, distribution alignment, and naive stop-word removal.

Removing iterative token-level compression drops GSM8K EM from 79.08 to 72.93. Removing the budget controller gives 73.62. Random selection inside the budget controller gives 72.78. These are large enough drops to show that the method is not just “delete many tokens and hope the LLM survives.”

The stop-word row is also useful. Removing stop words gives only 1.3x compression and lower EM. Prompt compression cannot be reduced to a surface-level text-cleaning trick.

Serving Cost

Prompt compression affects serving in two places:

  1. The target model receives fewer prompt tokens, so prefill compute and initial KV-cache allocation decrease.
  2. The target model may generate shorter answers because the compressed prompt often contains less redundant context.

The generation-length plot shows a downward trend as the compression ratio increases. This effect is application-dependent, but it matters for end-to-end latency because decode work is paid per generated token.

The paper also reports measured latency on GSM8K with a V100-32G GPU.

The reported end-to-end latency moves from 8.6 seconds without LLMLingua to 4.9 seconds at 2x compression, 2.3 seconds at 5x compression, and 1.3 seconds at 10x compression. The small LM compression step is not free, but in this setup it is much cheaper than running the large target model on the original prompt.

For serving systems, this makes LLMLingua complementary to KV-cache quantization, paged attention, continuous batching, and fast attention kernels. Those systems reduce the cost of serving a sequence. LLMLingua tries to reduce the sequence before those systems see it.

Failure Boundary

The limitation is semantic rather than numerical. Kernel optimization should not change the model’s input. Prompt compression does. If the compressor removes the one sentence that contains the answer, the target LLM can become confidently wrong.

The paper’s compression-ratio curve makes this visible.

Performance stays relatively strong up to moderate compression, then drops when the ratio gets too aggressive. Around very high ratios such as 25x to 30x on GSM8K, all methods degrade. LLMLingua shifts the degradation point later than the baselines, but it does not remove the tradeoff.

I would treat the compression ratio as a deployment knob, not as a fixed paper number. A RAG system should tune it against answer faithfulness, citation retention, and failure cases from its own traffic.

Practical Notes

Where I would try LLMLingua:

  • RAG prompts with long retrieved contexts and repeated boilerplate.
  • Agent traces where previous observations contain redundancy.
  • Demonstration-heavy prompts where examples can be ranked and removed.
  • API inference where prompt tokens are a direct cost center.

Where I would be careful:

  • Legal, medical, or financial prompts where one clause changes the answer.
  • Tool-use prompts where exact JSON schemas or command constraints must survive.
  • Debugging sessions where the model needs the full history, including failed attempts.
  • Any evaluation that only measures compression ratio and not evidence retention.

For production use, I would log both the original prompt and compressed prompt, then diff removed spans during debugging. Without that audit trail, a wrong answer is hard to attribute: it could come from the target LLM, the retrieved context, or the compressor deleting the necessary evidence.

Takeaway

LLMLingua is useful because it reframes part of LLM serving as input selection. The cheapest prefill token is the one never sent to the target model. The hard part is making sure that deleted tokens are actually redundant for the task, not just low-probability under a small proxy model.

entry.title: LQ-Nets: Learned Quantization for Highly Accurate and Compact Deep Neural Networks
LSQ: Learned Step Size Quantization
Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
entry.content:
Wang S, Li B Z, Khabsa M, et al. Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity. 2020.

Paper

Linformer is one of the clean efficient-attention papers: it makes a structural claim about self-attention, then turns that claim into a simple layer change. The claim is that the self-attention context mapping is often low-rank, so the model does not need to materialize the full n x n attention map for every head.

This is approximate attention. It is not the same kind of optimization as FlashAttention, which computes exact attention with better IO behavior.

Why This Matters

The standard Transformer attention pattern has quadratic time and memory in sequence length:

Linformer projects keys and values along the sequence dimension before attention:

If k is treated as a small fixed projection dimension, the layer becomes linear in n.

The comparison table frames Linformer against other sequence models. The pitch is not only lower asymptotic complexity; it also keeps one sequential operation like a standard Transformer layer, unlike recurrent models.

Low-Rank Evidence

The paper first inspects pretrained Transformer attention matrices from RoBERTa-base and RoBERTa-large. The singular-value curves show that much of the mass is concentrated in a relatively small number of directions, especially in higher layers. This is the empirical basis for replacing the full context matrix with a low-rank approximation.

I read this figure as a useful diagnostic, not a universal proof. Some heads, tasks, or positions may need higher-rank interactions. Linformer is betting that the common case can be compressed enough to make the tradeoff worthwhile.

Layer Design

The layer keeps the usual query projection, but applies learned projection matrices to keys and values across the sequence dimension. In the paper notation, each head can use matrices shaped like k x n to reduce the token axis before attention.

The authors also discuss sharing these projection matrices:

Sharing strategy Meaning Practical effect
Headwise sharing heads share projection matrices fewer extra parameters than per-head projections
Key-value sharing key and value projections share parameters reduces the projection overhead further
Layerwise sharing layers share projection matrices smallest projection-parameter footprint

The strongest practical setting in the downstream table uses shared key/value projections and layerwise sharing, which is a useful signal: the benefit is not only from adding more parameters.

Pretraining Curves

The pretraining plots check several knobs:

  • larger k improves the approximation;
  • k = 128 works reasonably for n = 512, while k = 256 is stronger for longer settings;
  • sharing projection matrices does not destroy convergence;
  • fixing k = 256 while increasing n still gives similar final validation perplexity.

The last point is the important one for the paper’s linear-time claim. If quality collapsed whenever n increased with fixed k, the asymptotic story would not matter much in practice.

Downstream Results

The downstream numbers are close to RoBERTa-base on SST-2, IMDB, QNLI, and QQP. The table reports a RoBERTa-base average of 92.25. A Linformer model with n = 512, k = 256, shared key/value projections, and layerwise sharing reaches 92.30. With n = 1024, k = 256, and the same sharing pattern, it reaches 92.18.

That is the core empirical bargain: similar benchmark quality while avoiding the quadratic attention map.

Efficiency

Table 3 measures inference-time speed and memory savings against a standard Transformer on a 16GB Tesla V100. Even at n = 512, k = 128, the paper reports 1.5x faster inference and 1.7x lower memory. At long sequence lengths the savings grow quickly; for example, n = 65536, k = 256 reports 18x faster inference and 52x lower memory.

These numbers depend on the benchmark setup and implementation, but the direction is expected. Once the full n x n attention map disappears, the long-sequence memory curve changes substantially.

Takeaway

Linformer is attractive because the change is easy to understand: compress the sequence axis of keys and values, then attend to the compressed representation. It gives a clean path from quadratic attention to approximate linear attention.

The risk is exactly the assumption that makes it work. If a task really needs high-rank token-token interactions, fixed low-rank projections can throw away information before attention has a chance to use it. I would treat Linformer as a strong efficient-attention baseline for long-context experiments, but not as a drop-in replacement for exact attention when output equivalence matters.

entry.title: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
entry.content:
Paper: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer

Code: https://github.com/allenai/longformer

Longformer is a practical long-context Transformer paper. It does not try to keep full attention and make it slightly faster. It changes the attention pattern so most tokens attend locally, while a small number of task-specific tokens receive global attention.

That design gives Longformer two properties that matter in real document tasks:

  • It scales roughly linearly with sequence length when the local window size is fixed.
  • It can reuse pretrained RoBERTa weights with minimal architectural changes.

Why It Matters

The standard Transformer attention matrix is dense. For sequence length , full self-attention has time and memory complexity. This is tolerable at BERT’s 512-token regime, but it becomes expensive for long QA, document classification, coreference, and summarization.

The paper compares full self-attention with several Longformer implementations. The full attention curve grows quickly and runs out of memory for longer sequences. The vectorized chunk implementation and CUDA implementation keep memory growth much closer to linear.

The important engineering point is that sparse attention only helps if the implementation matches the sparsity pattern. A local-window pattern implemented as many tiny inefficient gathers can lose the theoretical advantage.

Attention Pattern

Longformer combines three attention ideas: sliding-window attention, dilated sliding-window attention, and task-specific global attention.

With a fixed window size , each token attends to nearby tokens on both sides. The complexity becomes instead of . Stacking layers expands the receptive field, so a token can indirectly receive information from faraway tokens through multiple local hops.

Dilated sliding windows increase the receptive field without increasing the number of attended positions. This is similar to dilated convolutions: the model samples farther positions with gaps between them.

Global attention is the task escape hatch. Some tokens need to read or write across the whole document:

  • [CLS] for classification.
  • Question tokens for QA.
  • Candidate answer tokens for WikiHop.
  • The first token in LED summarization.

Those global tokens attend to the full sequence, and the full sequence can attend back to them. This keeps the model from becoming only a local text smoother.

Compared With Prior Long-Document Work

The paper positions Longformer against earlier efficient Transformer variants and long-document work.

The distinction is not only “sparse attention.” Longformer is designed for transfer learning on document-level NLP tasks. Prior long-sequence models often focused on autoregressive language modeling, or they required task-specific chunking and aggregation. Longformer aims to replace RoBERTa’s self-attention and keep the rest of the pretrained Transformer workflow familiar.

Pretraining From RoBERTa

The practical trick is simple but important: start from RoBERTa, replace full attention with Longformer attention, extend the position embeddings, and continue MLM pretraining on long documents.

The paper also tests how to configure attention windows.

Increasing the window size from lower to higher layers gives the best BPC in this ablation. Adding dilation on two heads helps in the small autoregressive language-modeling setup, though the paper notes that dilation was not used in the RoBERTa transfer setting because it did not fit the pretrained weights as well.

The position embedding story is especially useful. RoBERTa has learned absolute position embeddings up to 512 positions. Longformer extends to 4096 by copying the 512 learned embeddings repeatedly instead of random initialization.

The table shows why this is reasonable. A Longformer initialized with copied position embeddings is far better than one that starts with a random long-position setup, and continued MLM pretraining improves it further. For Longformer-base, BPC moves from 1.957 after copying position embeddings to 1.753 after 2K updates and 1.705 after 65K updates.

The Tasks Are Actually Long

Longformer is evaluated on tasks where the input length can exceed BERT’s 512-token limit by a large margin.

TriviaQA is the clearest example: the average context length is 6,589 wordpieces and the 95th percentile is 17,126. WikiHop and Hyperpartisan also have long tails. A truncation baseline may work on short examples, but it cannot be trusted as the sequence length grows.

This is where Longformer’s design is pragmatic. Instead of chunking the document, running RoBERTa repeatedly, and stitching chunk representations with task-specific logic, the paper can concatenate the available context and process it as one sequence.

Finetuning Results

The main finetuning table compares Longformer-base with RoBERTa-base.

The strongest gains appear where longer context matters. WikiHop improves from 72.4 to 75.0, and Hyperpartisan improves from 87.4 to 94.8. TriviaQA and HotpotQA improve more modestly because their useful evidence can often be found in shorter local regions or through task-specific pipelines. IMDB also improves slightly, which fits the dataset: many reviews are short, but a nontrivial tail is longer than 512 wordpieces.

This result shape is important. Longformer is not a magic upgrade for every NLP benchmark. It helps most when the task has useful information outside the short context window and the model can exploit that information through local plus global attention.

What The Ablation Says

The WikiHop ablation is the best diagnostic table in the paper.

The default Longformer with sequence length 4096 reaches 73.8 accuracy. Training longer reaches 75.0. Reducing the sequence length to 2048 drops to 73.1, and using sequence length 512 with full attention drops to 71.7. This supports the claim that performance is not only coming from extra pretraining; the model benefits from longer context.

The most severe row is “no linear projection, no global attention”, which drops to 65.5. Global attention is not a decorative feature. It gives task tokens a direct path to the whole document.

Longformer-Encoder-Decoder

The paper also introduces Longformer-Encoder-Decoder (LED) for long-document seq2seq tasks. LED uses Longformer-style local plus global attention in the encoder, while the decoder still attends fully to generated tokens and encoded representations.

On arXiv summarization, LED-large with sequence length 16,384 reports 46.63 ROUGE-1, 19.62 ROUGE-2, and 41.83 ROUGE-L in this table. The useful comparison is not only against prior systems, but also against the shorter LED setting.

Increasing the input size from 1K to 4K and then 16K improves both ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2. That is the cleanest evidence in the paper that the summarization task benefits from reading more of the source document.

Practical Notes

Longformer is a good fit when:

  • The task needs document-level context, not only a short answer span.
  • Most interactions are local, but a few task tokens need global access.
  • You want to reuse pretrained BERT/RoBERTa-style models instead of training a long-context architecture from scratch.
  • The model can tolerate a fixed attention pattern.

The limitation is also clear. Sliding-window attention is an inductive bias. It is efficient because most token pairs cannot directly interact. If a task requires arbitrary token-to-token interactions at many distant positions, a fixed local/global pattern may miss some dependencies unless enough layers or global tokens provide a path.

For implementation, I would pay attention to the kernel. The paper separates loop, chunk, and CUDA implementations because the same mathematical sparsity can have very different runtime behavior. The attention pattern and the memory layout have to be designed together.

Takeaway

Longformer is valuable because it makes long-document modeling feel like a controlled modification of pretrained Transformers. Local windows carry the text stream, global tokens carry the task interface, and copied position embeddings make RoBERTa adaptation practical. The result is not a universal replacement for dense attention, but it is a clean engineering tradeoff for document NLP.

entry.title: Mamba-2: Structured State Space Duality
Medusa: LLM Inference with Multiple Decoding Heads
MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile
MobileNetV3: Search-Assisted Engineering for Mobile CNNs
entry.content:
Howard A, Sandler M, Chu G, et al. Searching for MobileNetV3. ICCV 2019.

Paper

MobileNetV3 is easy to misread as “NAS found a better MobileNet.” That is not the main lesson. The paper is closer to a deployment engineering log: start from a platform-aware searched model, run a layer-wise adaptation procedure, inspect the expensive pieces, then make operator and layout changes that are outside the search space.

The result matters because the metric is not just MAdds. The paper measures single-thread latency on real Google Pixel phones through TFLite. That makes the work a useful bridge between architecture search papers and the kind of model surgery that actually determines mobile runtime.

What The Paper Is Optimizing

MobileNetV3 keeps the MobileNetV2/MnasNet lineage:

  • inverted residual blocks remain the basic building block;
  • depthwise separable convolution remains the compute-saving primitive;
  • squeeze-and-excitation is used, but selectively;
  • the final model is evaluated by measured Pixel latency, not only by operation count.

The pipeline has three layers:

Stage Role Why It Is Not Enough Alone
Platform-aware NAS Find a global block-level architecture under a latency-aware reward. The search space still cannot express every useful manual layout change.
NetAdapt Adjust channels layer by layer toward a target latency. It is a local adaptation method and depends on a good seed model.
Manual redesign Change activations, the first layer, the last stage, and SE details. These choices need profiling and implementation knowledge.

That last row is the part I care about most. MobileNetV3 is a strong model because the authors combine automated search with engineering constraints instead of pretending the search algorithm owns the whole design.

Accuracy And Real Latency

The front page result is the Pixel latency frontier. MobileNetV3-Large competes in the 40-100 ms range, while MobileNetV3-Small competes in the 20-40 ms range.

The important comparison is not just “higher accuracy.” The paper reports that MobileNetV3-Large reaches the same 75.2% ImageNet top-1 as MnasNet-A1 while reducing Pixel 1 latency from 71 ms to 51 ms. MobileNetV3-Small reaches 67.4% top-1 at 15.8 ms, compared with MnasNet-small at 64.9% and 20.3 ms.

Model Top-1 Pixel 1 latency
V3-Large 1.0 75.2 51 ms
MnasNet-A1 75.2 71 ms
V2 1.0 72.0 64 ms
V3-Small 1.0 67.4 15.8 ms
MnasNet-small 64.9 20.3 ms

The table makes the paper’s position clear. V3-Large is not merely a slightly larger model with better accuracy. It is a measured-latency improvement over another platform-aware NAS model at the same top-1 point.

The MAdds plot is still useful, but it is secondary.

MAdds tells us how many arithmetic operations a model nominally performs. Pixel latency tells us whether those operations map well onto the runtime, memory hierarchy, fused kernels, quantized operators, and thread setup. MobileNetV3 is designed against the second target.

From MobileNetV2 Blocks To V3 Blocks

MobileNetV2 uses the inverted residual and linear bottleneck block. The narrow representation sits at the input and output of the block, and the expensive work happens in the expanded channel space.

MobileNetV3 keeps this general form, but it brings in MnasNet-style squeeze-and-excitation and changes where nonlinearities are used.

This is not a cosmetic detail. SE is an accuracy booster, but it introduces extra small matrix/vector work and activation functions. Nonlinearity placement also matters because early feature maps are spatially large. An activation that looks cheap in a paper formula can become expensive when it is applied to many pixels.

Search Strategy

The paper uses two search/adaptation tools:

  1. Platform-aware NAS for block-wise global architecture search.
  2. NetAdapt for layer-wise channel adjustment.

For the large model, the authors reuse MnasNet-A1 as the starting point because the earlier MnasNet search already targets roughly the same 80 ms latency regime. For the small model, they adjust the reward because accuracy changes more sharply with latency in the small-model regime.

The MnasNet-style reward is:

Here is validation accuracy, is measured latency, is the target latency, and controls how strongly latency is penalized. The MobileNetV3 paper notes that the original setting was not ideal for small models and uses a smaller weight factor for that regime.

NetAdapt then performs a discrete channel search. At each step, proposals reduce either an expansion layer or a bottleneck size shared by residual-connected blocks. A candidate is selected according to the tradeoff slope between accuracy change and latency change:

This is a practical detail. The algorithm is not optimizing an abstract FLOPs proxy; it is trying to spend every millisecond of latency reduction where the accuracy damage is smallest.

The Last Stage Was Too Expensive

One of the most valuable pieces of the paper is the last-stage redesign. MobileNetV2-like networks often expand to a high-dimensional feature tensor before global pooling. That is expensive because the expansion is still applied at a spatial resolution such as 7x7.

MobileNetV3 moves the expensive feature generation after global average pooling. Once the tensor is 1x1, the 1x1 expansion is almost free compared with doing it over a spatial map.

The paper reports that this efficient last stage reduces latency by 7 ms, about 11% of runtime, and removes roughly 30M MAdds with almost no accuracy loss. This is exactly the type of edit a search space may miss: it is not just “choose another kernel size,” it is a structural observation about where expensive features are needed.

There is also an early-layer edit. The authors reduce the first convolution filters from 32 to 16 and find that hard-swish preserves accuracy there. That saves about 2 ms and 10M MAdds.

Hard-Swish

Swish is:

It often improves accuracy over ReLU, but sigmoid is not a friendly primitive on many mobile inference paths. MobileNetV3 replaces it with a piecewise-linear approximation:

This is not just an approximation for mathematical neatness. ReLU6 is widely optimized in mobile frameworks, and hard-swish avoids the precision and implementation variability of approximate sigmoid in quantized inference. The authors also avoid using h-swish everywhere. They use it mainly in the second half of the network because early activations have larger spatial maps and are more expensive.

The ablation table shows why the placement matters.

Variant Top-1 Pixel 1 latency
V3-Large 1.0 75.2 51.4
ReLU 74.5 50.5
h-swish @16 75.4 53.5
h-swish @112 75.0 51.0

Using h-swish from the 16-channel point gives a slight accuracy gain but costs more latency. Starting it later at the 112-channel point is closer to the final design tradeoff. The paper’s final choice is not “h-swish is always better”; it is “h-swish is worth it where the accuracy gain buys enough latency budget.”

The optimized implementation also matters:

Without an optimized h-swish kernel, the same architecture can move to a worse point on the latency curve. That is a useful warning for reproduction: changing the runtime implementation can change the conclusion.

Architecture Definitions

The final paper defines two model families. The large model targets higher accuracy under moderate mobile latency, and the small model targets lower-resource cases.

The large architecture has a mixed block layout: 3x3 and 5x5 bottlenecks, selective SE, ReLU in earlier blocks, and h-swish in later blocks. The tail uses the efficient last-stage pattern discussed above.

The small model is not just a width multiplier of the large one. It has its own searched/adapted structure, uses more 5x5 blocks in the middle, and is tuned for a different part of the latency curve.

Main ImageNet Results

The main floating-point table is the best compact evidence for the paper.

Three observations stand out:

  • V3-Large 1.0 and MnasNet-A1 both report 75.2% top-1, but V3-Large is 20 ms faster on Pixel 1.
  • V3-Small 1.0 is much smaller in MAdds than MnasNet-small while being both more accurate and faster.
  • V2 1.0 has more MAdds and lower accuracy than V3-Large, and it is slower on Pixel 1.

The last point is a reminder that MobileNetV3 is not only a NAS story. The final-stage edit, activation implementation, SE scaling, and channel adaptation all contribute to the measured latency.

The quantized results are worth checking separately because the paper is targeting mobile inference, not just floating-point research models.

For the full-size model, quantized MobileNetV3-Large keeps 73.8% top-1 and runs at 44 ms on Pixel 1, while MobileNetV2 1.0 reports 70.9% and 52 ms. For the small regime, MobileNetV3-Small keeps 64.9% top-1 at 15.5 ms, compared with MobileNetV2 0.35 at 57.2% and 16.7 ms. This is also where the hard-sigmoid/hard-swish choice matters: the activation has to survive the actual inference path.

Resolution And Width Scaling

MobileNetV3 is also evaluated across width multipliers and input resolutions.

The paper notes that changing input resolution can provide a better accuracy-latency tradeoff than changing the width multiplier. That makes sense: resolution changes the spatial cost of almost every layer, while width changes channel dimensions. But resolution is not always a free tuning knob. Detection and segmentation often need higher spatial detail, so deployment constraints can force a resolution choice before the architecture is selected.

The appendix table makes the deployment menu explicit.

Model Accuracy Pixel 1 latency
large 224/1.25 76.6 77.0
large 224/1.0 75.2 51.2
large 160/1.0 71.7 27.8
small 224/1.0 67.5 15.8
small 160/1.0 62.8 8.6
small 96/1.0 51.7 4.4

For a mobile product, this table is more useful than a single headline model. It gives several operating points that can be selected according to latency, battery, memory, and task accuracy requirements.

Component Progression

The most honest figure in the paper is the component progression plot.

The path is roughly:

Step Effect
MnasNet seed Strong baseline around 75.2% top-1.
SE/4 Improves accuracy with modest parameter cost.
NetAdapt Moves the model to a lower latency region.
Compact / last-stage edits Saves latency without giving up much accuracy.
h-swish and optimized h-swish Recovers or improves accuracy while depending on runtime support.

This figure is why I would not describe MobileNetV3 as a fully automatic NAS method. The final point is reached by a sequence of searched, adapted, and hand-designed changes.

Detection Transfer

The paper also uses MobileNetV3 as a drop-in SSDLite backbone on COCO.

The interesting detail is the channel reduction between C4 and C5. The last part of the classifier backbone is tuned for 1000 ImageNet classes, but COCO detection has 90 classes and different feature needs. Reducing channels in the late feature layers improves latency with little or no mAP loss.

Backbone mAP Latency
V2 22.1 162 ms
MnasNet 23.0 174 ms
V3 22.0 137 ms
V3 with channel reduction 22.0 119 ms
V3-Small 16.0 52 ms
V3-Small with channel reduction 16.1 43 ms

This is another example of post-search adaptation. A backbone that is good for classification still needs task-specific trimming when transferred to detection.

Semantic Segmentation

For segmentation, the paper proposes Lite R-ASPP, a lightweight head designed for MobileNetV3.

The head keeps the ASPP intuition but removes expensive branches. It uses global-average-pooling-like context and a small number of 1x1 convolutions. The authors also use atrous convolution for denser features when output stride is 16.

On Cityscapes validation, the MobileNetV3 rows are broadly similar in mIOU to MobileNetV2 rows but usually faster. The small model is especially useful: MobileNetV3-Small with LR-ASPP reaches 68.38 mIOU at 327 ms half-resolution Pixel 3 latency in the table.

The Cityscapes test table shows the expected tradeoff. Output stride 16 is more accurate and slower; output stride 32 is faster and slightly less accurate. Again, the paper is not claiming one universal best point. It is giving a set of mobile operating points.

Reproduction Notes

For a faithful reproduction, I would record these details before comparing results:

  • Device model: the paper reports Pixel 1/2/3 single large core measurements.
  • Runtime: the paper uses TFLite benchmark tooling.
  • Threading: measurements are single-threaded, not multi-core throughput.
  • Batch size: latency is batch size 1.
  • Input resolution: changing resolution can dominate the measured curve.
  • Operator implementation: optimized h-swish changes the latency conclusion.
  • Quantization path: hard-swish and hard-sigmoid were chosen partly because they are quantization-friendly.

I would also separate five ablations: NetAdapt, SE ratio, efficient last stage, first convolution reduction, and h-swish placement. Without that separation, it is too easy to over-credit the architecture search and under-credit the manual deployment work.

Limitations

The paper is tied to a specific software and hardware stack. Pixel/TFLite latency is a useful target, but it is not a universal latency oracle. A GPU delegate, a different ARM core, a DSP/NPU backend, or a runtime without optimized h-swish can reorder the frontier.

The search process is also not cheap or simple to reproduce. The paper reuses MnasNet machinery, runs NetAdapt, and trains models at scale. The engineering lesson transfers more easily than the exact search recipe.

Another limitation is that the paper reports a strong final design but not a fully exhaustive decomposition of every design interaction. For example, activation placement, SE placement, and channel adaptation are coupled. A clean ablation of each dimension would be expensive.

Takeaway

MobileNetV3 is a search-assisted engineering paper. NAS provides a good seed, NetAdapt sharpens the layer widths, and profiler-aware manual edits remove the pieces that the search space did not express. The strongest message is simple: for mobile CNNs, the real objective is not FLOPs, and the best architectures usually come from search plus runtime-aware model surgery.

entry.title: Mooncake: KVCache-Centric LLM Serving
Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-Token Prediction
entry.content:
Gloeckle F, Idrissi B Y, Roziere B, Lopez-Paz D, Synnaeve G. Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction. ICML 2024.

  • Paper: arXiv PDF
  • Topic: pretraining objective, future-token heads, code generation, byte-level modeling, self-speculative decoding

This paper is a useful reminder that “next-token prediction” is not the only causal language-modeling objective worth taking seriously. The proposed change is small: at each sequence position, train the model to predict not only the next token, but the next future tokens. The implementation uses a shared Transformer trunk and lightweight output heads. At inference time, the model can either ignore the extra heads and behave like an ordinary autoregressive model, or use the extra heads as draft heads for self-speculative decoding.

The main result is not just “more supervision is good.” The interesting part is where the gain appears. Small models can get worse. Large code models improve clearly. Byte-level models improve a lot. Multiple-choice natural language benchmarks do not show the same benefit, while summarization and synthetic reasoning tasks are more positive. So the paper is really about when forcing a model to look ahead changes the representation it learns.

One-Picture Summary

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. The model predicts four future targets from the same shared trunk state. At inference time the extra heads may be discarded, or reused to accelerate decoding.

The upper half of the figure is the architecture idea. Input token produces a shared hidden state. Instead of only supervising token , the model also predicts token , token , and token . The lower half gives an early hint of the scale effect: on MBPP pass@1, 4-token prediction is worse than the next-token baseline for 0.3B and 0.6B models, but better for 1.3B and above, with the biggest gain at 13B.

My short read:

Question Answer
Is this an inference-only trick? No. The paper studies multi-token prediction as a pretraining objective.
Does inference require the extra heads? No. The next-token head can be used alone.
Why keep the extra heads? They can serve as draft heads for self-speculative decoding.
Where are the strongest gains? Large code models and byte-level code models.
Is larger always better? No. For 7B token-level code models, is the sweet spot in the main ablation.
Does it help every benchmark? No. Multiple-choice NLP benchmarks are flat or worse.

Objective

Standard language modeling trains on one supervised target per position. For a training sequence , the usual next-token objective is:

where the paper writes the history as:

Multi-token prediction changes the target from one future token to a block of future tokens:

If the model could represent the full joint distribution over the future block, this objective would be a direct block-prediction loss. The implementation in the paper makes it tractable by using a shared representation and independent prediction heads. Let the shared trunk produce a latent representation:

Then the paper writes the multi-token loss through the shared latent variable as:

The practical head-factorized form is:

Since is computed deterministically by the trunk in the actual neural network, the training code is best understood as cross-entropy losses sharing one trunk state:

The first head is the ordinary next-token head. The other heads predict farther offsets:

The important detail is that the future heads do not consume the future tokens as inputs. They are not doing a mini autoregressive rollout inside the model. They predict different future offsets from the same observed context. This is why the task becomes harder as grows, and why simply increasing is not guaranteed to help.

Architecture

The architecture is deliberately conservative. There is one shared Transformer trunk , one shared unembedding matrix , and independent heads . The prediction for the -th future token is:

for:

The head is the next-token prediction head:

This matters for inference. A multi-token predictor is still a normal autoregressive LM if we only keep the first head. The future heads are an auxiliary training signal and an optional decoding accelerator.

For fair model-size comparisons, the paper does not simply add many new parameters on top of a baseline. When adding future-prediction layers, it removes layers from the shared trunk. This makes the comparison closer to equal-parameter and equal-budget training. The tradeoff is: some capacity moves from the shared trunk into prediction heads that specialize in different lookahead offsets.

The appendix also discusses alternative head structures. The main architecture uses independent heads, but causal and anticausal head stacks are possible. In a causal variant, later heads are built on top of earlier heads:

In an anticausal variant, the model starts from the farthest head and refines toward nearer futures:

The paper’s main experiments use the simpler independent-head architecture, which is also the cleanest design if the future heads are later used as parallel draft heads.

Memory-Efficient Training

Naively training future heads can blow up memory. The reason is the unembedding. If the vocabulary size is and the trunk hidden dimension is , materializing logits and gradients for all heads at once can cost:

That is a bad scaling law because is large. The paper’s trick is to run the head losses sequentially while accumulating the gradient at the shared trunk output. This reduces the peak memory to:

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. The trunk state is computed once, detached, used by each head sequentially, and then its accumulated gradient is passed back into the shared trunk.

The code sketch in the figure is essentially:

There are two useful engineering points here.

First, this is not equivalent to training separate models. The expensive trunk is shared, and the future heads are small relative to the full model. Second, the implementation avoids keeping every head’s unembedding gradients live at the same time. That is why the method can be trained at LLM scale rather than only on toy models.

The appendix notes that their actual distributed training implementation had a small overhead because separate backward passes interacted imperfectly with Fully Sharded Data Parallel overlap. I would not read “no overhead” as a law of nature. The stronger claim is that there is no fundamental -times memory blowup if the backward order is implemented carefully.

Main Code Results

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Multi-token prediction is worse for the smallest code models but becomes better as model size grows.

The scaling result is the most important empirical part of the paper. The authors train code models from 300M to 13B parameters and evaluate MBPP and HumanEval. The behavior is not monotonic in the naive sense. At 0.3B and 0.6B, 4-token prediction often hurts. Around 1.3B the trend starts to flip. At 6.7B and 13B, the gains are clear.

This is a plausible reason the idea has not become standard earlier. If one only runs small ablations, multi-token prediction looks fragile or negative. The paper’s claim is that the representation-level benefit is mostly visible once the model has enough capacity to use the lookahead signal.

Table cropped from the paper PDF. The bold entries mark the best values within each setting.

Table 1 gives a denser view of the main 7B results. The token-level code setting trains 7B models on 200B tokens with a 32k-token vocabulary and tests:

The best token-level model in that setting is usually :

Benchmark Baseline Best main token setting Observation
MBPP pass@1 30.0 33.8 at clear gain
MBPP pass@10 53.8 55.9 at smaller but positive
MBPP pass@100 73.7 76.9 at positive
HumanEval pass@1 22.8 24.0 at positive
HumanEval pass@10 36.4 40.1 at strong gain
HumanEval pass@100 62.0 66.1 at strong gain

The paper summarizes the same ablation as:

for pass@1, pass@10, and pass@100, and:

APPS/Intro behaves differently. In the 200B-token setting, is best for APPS/Intro. That is an important caveat: the best prediction window depends on the data distribution and evaluation task. There is no universal “four tokens is optimal” rule.

The byte-level result is even more dramatic. With byte tokenization, the next-token objective has to learn many local byte transitions that are easy but not semantically useful. Multi-byte prediction forces the model to look past some of those local byte patterns. In Table 1, the 313B-byte setting has:

Model MBPP pass@1 HumanEval pass@1 APPS/Intro pass@100
next-byte, 19.3 18.1 2.4
8-byte, 32.3 21.8 14.0

The authors describe this as more MBPP pass@1 problems solved and more HumanEval pass@1 problems solved compared with next-byte prediction. My interpretation is that byte-level training exposes the weakness of pure next-token supervision most clearly: the model can spend too much training signal on tiny local continuations instead of learning larger program structure.

How Many Future Tokens?

The paper’s answer is empirical, not theoretical.

For 7B token-level code models trained on 200B tokens:

is the strongest setting across MBPP and HumanEval in the main table. But wins APPS/Intro in the same training regime, and is best for byte-level models. So I would treat as a modeling hyperparameter tied to token granularity:

Tokenization More local redundancy? Useful in paper
32k BPE tokens lower for MBPP/HumanEval
bytes much higher in main byte ablation

The intuition is simple. A byte is a smaller semantic unit than a BPE token, so looking eight bytes ahead may correspond to a similar semantic horizon as looking a few tokens ahead. But this is only an intuition. The actual optimum still depends on model size, data, and task.

Faster Inference

The future heads can be used as draft heads. This is not exactly the same story as Medusa, because the heads are trained during pretraining rather than attached afterward. But the serving idea is similar: use cheap lookahead predictions to propose several tokens, then verify them with the next-token head.

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. With more heads used during self-speculative decoding, throughput increases and relative latency decreases across batch sizes.

In the appendix experiment, the authors use a 4-token prediction model and vary how many heads participate in self-speculative decoding. The speedup is stable across batch sizes in their setup. This matters because many speculative decoding results are strongest at small batch sizes and fade when batching grows. Here, the future heads are attached to the same model, so the overhead profile is different from running a separate draft model.

Table cropped from the paper PDF. Token-level 4-token models reach about 2.7x to 3.0x relative speedup when using four heads.

For the token-level 4-token model:

Domain Heads used Relative speedup Tokens per forward
Wikipedia 4 2.74 3.12
Books 4 2.67 3.09
Code 4 3.05 3.50

The code setting is the strongest. With four heads, the model retrieves 3.50 tokens per forward on average and reaches a 3.05x relative speedup. The speedup is lower than the theoretical maximum of four because not every proposed token is accepted and each speculative step has overhead.

The byte-level results can go higher because byte predictions are more local and often easier to accept:

Table cropped from the paper PDF. Byte-level self-speculative decoding reaches much larger speedups when many byte heads are used.

For the byte model, using eight heads gives 6.39x relative speedup. For , using all thirty-two heads gives 10.84x relative speedup and 15.35 tokens per forward. These are byte tokens, so the numbers are not directly comparable to BPE-token speedups, but they show why multi-byte prediction is appealing: byte-level training normally hurts inference length, and self-speculative decoding can recover much of that cost.

Finetuning

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. A model pretrained with 4-token prediction remains better after CodeContests finetuning.

The paper also checks whether the multi-token pretraining benefit survives finetuning. The setup compares:

Pretraining Finetuning target Legend
next-token next-token
4-token next-token
4-token 4-token

Both finetuned versions of the 4-token pretrained model beat the next-token baseline on CodeContests pass@k. The strongest line is , meaning: pretrain with the auxiliary lookahead task, then strip or ignore the future heads and finetune with the classical next-token objective.

This is a useful pattern. It suggests the future-token loss is valuable as a representation-shaping pretraining signal, even if the downstream finetuning objective returns to ordinary next-token modeling.

Natural Language Results Are Mixed

The paper does not claim universal improvement on all natural language benchmarks.

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. On six standard multiple-choice NLP benchmarks, 2-token prediction is roughly on par with the baseline and 4-token prediction is worse.

This negative result is important. Multiple-choice and likelihood-based evaluations reward calibrated preferences over fixed answer options. A lookahead objective may help generation and reasoning without improving this particular evaluation format. Or the natural language setting may simply require a different , larger model scale, or more data before the benefit appears.

For generative natural language, the paper reports a more positive summarization result:

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. On eight abstractive summarization benchmarks, 2-token and 4-token models improve average ROUGE-L F1 over the next-token baseline.

The average ROUGE-L F1 gains are not huge, but they are consistent in the plotted summarization aggregate. The gap shrinks at 500B training tokens, which fits the broader theme: multi-token prediction can improve sample efficiency, but the advantage may shrink as the baseline sees more data.

My read is that natural language results are task-dependent. If the benchmark is mostly about choosing among given labels, the extra lookahead supervision is not clearly useful. If the benchmark requires generating structured output, the result is more promising.

Synthetic Diagnostics

The authors use synthetic tasks to probe why lookahead might help. These experiments are not meant to replace large-scale evaluations, but they make the paper easier to reason about.

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. On a controlled induction task, 2-token prediction helps small models learn the second token of repeated two-token names.

The induction task asks whether a model can complete repeated patterns. If a story has already mentioned a two-token name, predicting the second token of a later occurrence is mostly an induction problem. The figure shows that 2-token prediction helps small models substantially. The advantage disappears around 100M nonembedding parameters.

That disappearance is not a contradiction. Once a model has enough capacity, or once the data makes induction easy enough, next-token training can learn the required feature. Multi-token prediction seems most useful when the model would otherwise underinvest in such longer-range features.

The arithmetic task pushes this further:

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Multi-token prediction improves accuracy on a polynomial arithmetic task, including out-of-domain expressions with more operations than seen during training.

The task works in the polynomial ring:

Training expressions contain one to five operations. Evaluation includes both in-domain cases and harder out-of-domain cases with more than five operations. The absolute out-of-domain accuracy is still low, but multi-token prediction improves it more than increasing the small model size from 30M to 100M in the related appendix comparison.

The useful lesson is not that multi-token prediction solves arithmetic. It does not. The lesson is that forcing lookahead can change which algorithmic features the model learns under the same parameter budget.

Why Might It Work?

The paper gives two related explanations. I find both useful, but neither should be read as a complete theory.

Choice Points

Some token decisions matter much more than others. In code, choosing a function name, branch condition, API call, loop bound, or variable update can constrain many future tokens. Other tokens are local formatting or syntactic glue. A next-token objective gives every target one direct loss term. A multi-token objective gives more indirect weight to tokens whose consequences affect the future.

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. If the hard transition is , then future-token losses also penalize earlier predictions that should have anticipated .

For an -token objective, the paper argues that a consequential choice point receives:

loss terms through its future correlates. An inconsequential transition receives only:

reinforcements. The relative emphasis on choice points is therefore:

For , that is a 2.5x relative emphasis on consequential decisions in this simplified counting argument. This connects nicely to code generation. One wrong high-level token can derail the entire solution even if the next few syntax tokens remain locally plausible.

The appendix gives a more formal reinforcement-learning style definition of a choice point. Let be the current partial sequence and be the generation policy. In shorter notation, define a state value $V_\pi(s_t)=\mathrm{E}\pi G_tG_t=\sum{j\ge0}R(s_{t+j})\sigma_\pi(s_t)=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(V_\pi(s_{t+1}))}\sigma_\pi(s_t)$ is large. This formalization is not directly used as a training objective, but it clarifies what the paper means by a token whose choice matters for the future trajectory.

Information-Theoretic View

The second explanation is about mutual information between adjacent future tokens. Let be the next token and be the second-next token, with the observed prefix omitted from notation.

Next-token prediction focuses on:

Two-token prediction adds the next future token:

The paper decomposes the single-token entropy as:

For two-token prediction:

The interpretation is that two-token prediction increases the relative weight of the mutual information term . In plain terms, the model is pushed to learn features of that are useful for predicting , not just features that make locally likely.

The appendix makes this argument closer to the actual cross-entropy loss. Let be the empirical data distribution and be the model distribution. The conditional cross-entropy is:

The relative mutual information term is defined as:

Then the relative version of the one-token decomposition is:

And the relative two-token decomposition is:

I would not over-interpret this as a complete proof of better reasoning. It is still an explanatory decomposition. But it gives a precise way to say what the objective changes: the future-token loss makes the model pay more attention to information that couples nearby future tokens.

Relation to Medusa and DeepSeek-V3

This paper sits between training objectives and inference systems.

Medusa also attaches future-token heads to a model, but its main framing is inference acceleration. The heads propose candidates and a tree attention pass verifies them. Multi-token prediction is more fundamental: the heads are part of pretraining, and the main question is whether the objective improves the base model even when the heads are discarded.

DeepSeek-V3 later uses an MTP module as part of its training recipe. The connection is direct at the conceptual level: force the model to predict more than one future token. The difference is implementation scale and integration with the rest of the model recipe. I read this paper as one of the clearest controlled studies showing why MTP is not just a decoding trick.

The clean mental model is:

Method Main role of future heads
Medusa inference-time candidate generation
Multi-token prediction paper pretraining objective and optional self-speculative decoding
DeepSeek-style MTP large-scale recipe component for stronger training signal

Practical Notes

If I were trying to reproduce or reuse this idea, I would watch the following details.

First, compare at a fixed parameter and compute budget. If we simply add heads and parameters to the baseline, the result is harder to interpret. The paper removes trunk layers when adding future head layers, which makes the comparison more meaningful.

Second, tune for tokenization. The right window for byte-level code is not necessarily the right window for BPE-token natural language. Larger creates harder prediction targets and can inject noisy gradients.

Third, keep the memory schedule. The method is appealing only if it avoids materializing all vocab-sized outputs at once. The difference between and is the difference between a neat idea and a trainable LLM recipe.

Fourth, evaluate both direct model quality and decoding speed. The future heads can help in two separate ways: they may improve the representation learned by the trunk, and they may provide high-quality drafts for self-speculative decoding. Those are related but not identical claims.

Fifth, do not expect every benchmark to improve. The multiple-choice result is a useful warning. Multi-token prediction seems especially aligned with generation, code, byte-level modeling, and synthetic tasks where local next-token correctness is not enough.

Takeaways

The paper’s strongest contribution is showing that multi-token prediction is a serious pretraining objective at scale. The gains are not universal, but they are large enough on code and byte-level modeling to matter. The method also creates a natural bridge from training to inference: the same future heads that shape representations during pretraining can later draft tokens for self-speculative decoding.

The part I like most is the choice-point interpretation. Next-token prediction treats every position as a local prediction problem under teacher forcing. Multi-token prediction asks the representation to carry information that will still matter a few steps later. That is a small objective change, but for code and algorithmic sequences, it changes the training pressure in exactly the place where one bad local decision can derail the whole continuation.

entry.title: Neural Architecture Optimization
NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Ying C, Klein A, Christiansen E, Real E, Murphy K, Hutter F. NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search. ICML 2019.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.09635.pdf
  • Code: https://github.com/google-research/nasbench

NAS-Bench-101 is a benchmark paper rather than a new NAS optimizer. Its main contribution is to turn a large but still controlled cell search space into a queryable table. The table maps each valid architecture to fixed training results, so an optimizer can be evaluated without retraining thousands of CIFAR-10 models.

That sounds simple, but it fixes a real problem in early NAS papers: algorithm comparisons were often dominated by GPU budget, implementation choices, and hidden training recipes. NAS-Bench-101 changes the experiment into a cleaner question: under the same query budget, which optimizer finds better architectures, and how stable is that behavior over many independent runs?

Search Space

NAS-Bench-101 uses the familiar cell-based CNN setup. A macro skeleton repeats a learned cell several times, and the cell itself is a directed acyclic graph. The original encoded space contains about 510 million possible graphs before validity checks and canonicalization. After removing invalid and isomorphic cases, the benchmark contains 423k unique valid architectures.

The cell has at most 7 vertices and at most 9 edges. The input and output nodes are fixed, while intermediate nodes select one of three operations:

  • 3x3 convolution;
  • 1x1 convolution;
  • 3x3 max pooling.

This is intentionally narrower than a production architecture search space. It does not include inverted residual blocks, device latency choices, width multipliers, activation choices, or Transformer-style dimensions. The point is controlled diagnosis, not direct deployment search.

Query Protocol

For every architecture, NAS-Bench-101 stores multiple training budgets: 4, 12, 36, and 108 epochs. Each architecture is trained and evaluated three times, so the API can return either repeated observations or a particular trial index. This matters because a realistic search algorithm should see noisy observations, not an oracle with the exact mean performance.

The paper is also explicit about validation and test usage. During search, the optimizer should use training and validation metrics. Test accuracy should only be queried offline after the search has selected an architecture. If an algorithm uses test accuracy during search, it is no longer measuring generalization; it is optimizing the benchmark’s hidden answer key.

The stored metrics include:

  • training time;
  • train accuracy;
  • validation accuracy;
  • test accuracy.

The cleanest evaluation is a best-so-far curve under a fixed budget. Reporting only the final architecture hides whether the method was sample efficient or just used enough queries to eventually stumble into a good cell.

Dataset Shape

The ECDF plots show two useful properties. First, most valid architectures are not terrible after 108 epochs; a large fraction already exceeds 90% validation and test accuracy. Second, stochastic training noise shrinks with longer training budgets, which is why early-epoch signals are useful but not equivalent to final ranking.

The best architecture in the table reaches 94.32% mean test accuracy. The paper compares this with two hand-designed cells: a ResNet-like cell at 93.12% and an Inception-like cell at 92.95%. The final validation and test accuracies are almost perfectly correlated at 108 epochs, with correlation around 0.999. That makes NAS-Bench-101 a good place to study optimizer behavior without getting too distracted by validation/test mismatch.

Training time is not just a function of parameter count. The plot below shows that more parameters usually cost more time, but topology still matters: two cells with similar parameter counts can have different runtime because of branching and operation placement.

That is one reason a benchmark table is useful. If the only feedback is accuracy, an optimizer may overfit to expensive cells. If the table also exposes time, one can evaluate regret over estimated wall-clock time instead of only over number of queries.

Architecture Diagnostics

The operation replacement experiment is one of the most useful parts of the paper. The authors replace one operation type with another across architectures and measure the average effect on validation accuracy and training time.

Replacing 3x3 convolution with 1x1 convolution drops average validation accuracy by about 1.16%, while replacing it with max pooling drops it by about 1.99%. The training-time changes go in the opposite direction: 1x1 convolution and max pooling are cheaper. A simple search algorithm can therefore get an apparent speed benefit while moving into a weaker region of the space.

The depth/width analysis is also a useful sanity check. In this benchmark, average validation accuracy peaks around depth 3, while increasing width helps up to the maximum width considered in the space.

This is a reminder that “deeper is better” is not a universal claim inside a constrained DAG cell. The combine semantics and edge constraints shape the distribution of architectures. A benchmark should be interpreted together with its encoding rules.

Locality

NAS algorithms often assume locality: a small architecture edit should usually cause a small performance change. NAS-Bench-101 lets the paper test that assumption directly.

The random-walk autocorrelation and fitness-distance correlation suggest locality up to a rough edit distance of about 6. The paper also notes that high-performing cells are rare in the encoded space: the chance of sampling one of the top graphs is roughly 1 in 50,000, while about 35.4% of the search space lies within distance 6 of the closest top graph. This explains why local search can be meaningful here, but also why pure random search needs many queries.

Search Algorithm Benchmarking

The benchmark section compares random search, regularized evolution, reinforcement learning, SMAC, TPE, BOHB, and Hyperband-like methods. Each algorithm is run 500 times, and performance is plotted as test regret over estimated wall-clock time.

This presentation is more informative than a single best score. The left plot captures convergence speed. The right ECDF shows how often an optimizer ends near the optimum. A method with a strong median but a bad tail may be unreliable, while a method with slower median progress but high robustness may be preferable for expensive real searches.

The comparison also highlights a subtle issue: algorithms that exploit lower training budgets, such as Hyperband and BOHB, are using a different kind of signal from optimizers that query only 108-epoch results. That is legitimate, but it must be stated. Otherwise “query count” is not a fair budget unit.

Mini-Benchmark and Early Epochs

The paper bootstraps a smaller NASBench-Mini with at most 6 vertices, giving around 64.5k cells instead of the full 423k. The relative ranking of random search, non-regularized evolution, and regularized evolution remains consistent across the smaller and larger tables.

This is useful because it suggests that a reduced space can still preserve some optimizer-ordering signal. It does not mean every algorithm conclusion transfers, but it gives evidence that the benchmark is not completely brittle to space size.

Early-epoch correlation is more complicated. The appendix reports Spearman rank correlations between early and final accuracies under different percentile slices.

The full-space 36-to-108-epoch correlation is high, around 0.902. But within the top 10% of architectures it drops sharply, to about 0.495. That is exactly the regime where strong NAS algorithms operate. Early training is useful for pruning weak models, but it is much less reliable for sorting the best models.

How I Would Use It

For a new black-box NAS optimizer, I would use NAS-Bench-101 as a first diagnostic step:

  1. Fix a query budget and wall-clock budget model.
  2. Run at least dozens of independent seeds, not just one or three.
  3. Use validation accuracy for search and reserve test accuracy for post-search reporting.
  4. Report best-so-far curves, not only the final best cell.
  5. Compare against random search and regularized evolution.
  6. State whether the optimizer can query 4/12/36-epoch results or only 108-epoch results.
  7. Check whether improvements survive on NAS-Bench-201 or a larger surrogate benchmark.

The important part is not to claim too much. A win on NAS-Bench-101 says that the optimizer navigates a small CIFAR-10 cell space well. It does not prove that the method will discover strong ImageNet, mobile, language, or hardware-aware architectures.

Limitations

NAS-Bench-101 is deliberately constrained:

  • only CIFAR-10 is used;
  • the operation set has only three choices;
  • the macro skeleton is fixed;
  • latency and memory are not first-class objectives;
  • the benchmark is small enough that repeated querying can turn into table exploitation;
  • the top region is narrow enough that early-epoch ranking becomes noisy.

These limitations do not make the benchmark weak. They define what the benchmark is for: controlled, reproducible optimizer analysis.

Takeaway

NAS-Bench-101 made NAS evaluation much more scientific. It replaced many expensive and hard-to-reproduce claims with a shared table, a clear query protocol, and enough repeated runs to study robustness. I would treat it as a unit test for NAS optimizers. Passing that unit test is not enough for real architecture design, but failing it is a strong warning sign.

entry.title: NAS-Bench-201: Extending the Scope of Reproducible Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Dong X, Yang Y. NAS-Bench-201: Extending the Scope of Reproducible Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2020.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00326.pdf
  • Code/API: https://github.com/D-X-Y/NAS-Bench-201
