NAS-Bench-201 is the natural follow-up to NAS-Bench-101. NAS-Bench-101 made a large cell space queryable, but it used only one dataset and imposed graph constraints that excluded some NAS algorithms. NAS-Bench-201 chooses a smaller fully enumerated space, then spends the saved budget on cleaner diagnostics: multiple datasets, more operations, and better support for different optimizer families.

The result is one of the most useful sanity-check benchmarks for NAS. It is small enough to be completely tabular, but rich enough to expose failure modes such as skip-connection collapse, weak transfer across datasets, and misleading early validation signals.

Search Space

NAS-Bench-201 uses a four-node cell. Every directed edge chooses one operation from a fixed set:

  • zeroize;
  • skip connection;
  • 1x1 convolution;
  • 3x3 convolution;
  • 3x3 average pooling.

There are 6 edges and 5 possible operations per edge, so the encoded search space has architectures.

The macro network repeats the searched cell inside a fixed skeleton. Compared with NAS-Bench-101, the cell is smaller, but the operation set is broader and the graph is unconstrained enough to support reinforcement learning, evolution, differentiable NAS, and hyperparameter-optimization-style search.

The paper also reports fewer unique topologies after accounting for equivalence: 12,751 if skip-connection isomorphism is considered, and 6,466 if both skip and zeroize isomorphisms are considered. That is a good reminder that an encoded search space and a semantic search space are not always the same thing.

What It Adds Over NAS-Bench-101

The paper includes a concise comparison table. The main differences are not only size. NAS-Bench-201 is multi-dataset, supports more NAS families, and exposes more diagnostic information.

NAS-Bench-201 stores results on:

  • CIFAR-10;
  • CIFAR-100;
  • ImageNet16-120.

For each architecture, it stores training, validation, and test loss/accuracy, plus compute-related properties such as parameter count, FLOPs, and latency. The latency measurement in the released benchmark was collected on a GTX 1080 Ti with batch size 256 for the non-CIFAR-10 settings.

This changes the kind of question the benchmark can answer. Instead of asking only “which method wins on CIFAR-10?”, we can ask whether a search method finds architectures that transfer across datasets and whether its behavior is stable when the target distribution changes.

Distribution of Architectures

The full enumeration gives a view of the entire space, not just the subset visited by a search algorithm.

The scatter plots show training, validation, and test behavior over all 15,625 architectures on all three datasets. The orange ResNet marker is a useful anchor. It is competitive, but not optimal: the paper notes that there is still about a 2% gap to the best architecture on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet16-120, and about a 1% gap among models with comparable parameter count.

The benchmark therefore has room for search algorithms to improve over a hand-designed baseline, while still being small enough that we can know the actual optimum.

Cross-Dataset Transfer

One of the strongest reasons to use NAS-Bench-201 is cross-dataset analysis. The paper sorts architectures by CIFAR-10 ranking and then shows where the same architectures rank on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet16-120.

The rankings are broadly correlated, but not identical. This matters for NAS claims. An optimizer that looks strong on CIFAR-10 may be exploiting a region that does not transfer cleanly to the other two datasets.

The correlation matrices make the same point more explicitly.

Within-dataset validation/test correlation is high. Cross-dataset correlation is lower, and it becomes weaker when focusing only on high-performing subsets. That is the practical regime of NAS: after a method filters out weak models, it still needs to rank good models, and that ranking is much harder to transfer.

Dynamic Ranking During Training

NAS-Bench-201 also records training curves, which makes it possible to ask how early validation accuracy relates to final test ranking.

The rank ordering becomes clearer as training progresses. At 1 epoch, the ranking is noisy. By 150 to 200 epochs, the validation ranking is much closer to final test ranking. This is the same lesson as NAS-Bench-101: early signals are useful, but using them as exact rank labels for the top architectures is risky.

Search Algorithm Results

The paper evaluates ten search algorithms, including random search, regularized evolution, REINFORCE, BOHB, DARTS variants, GDAS, SETN, ENAS, and random search with parameter sharing.

The table is valuable because it includes both search time and final validation/test performance across all three datasets. A few points stand out:

  • Random search is already a strong baseline in this compact space.
  • Regularized evolution is consistently competitive and extremely cheap when evaluated through the benchmark API.
  • Differentiable and parameter-sharing methods can fail badly if their search dynamics collapse to degenerate cells.
  • The optimal row is known, so the gap to the true best architecture is visible.

The paper also runs 500 trials for several non-weight-sharing search methods and plots trajectories across datasets.

This plot is closer to how NAS optimizers should be compared: many runs, explicit distribution, and both validation and test behavior. A single lucky search run is not enough evidence.

Parameter-Sharing Failure Mode

NAS-Bench-201 is especially useful for diagnosing parameter-sharing methods. In the reported experiments, DARTS-V1 and DARTS-V2 quickly move toward architectures dominated by skip connections, causing poor final performance.

The batch-normalization statistic strategy also matters. When using batch statistics instead of keeping running estimates for BN layers in each searched cell, the trajectories change.

This is a good example of why benchmarks need fine-grained traces. If a paper reports only the final architecture, we cannot tell whether the method failed because the search space is bad, the optimizer is bad, or the shared-weight evaluation protocol is biased.

Early Training Correlation

The appendix compares early-budget correlations with full-budget metrics.

Twelve-epoch training already gives a useful signal. For example, the 12-epoch diagnostic setting has strong correlations with full validation/test metrics across the three datasets. But the correlations are not perfect, especially for transfer to ImageNet16-120. Early stopping is a useful accelerator, not a replacement for final evaluation.

API Shape

The released API makes the benchmark easy to use from a script. The paper includes a short example showing architecture lookup, metric access, compute-cost access, and query by architecture string.

A typical use should keep the protocol explicit:

When reporting results, it is worth stating the dataset split, search budget, number of seeds, whether validation or test accuracy was queried during search, and whether any training-curve information was allowed.

Limitations

NAS-Bench-201 is controlled and compact, which is exactly why it is useful. But the same design also limits its scope:

  • the search space has only 15,625 encoded architectures;
  • all tasks are image classification;
  • the macro skeleton is fixed;
  • latency is measured in a limited hardware setting;
  • operation choices are small compared with modern mobile or Transformer spaces;
  • parameter-sharing results can depend strongly on implementation details.

Success on NAS-Bench-201 is therefore not proof that a method will work on every large real search space. It is evidence that the method survives a clean, fully observable diagnostic environment.

Takeaway

NAS-Bench-201 is a stronger NAS sanity check than a single-dataset benchmark. It tests whether a search algorithm beats simple baselines, avoids degenerate skip-heavy cells, and transfers across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120. I would use it after NAS-Bench-101 and before moving to larger surrogate or real-training benchmarks.

entry.title: NAS-BERT: Task-Agnostic and Adaptive-Size BERT Compression with Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Reference

  • Paper: NAS-BERT: Task-Agnostic and Adaptive-Size BERT Compression with Neural Architecture Search
  • Venue: KDD 2021

NAS-BERT is a BERT compression paper, but the interesting part is not simply that it produces a smaller encoder. The paper changes the compression setting:

  • the compressed models should come in many sizes, not one fixed student;
  • the search should happen at the pre-training stage, not separately for every downstream task;
  • the final model should be selected under parameter and latency constraints;
  • the search space is allowed to change the block type, not only width and depth.

This makes the paper closer to Once-for-All / BigNAS than to ordinary BERT distillation. NAS-BERT trains a supernet once, then selects subnets such as 60M, 30M, 10M, and 5M parameter models for different deployment budgets.

One Sentence

NAS-BERT is a task-agnostic, adaptive-size BERT compression framework:

  1. build a supernet over MHA, FFN, separable convolution, identity, and hidden-size choices;
  2. train it block by block using a BERT teacher;
  3. progressively shrink weak candidate architectures while preserving different model-size bins;
  4. approximate latency and loss with lookup tables;
  5. select a subnet that satisfies a target size and latency budget, then pre-train/fine-tune it.

My short reading: the paper is valuable because it treats compressed BERT as a model family, not as a single distilled model.

Why This Setting Matters

Most BERT compression papers choose a single student. DistilBERT, TinyBERT, MiniLM, and BERT-PKD each define one typical compressed size around 60M to 66M parameters. That is convenient for comparison, but deployment usually has more than one target:

Scenario Constraint that matters
online service latency and throughput
mobile device memory, energy, and CPU latency
offline batch inference total compute cost
edge device strict parameter and memory budget

A fixed compressed model cannot be optimal for all of these. A 60M model may be fine for server inference but too large for an embedded device. A 5M model may fit memory but sacrifice too much accuracy for a normal CPU service.

The other issue is task-specific compression. AdaBERT and DynaBERT can adapt to downstream tasks, but that means extra work per task. NAS-BERT tries a different tradeoff: do the expensive compression/search work during pre-training, then reuse the resulting model family across downstream tasks.

The phrase “task-agnostic” needs a careful reading. In this paper it mainly means the architecture search and compression are not repeated for each downstream task. The authors still evaluate optional downstream knowledge distillation. Their ablation later shows a stricter setting without fine-tuning-stage distillation.

Search Space

The search space is chain-structured. A supernet has layers, and each layer chooses one operation from a candidate set :

Here is one architecture path through the supernet. is the operation selected at layer . If there are candidate operations per layer and no further restrictions, the number of possible paths is:

This formula is simple but important. The architecture count grows exponentially with depth. NAS-BERT uses searchable layers because BERT-base has 12 Transformer layers, and each Transformer layer can be viewed as two sub-layers: MHA and FFN. With 26 operation choices, direct full-supernet search would have:

candidate paths. That number explains why the rest of the method is mostly about making supernet training and selection feasible.

The candidate operation set is:

The terms mean:

  • 1 for MHA;
  • 1 for FFN;
  • 3 for separable convolution with kernel size 3, 5, or 7;
  • 5 hidden sizes: 128, 192, 256, 384, and 512;
  • +1 for identity.

MHA and FFN keep the search space connected to the original Transformer. SepConv adds a cheaper non-attention operation with local context. Identity allows shallow networks because an identity operation can be removed after selection.

The hidden-size table is also structured. MHA uses 2, 3, 4, 6, or 8 heads as hidden size grows from 128 to 512. FFN uses intermediate sizes from 512 to 2048. This means the search is not merely “drop layers from BERT”; it can choose a different computation type and a different width at each block.

Why SepConv Appears Here

The appendix gives the practical reason for adding separable convolution. A standard 1D convolution with kernel size and hidden size has parameter scale:

A depthwise separable convolution has scale:

The first formula grows with both kernel size and the square of hidden size. The second separates channel mixing from depthwise local filtering. For BERT compression, this matters because a larger kernel can increase local receptive field without paying the full cost of standard convolution.

My interpretation: SepConv is a way to let the search escape the pure Transformer template while still remaining cheap. If the task does not need a full attention/FFN pair at every layer, the architecture can replace some blocks with local convolutional mixing.

Block-Wise Supernet Training

Directly training the entire supernet is too expensive. Weight sharing gives many paths access to the same operations, but with a search space around , random single-path optimization would give each architecture too little training signal.

NAS-BERT therefore divides the 24-layer supernet into blocks. Each block has 6 searchable layers. The BERT-base teacher is also divided into 4 corresponding blocks. For the -th student block, the training target is the output hidden state of the -th teacher block.

The paper’s block-wise distillation loss is:

Meaning of the terms:

  • is the teacher hidden state before block .
  • is the teacher hidden state after block .
  • is the student search block.
  • is the output of the student block when it receives the teacher’s input hidden state.
  • The squared norm is a mean-square style matching loss.

The formula says: “given the teacher’s input to this block, make the student block reproduce the teacher’s output.” This is not task-label supervision. It is representation matching inside the pre-trained BERT computation graph.

There is one extra engineering detail: student hidden size may be 128, 192, 256, 384, or 512, while the BERT-base teacher hidden size is 768. The paper uses learnable linear transformations before and after each student block to map hidden dimensions into the teacher-compatible space. Without these transformations, block-wise hidden-state matching would not be dimensionally valid.

Search Space Reduction From Blocking

Blocking changes the search problem from one enormous path to a composition of smaller sub-architectures.

Inside each block, NAS-BERT keeps the hidden size consistent across the 6 layers. The rough number before removing redundant identity-order variants is:

The 5 is the number of hidden-size choices. The term comes from 6 operation choices per layer over 6 layers, where the operation categories are MHA, FFN, SepConv3, SepConv5, SepConv7, and identity.

The paper then removes redundant identity permutations. For example:

and:

represent the same effective architecture after identity layers are removed. Keeping identities only at the end of a block reduces each block from 233,280 to 97,650 candidate sub-architectures.

The full combination count becomes:

This is still huge, but much smaller than . The key is that block-wise training lets NAS-BERT evaluate and prune candidate sub-architectures per block, then assemble full models later.

Progressive Shrinking

Block-wise training reduces the search space, but each block is still large. NAS-BERT uses progressive shrinking: after training epochs, it evaluates sampled architectures and removes weak candidates. This gives surviving architectures more training budget.

The figure is a useful sanity check. Progressive shrinking starts at epoch 4. After that, the red curve drops lower than the no-shrinking baseline. The interpretation is not that shrinking magically improves the model; it improves the allocation of training. Weak candidates are removed, so the remaining candidates receive more effective optimization.

Naive pruning has a problem: it may remove large models early because they are harder to train, and remove small models late because they have less capacity. Then the final supernet would lose the ability to serve different deployment budgets.

NAS-BERT solves this by dividing each block’s architectures into bins by parameter size and latency. For bin , the maximum parameter and latency thresholds are:

Here:

  • is the number of bins;
  • is the largest model in the search space;
  • is the parameter-size function;
  • is the latency function;
  • and define the upper boundary of bin .

An architecture belongs to bin only if:

This formula is the diversity guardrail. Pruning is performed inside each bin, so the method does not collapse into only one size range. If the binning works, the final supernet keeps candidates for small, medium, and large budgets.

The paper uses bins. It first trains for 3 epochs without progressive shrinking as a warm start. Then at the end of each later epoch, it samples architectures for validation and removes architectures per bin. The process stops when only architectures remain in each bin.

Model Selection

After progressive shrinking, each block contains sub-architectures. A complete architecture is formed by choosing one sub-architecture from each of the blocks, so the final candidate count is:

With , , and , this is:

Measuring full validation loss and actual latency for candidates is still not practical. NAS-BERT builds a lookup table with approximate metadata: architecture, parameter count, latency, and loss.

Latency is approximated additively:

This says the latency of the whole architecture is estimated by summing the measured latency of its operations. It is not perfect because real systems have memory effects, kernel launch overhead, batching behavior, and cache behavior. But it is cheap and hardware-specific: one can measure the 26 candidate operations on a target device and use that device’s latency table.

Loss is also approximated additively from block-wise losses:

This is my notation for the paper’s procedure. The method evaluates sub-architectures in each block on the dev set, then adds those block losses to estimate a complete architecture’s quality. The approximation is only valid if block-wise losses are informative enough after teacher-guided training. This is exactly why the earlier block-wise distillation matters.

The final selection pipeline is:

  1. build the architecture lookup table;
  2. filter candidates that violate parameter or latency constraints;
  3. choose the top candidates with low approximate loss;
  4. evaluate those full architectures on the dev set;
  5. select the best compressed model.

The paper uses .

Two-Stage Distillation

NAS-BERT’s architecture search is task-agnostic, but the paper also evaluates knowledge distillation during both pre-training and fine-tuning. The appendix summarizes the two-stage pipeline:

  1. pre-train the teacher;
  2. pre-train the student with distillation from the pre-trained teacher;
  3. fine-tune the teacher on the downstream task;
  4. fine-tune the student with distillation from the fine-tuned teacher.

The paper uses a general distillation objective:

In MathJax form:

The terms are:

  • and are student and teacher parameters.
  • is the normal supervised or language-modeling loss for the student.
  • matches the teacher output distribution and the student output distribution.
  • and are teacher and student predicted distributions.
  • balances ground-truth supervision and teacher matching.

The formula is not unique to NAS-BERT, but it matters for interpreting the experiments. The paper’s main claim is about architectures; the distillation objective helps train and evaluate them. The ablation later is important because it asks whether the searched architectures remain useful when one distillation stage is removed.

Training Cost

The training setup is large but not absurd for BERT-era compression:

Item Setting
Teacher BERT-base
Searchable layers 24
Blocks 4
Search bins per block 10
Warm start 3 epochs before shrinking
Validation samples during shrinking 2000 architectures
Stop condition 10 architectures per bin per block
Corpus English Wikipedia + BookCorpus
Supernet training 3 days on 32 NVIDIA P40 GPUs
Teacher training in paper 5 days

The cost story is central. Training a supernet on masked language modeling is expensive, but the cost is amortized over many final model sizes. If one needed to repeat the entire search per downstream task or per device, the method would be much less attractive.

Results: Adaptive Sizes

Table 2 is the cleanest evidence that the search space is doing something useful. The hand-designed baselines are BERT-like models with similar size and latency. NAS-BERT is compared at four sizes and two training settings:

  • PF: pre-training and fine-tuning;
  • KD: pre-training and fine-tuning with two-stage distillation.

The average GLUE score improvements are:

Size Setting BERT avg NAS-BERT avg Difference
60M PF 82.5 83.2 +0.7
60M KD 83.5 84.2 +0.7
30M PF 79.2 80.0 +0.8
30M KD 79.7 80.3 +0.6
10M PF 74.0 75.2 +1.2
10M KD 74.6 75.5 +0.9
5M PF 68.4 72.3 +3.9
5M KD 68.5 72.7 +4.2

The gap is much larger at 5M. This is the most interesting part of the table. When the model is still fairly large, a hand-designed BERT-like stack is competitive. When the budget becomes tiny, allowing the search to mix SepConv, MHA, FFN, identity, and width choices becomes more valuable.

The 5M result is also faster in the paper’s latency proxy: NAS-BERT5 reports 23.6x speedup, while BERT5 reports 20.7x. So the smaller model is not gaining accuracy by secretly becoming slower.

Comparison With Prior Compression Work

The common-size comparison uses NAS-BERT60 against previous 60M to 66M models.

On the dev set:

  • Teacher: 84.4 average.
  • DynaBERT with augmentation: 82.7 average.
  • NAS-BERT: 84.2 average.
  • NAS-BERT with augmentation: 84.8 average.

On the GLUE test set:

  • BERT-of-Theseus: 79.4 average.
  • TinyBERT with augmentation: 80.6 average.
  • NAS-BERT: 81.1 average.
  • NAS-BERT with augmentation: 81.7 average.

This table should be read with some caution. Compression papers often differ in teacher strength, data augmentation, distillation details, and training budgets. The authors explicitly do not compare with MobileBERT in this table because MobileBERT uses a stronger teacher. Still, the table supports the main claim: NAS-BERT60 is competitive with strong BERT compression methods while being produced from an adaptive architecture search framework.

Extremely Small Models

Table 4 compares NAS-BERT5 with AdaBERT in a stricter small-model setting. The paper removes some sophisticated task-specific tricks for fairness: no two-stage distillation and data augmentation for NAS-BERT5, and no data augmentation or probe classifiers for AdaBERT.

The reported numbers:

Task AdaBERT NAS-BERT
QNLI 82.0 / 7.9M 83.9 / 5.0M
MRPC 77.2 / 7.5M 80.0 / 5.0M
RTE 56.7 / 8.6M 67.0 / 5.0M

This is where NAS-BERT’s task-agnostic design looks strongest. AdaBERT searches task-specific students, but NAS-BERT5 uses a single searched architecture family from pre-training and still obtains better scores with fewer parameters in these comparisons.

My reading: the absolute numbers are from the 2021 BERT compression ecosystem, but the qualitative lesson is useful. At very small sizes, architecture matters more than simply scaling down a Transformer template.

Ablations

The ablations answer three questions.

First, does progressive shrinking help? Table 5 says yes:

Setting AVG
without progressive shrinking 83.1
with progressive shrinking 84.2

The gain is +1.1 average GLUE points for NAS-BERT60. The explanation matches Figure 3: without shrinking, each candidate path is under-trained; with shrinking, the remaining paths receive more useful optimization.

Second, should shrinking prune whole architectures or operations? Table 6 favors pruning architectures:

Setting AVG
PS-arch 84.2
PS-op 82.8

This makes sense. Operation-level pruning is too coarse. Removing an operation globally from a layer can damage many potentially good paths. Architecture-level pruning keeps the operation set alive but removes weak paths inside each bin.

Third, how much does distillation matter? Table 7 compares pre-training distillation (PD) and fine-tuning distillation (FD). NAS-BERT60 stays better than the BERT60 baseline in all corresponding settings:

Setting BERT60 AVG NAS-BERT60 AVG
PD + FD 83.5 84.2
PD only 82.9 83.5
FD only 82.6 83.1

The PD only row is especially important. Without fine-tuning-stage distillation, the compressed model is closer to the fully task-agnostic story: search and compression happen during pre-training, and each downstream task only needs normal fine-tuning. NAS-BERT60 still reaches 83.5 average.

SQuAD Results

NAS-BERT is evaluated beyond GLUE on SQuAD v1.1 and v2.0. For the 60M model, the compact comparison is:

Model EM F1
TinyBERT on SQuAD v1.1 79.7 87.5
NAS-BERT on SQuAD v1.1 80.5 88.0
NAS-BERT dagger setting on SQuAD v1.1 81.2 88.4
Model EM F1
TinyBERT on SQuAD v2.0 69.9 73.4
NAS-BERT on SQuAD v2.0 73.2 76.3
NAS-BERT dagger setting on SQuAD v2.0 73.9 77.1

The dagger setting uses a larger training budget for fair comparison with MiniLM’s larger pre-training run. The important point is not only that NAS-BERT beats several baselines; it also transfers from classification-style GLUE evaluation to span extraction QA.

That supports the paper’s task-agnostic claim. The architecture family is not searched for one GLUE task and then overfit to that task.

What The Selected Architectures Look Like

Table 10 is useful because it shows the selected architectures are not just shallow BERTs. The notation is:

  • E: embedding size;
  • M: MHA;
  • F: FFN;
  • S3, S5, S7: SepConv with kernel size 3, 5, or 7;
  • the subscript is the hidden size.

Several observations stand out:

  • Large models such as 60M and 55M still contain many MHA and FFN operations.
  • Middle-size models start mixing in more SepConv while keeping some MHA/FFN.
  • Very small models use mostly SepConv and a few MHA operations.
  • Embedding size also shrinks: the 5M model uses E64, while larger models use E512, E384, E256, or E128.

This is the core architectural result. NAS-BERT is not only choosing “how many BERT layers”. It is changing the composition of the encoder under size constraints.

My Reading Notes

The paper is strongest when read as an amortized deployment method. If I only need one 60M BERT student, a strong distillation method may be simpler. If I need many models under different latency and memory budgets, a trained supernet becomes more attractive.

The most important engineering ideas are:

  • Block-wise distillation turns a huge pre-training search into smaller block searches.
  • Progressive shrinking improves training allocation and search accuracy.
  • Size/latency bins preserve diversity so the supernet does not collapse into one budget range.
  • Lookup-table selection makes final architecture selection cheap enough.
  • Mixed operations let tiny models move away from pure Transformer structure.

The limitations are also clear:

  • The supernet still costs 3 days on 32 P40 GPUs in the paper.
  • Latency lookup is hardware-specific and approximate.
  • The results are for BERT-base-era encoder compression, not decoder-only LLMs.
  • The “task-agnostic” claim has a practical caveat: optional fine-tuning-stage distillation still uses downstream-task teachers, although the architecture search itself is task-agnostic.
  • The search space is manually designed. NAS decides within that space; it does not invent arbitrary efficient Transformer blocks.

Overall, I would place NAS-BERT between AdaBERT and Once-for-All. Compared with AdaBERT, it moves compression earlier and avoids per-task search. Compared with Once-for-All, it brings the elastic-supernet idea into BERT compression and adds block-wise teacher supervision to make the pre-training search feasible.

entry.title: NAS-Bench-301 and the Case for Surrogate NAS Benchmarks
entry.content:
Siems J, Zimmer L, Zela A, Lukasik J, Keuper M, Hutter F. NAS-Bench-301 and the Case for Surrogate Benchmarks for Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2022.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.09777.pdf
  • Code: https://github.com/automl/nasbench301

NAS-Bench-301 attacks the scaling limit of tabular NAS benchmarks. NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 are exact lookup tables, which is excellent for reproducibility, but their spaces are deliberately small. Real NAS spaces such as DARTS or FBNet can contain to architectures. Exhaustive training is impossible.

The paper’s solution is a surrogate NAS benchmark. Instead of evaluating every architecture, it samples a large but finite set of architectures, trains them with a fixed recipe, fits performance predictors, and uses those predictors as cheap benchmark oracles.

The tradeoff is clear: a tabular benchmark is exact but small; a surrogate benchmark is approximate but much larger.

Why Surrogate Benchmarks

The motivating experiment uses NAS-Bench-101 itself. A graph neural network surrogate is trained on subsets of the NAS-Bench-101 table and compared with single tabular observations. Once enough architectures are used for training, the surrogate can beat a one-seed table lookup because it smooths out evaluation noise.

The crossover happens around 21,500 NAS-Bench-101 architectures in the paper’s experiment. That is the conceptual hook: if architecture evaluations are noisy, a learned predictor can sometimes provide a better estimate of expected performance than a single real training run.

This does not mean surrogates are automatically safe. It means they can be useful if their ranking behavior, uncertainty, and optimizer trajectories are validated carefully.

Benchmark Construction

The general pipeline is:

  1. Choose a large search space, such as DARTS or FBNet.
  2. Sample architectures with a mixture of random search and NAS optimizers.
  3. Train and evaluate those architectures with a controlled recipe.
  4. Fit surrogate models from architecture encoding to validation performance.
  5. Validate the surrogates with error metrics, rank metrics, and optimizer trajectory tests.
  6. Release both the benchmark oracle and enough data to audit it.

The main dataset is SNB-DARTS, built on the DARTS search space and CIFAR-10. The paper collects roughly 60k architectures. The sampling mixture includes random search and optimizer traces from methods such as BANANAS, DARTS, PC-DARTS, GDAS, DrNAS, regularized evolution, TPE, differential evolution, and COMBO.

The second dataset is based on FBNet and CIFAR-100. The FBNet space is even larger: the paper describes 22 searchable layers, each with 9 operation choices, giving roughly possible architectures, around .

Surrogate Model Choice

The paper compares several surrogate families, including graph neural networks and gradient-boosted trees. The strongest models include graph isomorphism networks, LightGBM-style boosting, and XGBoost-style boosting.

The authors evaluate both prediction quality and ranking quality. Mean absolute error is useful, but for NAS the ranking is often more important. A surrogate that predicts exact errors poorly but preserves the ordering of architectures can still be useful for optimizer comparison. Conversely, a low average error can hide bad behavior in the high-performing tail.

The noise-modeling table is important because architecture evaluations are stochastic. The paper compares a tabular single-observation baseline with learned surrogate ensembles on 500 architectures evaluated five times.

The GIN surrogate has the best MAE in this table and a much better KL divergence than the boosting models, suggesting better uncertainty modeling. This is one reason the paper does not rely on a single surrogate type. Multiple surrogate families reduce the chance that a NAS optimizer simply exploits one model’s bias.

True Benchmark vs Surrogate Trajectories

The central validation question is not only “does the surrogate predict held-out architectures?” It is “does an optimizer behave similarly on the surrogate as it does on the expensive real benchmark?”

The figure compares trajectories on the real benchmark with trajectories on GIN and XGBoost surrogate benchmarks trained with optimizer data. The broad convergence behavior is preserved. BANANAS improves strongly, random search stagnates, and the surrogate trajectories follow the same qualitative ordering.

The paper then repeats the experiment using surrogates trained only on random-search data.

Random-only training still gives plausible trajectories, but it is weaker in the best-performing regions. That makes sense: random sampling covers the global space, but strong optimizers concentrate in small regions that random search may undersample. A robust surrogate benchmark needs broad coverage and enough data near both good and bad boundaries.

Optimizer Data Distribution

The appendix gives an ECDF of validation error by optimizer.

The distribution is not uniform across optimizers. BANANAS samples many strong architectures; PC-DARTS, DrNAS, differential evolution, GDAS, and regularized evolution occupy different quality regions; TPE is only slightly better than random search in this plot; COMBO and DARTS include many weak architectures. This is useful for training surrogates because different optimizers expose different parts of the space.

The t-SNE visualization makes the coverage issue more concrete.

Random search covers the main cloud, while individual optimizers often explore specific regions. COMBO goes into areas less covered by random search. BANANAS concentrates outside the main cloud. Differential evolution finds a strong central region. This explains why leave-one-optimizer-out validation is necessary: a surrogate trained on one distribution may not extrapolate well to another optimizer’s candidates.

Leave-One-Optimizer-Out

The paper validates this directly with leave-one-optimizer-out experiments. The surrogate is trained without data from one optimizer and then tested on that held-out optimizer’s architectures.

The table shows a pattern that is easy to miss if one only reports average . Leaving out DARTS can hurt badly because DARTS contributes unusual skip-heavy architectures, but sparse Kendall tau can remain reasonably high. In other words, the surrogate may still rank bad DARTS architectures as bad even if it cannot predict exactly how bad they are.

The trajectory plot gives the practical version of the same test.

This is the kind of validation a surrogate benchmark needs. If a new optimizer searches in a region not represented in the training data, the surrogate may be overconfident or wrong. Holding out optimizer families is a stronger test than a random train/test split.

FBNet Surrogate Benchmark

The paper also constructs a surrogate benchmark for the FBNet search space on CIFAR-100. Here the authors use an XGBoost surrogate trained on randomly sampled architectures. The scaling plot shows that more training data reduces MAE and improves rank correlation.

With transferred hyperparameters from the DARTS surrogate, the FBNet surrogate reaches about and sparse Kendall tau around 0.75 on the test set. That is not perfect, but it is enough to reproduce broad optimizer trajectories.

This part of the paper is important because it argues that surrogate NAS benchmarks are not a one-off trick for DARTS. The same methodology can be applied to a different, much larger search space, as long as the data collection and validation protocol are careful.

Failure Cases and Boundary Checks

The paper does not pretend that surrogates are exact. It studies a constrained DARTS failure case where DARTS can diverge toward cells with only skip connections.

The surrogate can capture the broad divergent trajectory, especially when the relevant data is included. But uncertainty grows when the surrogate is asked to extrapolate into regions it has not seen. This is the main operational risk of surrogate benchmarks: a NAS method can optimize the benchmark model rather than the real architecture performance.

The parameter-free operation analysis is another useful boundary test.

The ground truth and surrogate predictions both show that too many parameter-free operations, especially skip connections, lead to worse validation error. This is exactly the kind of degenerate region that differentiable NAS methods can exploit if the benchmark or search objective is not robust.

The one-shot optimizer trajectory plot checks whether the surrogate can monitor methods such as DARTS, PC-DARTS, and GDAS through the search process.

The curves are not a perfect replacement for real training, but they are informative enough to diagnose behavior at much lower cost.

How I Would Use It

For benchmarking a new NAS method, I would use NAS-Bench-301 differently from a tabular benchmark:

  1. Report both GIN and XGBoost surrogate results when possible.
  2. Use validation performance during search and reserve final real training checks for selected candidates.
  3. Track uncertainty or at least avoid making claims from a single surrogate prediction.
  4. Compare against random search, regularized evolution, BANANAS, and simple Bayesian optimization baselines.
  5. Inspect whether the method visits regions covered by the surrogate training data.
  6. Run a small number of real evaluations for final architectures if the claim is about actual model quality.
  7. Treat surprising superhuman surrogate scores as suspicious until verified.

The last point is the most important. A surrogate benchmark is a model. It can be exploited.

Limitations

NAS-Bench-301 expands the search space dramatically, but it introduces new limitations:

  • surrogate predictions are approximate;
  • training data coverage affects every conclusion;
  • strong optimizers can search out-of-distribution regions;
  • random train/test splits can overestimate reliability;
  • one surrogate family can bias the benchmark;
  • final deployment claims still need real training and hardware checks.

These limitations are not a reason to avoid the benchmark. They define the right level of evidence. NAS-Bench-301 is excellent for comparing optimizer behavior in a large search space. It is not a final oracle for architecture quality.

Takeaway

NAS-Bench-301 is the bridge between exact tabular NAS benchmarks and expensive real architecture search. It keeps the reproducibility benefit of benchmarks while moving into search spaces that are orders of magnitude larger than NAS-Bench-101 or NAS-Bench-201. The price is approximation, so the benchmark must be used with surrogate validation, optimizer holdout tests, and real checks for final claims.

entry.title: Learning Transferable Architectures for Scalable Image Recognition
entry.content:
Paper

NASNet is the paper that turns the expensive NAS-RL idea into a more transferable design pattern. Instead of searching a whole ImageNet-scale network directly, it searches for small convolutional cells on CIFAR-10, then stacks those cells to build larger ImageNet models.

The important contribution is the search space. Once the cell is found, the number of cell repeats and filter counts can be scaled without changing the cell topology.

Motivation

The original NAS-RL paper could discover good architectures, but searching directly over a large full network is expensive. NASNet asks a more reusable question:

Can we search for a small building block on CIFAR-10 and transfer that block to ImageNet?

The answer depends on constraining the search space. If the controller searches arbitrary whole networks, transfer is fragile. If it searches repeated motifs, the learned component can be reused at different depths, resolutions, and compute budgets.

Contribution

The paper contributes:

  1. The NASNet search space: architectures are built from repeated Normal Cells and Reduction Cells.
  2. A transfer recipe: search the cell on CIFAR-10, then stack it for ImageNet.
  3. ScheduledDropPath, where the probability of dropping a path increases during training.
  4. Strong results on CIFAR-10, ImageNet classification, and COCO detection with NASNet features.

The headline numbers:

Task Result
CIFAR-10 2.40% error
ImageNet 82.7% top-1 / 96.2% top-5
ImageNet mobile-scale setting 74.0% top-1
COCO detection 43.1% mAP test-dev

Methodology

Normal and reduction cells

NASNet fixes the macro layout and searches the repeated cell structure. There are two cell types:

  • Normal Cell: keeps the feature map resolution.
  • Reduction Cell: reduces spatial resolution by using stride-2 operations.

For CIFAR-10, cells are stacked between a few reduction points. For ImageNet, the image is larger, so the network uses more reduction stages. The topology of each cell is learned; the number of repeats and initial filters are scaling knobs.

Controller block

Each cell is built from blocks. In the paper’s main NASNet-A search, . For each block, the controller predicts five decisions:

  1. Select the first hidden state.
  2. Select the second hidden state.
  3. Select an operation for the first hidden state.
  4. Select an operation for the second hidden state.
  5. Select how to combine the two outputs.

The operation set includes identity, pooling, standard convolution, factorized convolution, dilated convolution, and depthwise-separable convolution. At the end of the cell, unused hidden states are concatenated to form the output.

NASNet-A cell

The found NASNet-A cells contain many separable convolutions and learned skip-style connections. There are no manually inserted residual links between cells; the searched cell already learns its own internal connectivity.

ScheduledDropPath

The authors found ordinary DropPath was not enough. ScheduledDropPath drops paths in a cell with a probability that increases linearly over training. This is a small but practical detail: without strong regularization, these searched cells can overfit.

Results

CIFAR-10

Model Params Error
NAS v3 + more filters 37.4M 3.65%
NASNet-A (6 @ 768) 3.3M 3.41%
NASNet-A (6 @ 768) + cutout 3.3M 2.65%
NASNet-A (7 @ 2304) + cutout 27.6M 2.40%
NASNet-C (4 @ 640) 3.1M 3.59%

The large NASNet-A with cutout reaches 2.40% error averaged across 5 runs, and the best single run reported in the paper is 2.19%.

ImageNet transfer

The key claim is transfer: the cells are searched on CIFAR-10, then all ImageNet models are trained from scratch with those cells.

Model Params Mult-Adds Top-1
Inception ResNet V2 55.8M 13.2B 80.1
NASNet-A (7 @ 1920) 22.6M 4.93B 80.8
SENet 145.8M 42.3B 82.7
NASNet-A (6 @ 4032) 88.9M 23.8B 82.7

NASNet-A reaches 82.7% top-1 and 96.2% top-5 on ImageNet with fewer mult-adds than SENet in the comparison table.

Smaller compute setting

For the <1.5B mult-add regime, the paper reports:

Model Params Mult-Adds Top-1
MobileNet-224 4.2M 569M 70.6
ShuffleNet (2x) ~5M 524M 70.9
NASNet-A (4 @ 1056) 5.3M 564M 74.0

This is one reason NASNet mattered: the same cell family could scale down and still beat mobile-oriented baselines from that period.

Detection transfer

The paper also plugs NASNet-A ImageNet features into Faster R-CNN on COCO. The best reported test-dev mAP is 43.1%, which supports the claim that the learned features transfer beyond classification.

Takeaway

NASNet’s main lesson is that the search space can matter more than the controller. By forcing architectures to be made of reusable cells, the paper makes search results transferable across scale.

There are still limitations. The search is expensive, and the method assumes a hand-designed macro skeleton with normal/reduction cell placement. But the cell-based formulation became the template for many later NAS papers because it turns an architecture into something you can scale, compare, and reuse.

entry.title: NATS-Bench: Benchmarking NAS Topology and Size
OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated LLM Quantization
entry.content:
Shao W, Chen M, Zhang Z, Xu P, Zhao L, Li Z, Zhang K, Gao P, Qiao Y, Luo P. OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated Quantization for Large Language Models. ICLR 2024.

  • Paper: arXiv PDF
  • Code: OpenGVLab/OmniQuant
  • Topic: post-training quantization, learnable clipping, equivalent transformation, low-bit LLM deployment

OmniQuant is a useful paper because it sits between lightweight PTQ and expensive QAT. It does not update the full-precision model weights like quantization-aware training. It also does not rely only on handcrafted calibration rules like plain MinMax, SmoothQuant-style fixed migration strength, or grid-searched scaling. The main idea is narrower and more practical: freeze the original LLM weights, add a small set of learnable quantization parameters, optimize those parameters block by block on calibration samples, then fold the learned parameters away so the exported model has no extra runtime modules.

That design matters most in the hard cases. W4A16 is already reachable by strong weight-only methods such as GPTQ and AWQ. W8A8 is the target of SmoothQuant. OmniQuant tries to cover a wider set of formats, especially W2A16 and W4A4, where ordinary PTQ collapses. The method has two knobs:

  • Learnable Weight Clipping, or LWC, learns relative clipping strengths for weights.
  • Learnable Equivalent Transformation, or LET, learns scale/shift transformations that move activation quantization difficulty into weights while preserving the floating-point function before quantization.

The paper’s name is a little grand, but the technical point is concrete. “Omni” means the same calibration framework is used across weight-only, weight-activation, and attention/KV-related quantization positions.

One-Picture Summary

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. OmniQuant tries to keep PTQ-level calibration cost while getting much closer to QAT-quality low-bit results.

Figure 1 is the best starting point. The left panel compares three points for LLaMA-7B W4A4:

Method Calibration data Time Average accuracy
SmoothQuant 128 samples 10 min 38.41%
LLM-QAT 100k samples 90 h 46.43%
OmniQuant 128 samples 1.6 h 52.65%

The two right panels show why the paper focuses on low bit widths. In the weight-only curve, GPTQ is reasonable at W4A16 and W3A16, then breaks badly at W2A16. In the weight-activation curve, SmoothQuant is fine around W8A8/W6A6 but degrades sharply at W4A4. OmniQuant’s claim is not that every quantization setting becomes lossless. The claim is that optimizing a small number of calibration parameters gives much better low-bit behavior than fixed rules, while staying far cheaper than QAT.

Quantization Target

The notation WbAa means:

So:

Format Meaning Typical deployment reading
W4A16 4-bit weights, FP16/BF16 activations weight-only compression
W3A16 3-bit weights, FP16/BF16 activations more aggressive weight-only compression
W2A16 2-bit weights, FP16/BF16 activations extreme weight-only compression
W8A8 8-bit weights and activations dense INT8 inference target
W6A6 6-bit weights and activations low-bit activation quantization
W4A4 4-bit weights and activations very hard low-bit compute target

For weight-only quantization, reducing the weight bit width attacks model memory and weight bandwidth. The approximate raw weight storage ratio against FP16 is:

ignoring scale, zero-point, group metadata, and packing overhead. This is why W4A16 is attractive: a nominal 4x weight-size reduction is possible before metadata. W2A16 is even more attractive on paper, but the accuracy loss is usually severe.

For weight-activation quantization, the goal is broader. If both weights and activations are low-bit, the matrix multiplication itself can move toward low-bit kernels. This is also where outliers are most damaging. LLM activations often have large channel-wise outliers, and naive per-token activation quantization must choose a scale large enough to cover them, wasting resolution on ordinary values.

A generic affine uniform quantizer can be written as:

The hard part is not writing this formula. The hard part is choosing the scale, zero point, clipping range, and equivalent transformations so that the quantized block still behaves like the original block on real activations.

PTQ, QAT, And Where OmniQuant Fits

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. The paper positions OmniQuant as learning a small set of quantization parameters with 128 calibration samples on a single A100-40G.

The practical tension is:

Approach What is optimized Cost Low-bit behavior
Plain PTQ fixed quantization parameters low often fails at W2A16/W4A4
Heuristic PTQ scales/clips searched by proxies low to medium better, but limited by proxy quality
QAT all model weights under quantization simulation very high strong but expensive
OmniQuant only quantization parameters medium PTQ-like strong in low-bit settings

OmniQuant’s calibration setup in the paper is intentionally small: 128 randomly selected 2048-token segments from WikiText2, batch size 1, AdamW, and block-wise optimization. The original FP weights are frozen. The learned parameters are:

The central implementation question is whether these parameters stay in the runtime graph. OmniQuant’s answer is no: clipping affects the final quantized weights, and equivalent transformations are folded into adjacent normalization or linear layers. If these parameters remained as extra floating-point operations during serving, the method would be much less attractive.

Block-Wise Reconstruction Objective

OmniQuant calibrates one transformer block at a time. For a block mapping , full-precision weights , and calibration activations , the paper writes the optimization objective as:

I read this as a local reconstruction loss. The full-precision block output is the teacher, and the quantized block output is the student:

The important engineering choice is the block boundary. Optimizing an entire 7B-70B model with differentiable quantization would be too large. Optimizing only a layer or a small operator can miss error propagation across residual paths, attention, and MLP sublayers. A transformer block is a reasonable middle point: large enough to see the effect of several quantized operators, small enough to calibrate sequentially.

The gradient is applied to quantization parameters, not to the original pretrained weights:

As usual for differentiable quantization, the rounding operation itself needs a straight-through-style gradient in practice. The paper’s contribution is not a new rounding estimator; it is the choice of learnable parameters and where they are inserted.

Learnable Weight Clipping

Weight quantization fails when a few extreme values force the quantization range to become too wide. MinMax quantization uses the observed min and max as the clipping range. OmniQuant keeps the MinMax structure but learns relative clipping strengths for the upper and lower bounds.

The LWC quantizer is:

Here:

Symbol Meaning
target bit width
original full-precision weights
quantized integer weights
normalization factor / scale
zero point
learnable upper clipping strength
learnable lower clipping strength

The constraints are:

The paper instantiates them through a sigmoid:

So the trainable variables can be unconstrained, while the actual clipping strengths stay in . If and , LWC reduces to the ordinary MinMax range. If either value becomes smaller, the effective range shrinks and extreme weights are clipped.

The dequantized weight can be read as:

This design is more stable than directly learning absolute clipping thresholds, because the threshold is parameterized relative to the current weight range. That matters when LET changes the equivalent weight distribution during calibration.

Learnable Equivalent Transformation

LWC helps weights. LET targets activations. The core observation is the same one used by SmoothQuant: activation outliers can be made smaller by an equivalent transformation that moves scale into weights. OmniQuant makes the transformation learnable and extends it beyond ordinary linear layers.

For a linear layer:

OmniQuant inserts channel-wise shifting and scaling:

where:

The operators and are elementwise division and multiplication with channel-wise broadcast. The equality is exact in floating point:

After transformation, quantization is applied to the transformed activation and weight:

The intuition is simple:

  • divide hard activation channels by so they become easier to quantize;
  • multiply the corresponding weight channels by so the floating-point function is unchanged;
  • let LWC handle the harder transformed weight distribution;
  • learn and through block reconstruction, instead of choosing them only by a fixed heuristic.

SmoothQuant uses a scale initialized from activation and weight maxima. A common form is:

where is a channel index and controls how much difficulty moves from activations to weights. OmniQuant uses SmoothQuant-style scaling as an initialization, but then optimizes the equivalent parameters with the block-wise loss.

LET Inside Attention

The attention score matrix is:

OmniQuant applies an equivalent transformation to the affinity multiplication:

Define:

The quantized attention-affinity computation becomes:

The paper notes that the scale factors in and can be absorbed into the query and key projection weights. The explicit transformation for is omitted because the inverse transformation associated with the output projection already changes the value distribution.

This attention LET is one of the reasons the method is broader than a direct SmoothQuant clone. It touches the Q/K path and therefore relates to the difficulty of quantizing attention computation and KV-cache-related tensors.

Transformer Block Placement

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Red modules are learnable during calibration, blue snowflake markers are fixed, and pink modules can be eliminated after quantization.

The placement diagram is dense, but it is the most useful implementation figure in the paper. The learnable pieces appear around:

  • weight clipping before weight quantization;
  • normalization-to-projection transformations;
  • Q/K transformations before attention affinity;
  • value/output projection transformations;
  • MLP transformations around fc1.

The paper explicitly avoids LET on the second FFN linear layer. Its explanation is that the activation after the nonlinear layer is sparse, which can make LET gradients unstable there. That is a good reminder that equivalent transformations are not free to place everywhere. They need numerically stable statistics and a neighboring operation where the transform can be folded.

Calibration Algorithm

Algorithm cropped from the paper PDF. OmniQuant runs a full-precision stream and a quantized stream through blocks, optimizing LWC/LET parameters for each block before moving on.

The algorithm keeps two activation streams:

For each transformer block :

  1. Run the full-precision block to update .
  2. Initialize LWC parameters and LET parameters .
  3. For several epochs, transform the block, quantize it, run it on , and minimize .
  4. Fold the learned LET parameters and quantize the block with LWC.
  5. Run the final quantized block to update for the next block.

A simplified pseudocode view:

This sequential design is important because errors accumulate. If every block were calibrated only against the original full-precision input distribution, later blocks would see a cleaner distribution than they will see at inference time. By updating after each quantized block, the next block calibrates on the actual quantized prefix distribution.

Main Weight-Only Results

Table cropped from the paper PDF. WikiText2 perplexity for LLaMA-1 and LLaMA-2 weight-only quantization.

Table 1 is the most important weight-only result. The easy setting is W4A16, where GPTQ/AWQ/RTN are already close to FP16. The interesting setting is W2A16.

Some representative rows:

Setting Model GPTQ PPL AWQ PPL OmniQuant PPL
W2A16 LLaMA-1-13B 5.5e3 - 13.21
W2A16 LLaMA-1-30B 499.75 - 8.71
W2A16 LLaMA-2-70B 77.95 - 7.81
W2A16g128 LLaMA-1-13B 15.60 2.8e5 7.93
W3A16 LLaMA-1-13B 6.76 7.45 5.68
W4A16g128 LLaMA-2-70B 3.42 - 3.40

The pattern is:

  • At W4A16, the gap is small because the format is not extremely hard.
  • At W3A16, OmniQuant is consistently strong but the baseline methods remain usable.
  • At W2A16, the learned clipping becomes crucial; GPTQ and AWQ can collapse depending on model and grouping, while OmniQuant keeps perplexity in a usable range.

I would not read this table as “OmniQuant replaces GPTQ everywhere.” For ordinary W4A16 deployment with mature kernels, GPTQ/AWQ may still be simpler. The reason to care about OmniQuant is the lower-bit frontier and the fact that the same calibration machinery also supports weight-activation quantization.

Weight-Activation Results

Table cropped from the paper PDF. Six zero-shot task accuracy for LLaMA W6A6 and W4A4 quantization.

W4A4 is the table I care about most. Once activations are also 4-bit, activation outliers become unavoidable. SmoothQuant helps at W8A8, but W4A4 is much harsher.

For average zero-shot accuracy:

Model SmoothQuant W4A4 OS+ W4A4 OmniQuant W4A4 FP16
LLaMA-1-7B 38.41 48.43 52.65 64.09
LLaMA-1-13B 49.36 49.86 54.37 66.33
LLaMA-1-30B 44.83 52.62 56.63 67.44
LLaMA-1-65B 47.71 52.52 59.22 71.04

The 7B row also includes LLM-QAT:

Method LLaMA-1-7B W4A4 average accuracy
SmoothQuant 38.41
LLM-QAT 41.27
LLM-QAT + SmoothQuant 46.43
OS+ 48.43
OmniQuant 52.65

This is the headline result: with 128 calibration samples and 1.6 hours for LLaMA-7B, OmniQuant beats the listed QAT baseline in that W4A4 comparison. The reason is not that tiny PTQ optimization is more expressive than full QAT in general. It is that optimizing the right local quantization parameters can be a better use of calibration budget than doing broad weight updates under a limited QAT setup.

W6A6 is less dramatic. It is usually close to FP16 and SmoothQuant/OS+ are already reasonable. Again, OmniQuant is most interesting where handcrafted parameters stop being enough.

Instruction-Tuned Models

Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Vicuna-Bench pairwise comparison for LLaMA-2-chat W3A16g128.

The instruction-tuned experiment is useful because perplexity is not the whole story. On Vicuna-Bench, the authors compare RTN, AWQ, and OmniQuant with GPT-4 judging over both answer orders.

For LLaMA-2-7B-chat:

  • AWQ vs RTN: 69.4% win rate for AWQ.
  • OmniQuant vs RTN: 80.3% win rate for OmniQuant.
  • OmniQuant vs AWQ: 50.0% win rate.

For LLaMA-2-13B-chat:

  • AWQ vs RTN: 46.6% win rate for AWQ.
  • OmniQuant vs RTN: 54.4% win rate for OmniQuant.
  • OmniQuant vs AWQ: 56.2% win rate for OmniQuant.

The result is not an overwhelming sweep, but it supports the claim that the calibration is not only overfitting WikiText2 perplexity. For instruction-tuned models, OmniQuant remains competitive or better in a pairwise chat evaluation.

Deployment Result

Table cropped from the paper PDF. Weight-only quantized LLaMA models deployed through MLC-LLM on an NVIDIA A100-80G.

The deployment table matters because a quantization method can look good in perplexity and still be awkward to serve. OmniQuant’s learned parameters are designed to be folded, so weight-only models can be exported into existing low-bit deployment stacks.

The paper reports memory and generation speed through MLC-LLM. For LLaMA-7B:

Setting Weight memory Running memory token/s
FP 12.6G 14.4G 69.2
W4A16g128 3.8G 5.7G 134.2
W3A16g128 3.2G 5.1G 83.4
W2A16g128 2.2G 4.1G 83.9

For LLaMA-65B, the FP model is OOM under the measured setup, while quantized variants run:

Setting Weight memory Running memory token/s
W4A16g128 33.0G 41.0G 24.3
W3A16g128 27.0G 35.1G 15.2
W2A16g128 18.0G 25.6G 24.8

The speed numbers are not monotonic with bit width because kernel support matters. INT3/INT2 support was weaker in the reported MLC-LLM stack. This is a deployment lesson: lower bits reduce memory, but latency depends on packing, dequantization, kernel quality, and hardware support.

The paper only demonstrates deployment for weight-only quantization. It explicitly notes that W4A4 and W6A6 lacked out-of-the-box hardware support in that study. So OmniQuant’s W4A4 accuracy result should be separated from actual production W4A4 serving speed.

Why LWC And LET Need Each Other

Table cropped from the appendix. LET and LWC work best when optimized together under the same differentiable block-wise framework.

Table A2 is one of the most useful ablations:

LLaMA-7B W4A4 method Average PPL Average accuracy
SmoothQuant 28.78 38.41
LET 16.97 48.83
LET + grid-searched weight clipping 15.82 49.59
SmoothQuant + LWC 15.80 50.15
LET + LWC 12.87 52.65

The point is not simply “clipping helps” and “equivalent transformation helps.” LET changes the activation and equivalent weight distributions. LWC then has to clip the transformed weights, not the original weights. If clipping is found by a separate grid search or if the equivalent transform is fixed, the two knobs are not co-adapted.

This is the most convincing argument for OmniQuant’s differentiable setup. It is not learning many parameters, but it is learning coupled parameters.

Component Ablation

Table cropped from the appendix. Removing LET is catastrophic for W4A4; removing LWC is also harmful.

The component ablation is blunt:

Model / setting LWC+LET without LWC without LET without both
LLaMA-13B W4A4 10.87 20.75 5.4e3 1.8e3
LLaMA-13B W3A16 5.65 7.65 5.68 10.68
OPT-13B W4A4 11.65 15.23 7.8e3 7.8e5
OPT-13B W3A16 10.87 12.98 11.29 4.6e3

For W4A4, removing LET causes a collapse because activation quantization remains unsolved. For W3A16 weight-only quantization, LET is less important for LLaMA, which is why the paper often uses only LWC for LLaMA weight-only settings to save time. OPT is more sensitive to LET even in weight-only W3A16.

This is a good practical rule:

  • If activations are quantized, LET is not optional.
  • If only weights are quantized, LWC is the core component, and LET may or may not pay for itself depending on the model family.

LET Design Choices

Tables cropped from the appendix. Channel-wise shifting, attention transformation, and LET placement each affect W4A4 quality.

Table A4 compares the two additions beyond a basic scale-only linear transformation:

Method LLaMA-13B W4A4 PPL OPT-13B W4A4 PPL
LWC + LET 10.87 11.65
without shifting 11.47 13.64
without attention LET 11.34 11.79

Channel-wise shifting helps, especially on OPT-13B W4A4. Attention LET helps too, though less dramatically in this table. That matches the paper’s explanation that the largest outliers often appear after normalization layers, so linear-layer LET carries most of the gain.

Table A5 removes LET at different positions in LLaMA-7B W4A4:

Removed LET position Average PPL Average accuracy
none 12.87 52.65
[ln1, (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj)] 19.87 46.79
[v_proj, out_proj] 13.03 51.68
[Q,K] 13.34 51.47
[ln2, fc1] 14.47 51.04

The most sensitive placement is the transform after the first LayerNorm and before Q/K/V projections. This is consistent with the activation-outlier story: if a normalization output has severe channel outliers, every downstream projection inherits the quantization problem.

Calibration Time

Table cropped from the appendix. Most configurations improve quickly; W2A16 needs more epochs.

The training-time ablation uses LLaMA-7B and reports WikiText2 perplexity:

Epochs W4A16 W3A16 W2A16 W6A6 W4A4
0 6.29 24.04 1.1e5 6.16 33.93
10 5.87 6.51 27.49 5.96 12.04
20 5.85 6.49 17.46 5.95 11.26
40 5.86 6.47 15.47 5.95 11.23
80 - - 14.77 - -

The fast convergence is important. W4A4 drops from 33.93 to 12.04 in 10 epochs, then only improves modestly. W2A16 is harder and keeps benefiting from longer calibration. This is exactly what I would expect: 2-bit weight quantization leaves so little representational room that the clipping parameters need more optimization.

The main paper uses 20 epochs for most settings and a longer schedule for W2A16. The deployment implication is that calibration cost is not zero, but it is still in the PTQ family rather than QAT.

What LWC Learns

Figure cropped from the appendix. Learned clipping strengths differ by bit width and grouping.

The learned clipping-scale visualization is a useful sanity check. LWC is not always clipping aggressively. In grouped quantization, many groups have clipping strengths close to 1, meaning little clipping. At lower bit widths, the distribution shifts toward more clipping because the quantizer has fewer representable values.

This fits the role of LWC. The method is not trying to erase all outliers. It is deciding where the quantization range should stop so that the block output is preserved on calibration data.

The appendix also reports that LWC reduces both weight distance and final activation distance. That second part matters more than the first. A small weight reconstruction error is not enough if it produces a large downstream activation error. OmniQuant’s block-wise loss directly sees that downstream effect.

What LET Changes

Figure cropped from the appendix. LET makes activation channels more homogeneous than the original distribution and the SmoothQuant-transformed distribution.

Figure A2 shows the activation-outlier story visually. Original activations have a few channels with much larger magnitude. SmoothQuant reduces the largest outliers, but the transformed distribution still has visible channel imbalance. LET reduces the disparity further because it is optimized under the block reconstruction objective rather than chosen by a fixed migration rule.

This is the activation-side reason W4A4 improves. If the activation quantizer must cover a few huge channels, ordinary channels lose resolution. LET reshapes the distribution before quantization, and LWC absorbs the corresponding weight-side difficulty.

Block-Wise Error

Figure cropped from the appendix. Gradient-based calibration produces lower block-wise error than grid-search-based methods in the reported settings.

Figure A3 compares block-wise quantization error against AWQ-style or OS+-style grid-search baselines. The curves make the main optimization argument concrete: a handcrafted proxy can find a useful scale, but directly optimizing block reconstruction can reduce the error more consistently across blocks.

This does not mean gradient-based PTQ is automatically better for every model. It means the optimization target is better aligned with what we care about: preserving the block’s actual output on representative activations.

Bit-Level Scaling Law

Figure cropped from the appendix. With stronger PTQ, 3-bit quantization can approach the tradeoff usually associated with 4-bit quantization.

The bit-level scaling plot is a more speculative but interesting result. Earlier empirical work often argues that 4-bit quantization is a good universal balance between total model bits and accuracy. OmniQuant’s appendix suggests that, with better calibration, 3-bit models can approach a similar tradeoff for perplexity.

I would read this cautiously. It depends on the quantizer, metadata, kernels, and model family. A 3-bit checkpoint with poor kernel support may be slower than a 4-bit checkpoint. Still, the result is important because it says the “4-bit is the natural floor” intuition is partly a method limitation, not only a model property.

LWC Versus PACT And LSQ

Table cropped from the appendix. LWC is compared against MinMax, PACT, and LSQ inside the same OmniQuant-style pipeline.

The paper compares LWC with older learnable clipping methods:

Method W3A16 PPL W4A4 PPL
MinMax 25.73 14.49
PACT 6.95 18.25
LSQ 6.63 15.03
LWC 6.47 11.26

PACT and LSQ were originally designed in a QAT context. They can help weight-only quantization, but W4A4 is different because LET changes the equivalent weight distribution during calibration. LWC’s relative clipping parameterization adapts better to that changing distribution.

Figure cropped from the appendix. LWC tracks changing weight ranges during training more stably than absolute-threshold clipping methods.

Figure A5 reinforces the same point. If the effective weight range changes during LET optimization, an absolute clipping threshold can become stale. Relative clipping strengths are a better parameterization when the scale of the transformed weights is moving.

Relation To Other LLM Quantization Methods

Table cropped from the appendix. OmniQuant differs from SmoothQuant/AWQ/OS+ by learning scale-and-shift transformations and applying them to both linear layers and attention.

Method Main target Calibration signal Runtime shape
LLM.int8() INT8 matmul with outlier rescue activation outlier detection INT8 path plus FP16 outlier path
SmoothQuant W8A8 activation/weight maxima, fixed smoothing strength dense INT8-friendly path
GPTQ W3A16/W4A16 second-order layer reconstruction weight-only low-bit kernels
AWQ W4A16 activation-aware salient weight protection weight-only low-bit kernels
OmniQuant W2A16/W3A16/W4A16/W6A6/W4A4 gradient-optimized block reconstruction over LWC/LET parameters folded quantized model

The closest conceptual relatives are SmoothQuant and AWQ:

  • Like SmoothQuant, OmniQuant uses equivalent transformations to migrate activation difficulty into weights.
  • Like AWQ, OmniQuant cares about activation-aware weight quantization and avoids updating the full original model.
  • Unlike both, OmniQuant directly optimizes the calibration parameters with gradients under a block-wise reconstruction loss.

Compared with GPTQ, OmniQuant is less about Hessian-based rounding compensation and more about making the quantization range and transformed distributions easier before quantization. They attack different parts of the PTQ problem.

Practical Reproduction Notes

If I were reproducing OmniQuant, I would not start with all settings at once. I would stage it like this:

  1. Implement LWC only for one linear layer and verify the LWC formula against MinMax when .
  2. Calibrate one transformer block in W4A16 or W3A16 and confirm the block reconstruction loss decreases.
  3. Add LET for a linear layer and verify exact floating-point equivalence before quantization:

  1. Check that folding removes the runtime transformation. The exported graph should not contain extra LET modules.
  2. Move from W4A16 to W3A16, then W2A16. Do not debug W2A16 first.
  3. Add activation quantization and test W6A6 before W4A4.
  4. Track both layer/block reconstruction and end metrics. A lower local loss is useful only if perplexity and task accuracy follow.

The calibration data also deserves attention. The paper uses 128 2048-token WikiText2 segments. That is enough for the reported setting, but deployment prompts may have different activation statistics. For a production model, I would calibrate on representative prompts and hold out a similar set to detect overfitting of the learned quantization parameters.

Takeaway

OmniQuant is best read as differentiable PTQ for LLMs. It keeps the original weights frozen, learns only a small set of quantization parameters, and calibrates them block by block. LWC learns how much weight range to clip. LET learns how to reshape activation distributions through equivalent transformations. Together, they make difficult formats such as W2A16 and W4A4 much more stable than fixed PTQ rules.

The caveat is systems support. Weight-only OmniQuant can be deployed through existing low-bit stacks after folding. W4A4 accuracy is promising, but real W4A4 serving also needs mature kernels and hardware support. In that sense, the paper is both a quantization-method paper and a reminder that quantization quality and quantized inference are related but separate engineering problems.
