PowerInfer: Fast LLM Serving on a Consumer GPU
entry.content:
Song et al. PowerInfer: Fast Large Language Model Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU. SOSP 2024.

Paper: PowerInfer: Fast Large Language Model Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU

PowerInfer is a local LLM serving paper. It is not trying to beat datacenter serving systems under large batches. It asks a narrower and very practical question:

If the model is too large for a single consumer GPU, can we use CPU memory without making every token wait on CPU-GPU weight transfer?

The paper’s answer is to exploit activation locality. A small subset of MLP neurons is activated frequently across inputs. PowerInfer treats these as hot neurons and keeps them on the GPU. The remaining cold neurons stay in CPU memory and are computed on the CPU only when an online predictor says they are needed.

This is different from quantization and different from layer-level offloading. Quantization shrinks all weights. Layer offloading moves whole Transformer layers between GPU and CPU. PowerInfer instead works at neuron granularity inside layers.

The Local Serving Problem

Consumer GPUs have much less memory than datacenter GPUs. An RTX 4090 has 24 GB of VRAM. That is large for games, but not large enough for many FP16 LLMs, and still tight for some quantized large models once runtime buffers are included.

The naive offloading solution is simple: keep part of the model in CPU memory and move weights to GPU when needed. The problem is that autoregressive decoding runs the full model for every generated token. If a token step repeatedly transfers large weights over PCIe, latency becomes dominated by data movement.

PowerInfer’s key claim is that LLM inference has enough neuron-level locality to use the GPU as a hot-neuron cache and the CPU as a cold-neuron executor.

What Is A Neuron Here?

The paper defines a neuron as a row or column in a weight matrix. In an MLP block, the simplified shape is:

For ReLU-style activations, many entries of are zero or near-zero for a given token. If an intermediate activation entry is inactive, the corresponding work in the following projection can be skipped.

Figure 1 shows this at the MLP level. The activation function gates FC1 outputs, and only the activated rows or columns contribute to the FC2 computation.

The paper reports substantial MLP sparsity even outside pure ReLU models.

Table 1 is the quick motivation:

Model Activation Reported MLP sparsity
OPT-30B ReLU 97%
LLaMA2-13B SwiGLU 43%
Yi-34B SwiGLU 53%

For ReLU-based models, sparsity means zero activation. For SwiGLU-based models, the paper measures the proportion of neurons that can be dynamically pruned with less than 1% perplexity impact. That distinction matters: PowerInfer is strongest on ReLU-family models, but the authors also test lower-sparsity non-ReLU settings.

Why Existing Offloading Is Slow

The paper separates two common approaches.

GPU-centric offloading stores overflow parameters in CPU memory, then transfers needed weights to GPU at runtime. This can make a large model fit, but every token can pay PCIe transfer cost.

Hybrid CPU-GPU offloading splits layers between CPU and GPU. This reduces transfer volume, but it gives the CPU too much compute when the GPU cannot hold enough of the model.

Figure 3 shows the failure on OPT-30B with an RTX 4090. FlexGen and DejaVu with unified memory are dominated by CPU-GPU movement. The paper states that more than 99.5% of FlexGen processing time is spent transferring LLM weights from CPU to GPU. The llama.cpp-style hybrid path avoids much of that transfer, but for OPT-30B on a 24 GB 4090 only about 37% of the model is on GPU, and the CPU ends up handling most of the computation time.

PowerInfer is trying to get the best of both:

  • Keep the most frequently useful weights in GPU memory.
  • Avoid moving cold weights to GPU for each token.
  • Compute cold activated neurons directly on CPU.
  • Skip inactive neurons entirely.

Insight 1: Power-Law Activation

The central observation is not only “activations are sparse.” It is that activation frequency is highly skewed.

Figure 4 profiles about 1M tokens from Wikipedia. In one MLP block, the paper reports that 26% of OPT-30B neurons, 43% of LLaMA2-ReGLU-70B neurons, and 69% of LLaMA2-SwiGLU-70B neurons account for 80% of activations. Across the entire model, the corresponding proportions are 17%, 26%, and 75%.

This is the hot/cold split:

Group Meaning Placement intuition
Hot neurons Frequently activated across many inputs Keep on GPU
Cold neurons Input-dependent and less frequently activated Keep on CPU, compute only when predicted active

The split is useful only if it is stable across tasks. The paper checks that too.

Figure 5 shows OPT-30B activation frequency by layer and across tasks. The paper reports more than 90% overlap in the top 20% most frequently activated neurons across the profiled downstream domains. That is the key evidence behind the offline placement step. If the hot set changed completely between tasks, static placement would be fragile.

Insight 2: CPU Computation Can Beat Weight Transfer

If a cold activated neuron lives in CPU memory, there are two options:

  1. Load the neuron’s weights to GPU and compute there.
  2. Compute the neuron directly on CPU and transfer only the result.

For small local-serving batches, PowerInfer chooses the second path.

Figure 6 compares load-then-execute with direct CPU execution for OPT-30B. For batch sizes under 32, direct CPU computation is faster than transferring those weights to the RTX 4090 and computing on GPU. This is the second reason the design is neuron-level rather than layer-level: the CPU should not own whole layers, but it can handle a small set of cold activated neurons.

System Overview

PowerInfer has an offline part and an online part.

The offline part profiles activation statistics, classifies neurons as hot or cold, trains adaptive activation predictors, and solves a placement problem under GPU memory and bandwidth constraints. The online part loads the selected hot neurons on GPU, keeps cold neurons on CPU, predicts active neurons per input, and runs GPU and CPU work concurrently.

The high-level workflow is:

The model is still the same model. PowerInfer is changing the runtime path, not replacing the LLM with a smaller model.

Single-Layer Execution

The single-layer example is the easiest way to understand the runtime.

In the example, neurons 3, 5, and 7 are classified as hot offline and are stored on GPU. At runtime, the predictor says neurons 3, 4, and 5 are active. The GPU computes 3 and 5. The CPU computes 4. Neuron 7 is hot but predicted inactive, so it is skipped. After CPU computation finishes, its output is transferred to GPU and merged with the GPU result.

This is why PowerInfer needs three pieces to work together:

  • The offline hot/cold split controls memory placement.
  • The online predictor controls which neurons are computed for a particular token.
  • The hybrid executor overlaps CPU and GPU work and merges partial results.

If any piece is weak, the design loses its advantage. A bad predictor computes too much or misses useful neurons. A bad placement policy leaves hot work on CPU. A bad executor spends the saved compute on synchronization.

Adaptive Predictors

PowerInfer inherits the idea of activation predictors from DejaVu, but local deployment changes the predictor budget. Fixed-size predictors can be too large. The paper gives a concrete example: predictors for OPT-175B would require around 27 GB of GPU memory, more than an RTX 4090 has.

The paper’s solution is to size predictors according to layer sparsity and skewness. Sparse, highly skewed layers need smaller predictors because the active set is easier to identify. Dense or less skewed layers need larger predictors.

Figure 9 shows the relationship for OPT-175B at a guaranteed 95% predictor accuracy level. Higher sparsity generally permits smaller predictors, while the error bars reflect skewness differences inside layers.

Later, the evaluation reports predictor sizes for several models.

The predictor ratio is not free, but it is bounded. The paper reports that predictor parameters are about 7.09% of model weights on average, and predictor execution contributes less than 10% of total inference time.

Placement Policy

The placement policy is more subtle than “put the hottest neurons on GPU.”

The GPU has limited memory and high bandwidth. The CPU has more memory and lower compute throughput. PCIe transfer is expensive. A placement policy therefore needs to balance:

Factor Why it matters
Activation frequency Hot neurons are likely to be used often
Neuron impact Some neurons matter more to model output
GPU memory capacity The hot set cannot exceed available VRAM
CPU-GPU transfer Too much split work can create communication overhead
Layer structure Partial placement inside a layer must still be executable efficiently

The paper formulates this as an integer linear programming problem. The objective is to maximize the impact of neurons placed on GPU while satisfying memory and communication constraints. That offline solver is what turns the activation profile into an actual memory layout.

The practical reading: PowerInfer is a cache placement system for neurons, but the cache item is not only chosen by frequency. It also needs to respect layer-level execution cost.

Neuron-Aware Operators

Normal sparse kernels are not automatically a good fit here. The sparsity is dynamic, neuron-granular, and split across CPU and GPU. Converting dense matrices into generic sparse formats at runtime can erase the win.

PowerInfer implements neuron-aware operators that directly compute activated neurons and their weights. On GPU, the operator maps individual activated neurons to thread blocks. On CPU, the operator assigns activated neuron work to available CPU cores.

Figure 16 compares PowerInfer’s operators with dense computation, PyTorch sparse on CPU, and PIT on GPU. The CPU result is the most striking: PyTorch sparse does not beat dense computation until sparsity is above 87%, while PowerInfer’s CPU operator beats dense even below 10% sparsity. On GPU, PowerInfer is close to PIT, but PowerInfer’s advantage is that the same framework supports hybrid CPU-GPU execution.

Evaluation Setup

The evaluation uses two local PC configurations.

Setup CPU Host memory GPU PCIe
PC-High Intel i9-13900K, eight 5.4 GHz cores 192 GB, 67.2 GB/s RTX 4090, 24 GB PCIe 4.0, 64 GB/s
PC-Low Intel i7-12700K, eight 4.9 GHz cores 64 GB, 38.4 GB/s RTX 2080Ti, 11 GB PCIe 3.0, 32 GB/s

The tested models cover ReLU, ReGLU, SwiGLU, and dReLU variants.

Table 3 is useful because it explains the result spread. OPT and Falcon are highly sparse. LLaMA2-ReGLU is less sparse but still favorable. SwiGLU models have lower sparsity, so PowerInfer still helps but with smaller speedups.

The baselines are llama.cpp and SpecInfer. The paper also analyzes FlexGen and DejaVu earlier, but they are not the main end-to-end baselines because their latency is poor in this local, batch-small setting.

FP16 Results

The main FP16 result is batch size 1 generation speed, which matches the local interactive setting better than a throughput-oriented server benchmark.

On PC-High with RTX 4090, the paper reports an average PowerInfer generation speed of 8.32 tokens/s and a peak of 16.06 tokens/s. It reports average speedups of 7.23x over llama.cpp and 6.19x over SpecInfer, with Falcon-40B reaching up to 11.69x over llama.cpp.

On PC-Low with RTX 2080Ti, PowerInfer still improves performance, but the margin is smaller because the 11 GB GPU can host fewer hot neurons. The paper reports average speedups of 4.71x over llama.cpp and 5.97x over SpecInfer, with peaks of 7.06x and 7.47x.

This is a useful boundary condition. PowerInfer benefits from GPU memory even though it is designed for limited VRAM. If the GPU is too small relative to the model, more hot neurons spill to CPU and the CPU becomes the bottleneck.

Where The Work Runs

Figure 12 explains why PowerInfer is faster than layer-level hybrid offloading.

The paper defines neuron load as the proportion of activated neuron computations executed by each device. On PC-High, PowerInfer increases the GPU’s share from about 20% in llama.cpp to about 70%. This is the runtime effect of hot-neuron placement: the GPU gets the common work even though the whole model does not fit in VRAM.

On PC-Low, the GPU share can fall. The paper gives the example of running a roughly 60 GB model on an 11 GB RTX 2080Ti, where the GPU handles about 42% of the neuron load because it cannot hold enough hot neurons.

Long Input And INT4

Long prompts change the behavior. During prefill, many tokens are processed together, and their combined active-neuron set is less sparse. PowerInfer switches to dense GPU computation in prefill, then uses sparse hybrid execution during generation.

For 1.5K input length and 256 output length on PC-High, the paper still reports 3.47x to 5.69x speedup over llama.cpp. This is not as clean as single-token decode, but it shows that the system is not only a short-prompt trick.

The paper also evaluates INT4 models.

With INT4 quantization, PC-High reaches 13.20 tokens/s on average and 29.08 tokens/s at peak. The average speedup over llama.cpp is 2.89x, with a maximum of 4.28x. On PC-Low, the average speedup is 5.01x and the peak is 8.00x. The OPT-175B result is especially interesting: PowerInfer nearly reaches 2 tokens/s on PC-High and is 2.66x faster than llama.cpp.

Quantization and PowerInfer are complementary. Quantization reduces the memory footprint of every weight. PowerInfer changes where and whether neuron computations happen.

Batching Boundary

PowerInfer is aimed at small-batch local serving. The batch-size result makes that explicit.

On Falcon-40B with PC-High, the paper reports strong speedups when batch size is below 32, with an average 6.08x improvement over llama.cpp. At batch size 32, PowerInfer still reports 4.38x speedup, but the ratio declines as batch size grows.

The reason is joint activation. With more requests in a batch, the union of active neurons grows. Eventually the batch activates enough of the model that sparsity is less useful. This is why PowerInfer should not be read as a replacement for high-throughput datacenter batching systems. It is a local, latency-sensitive path.

Ablation

The ablation separates three ideas:

  1. +PO: add predictors and neuron-aware operators, but keep layer-wise execution.
  2. +Engine: allow GPU and CPU to process neurons from the same layer concurrently.
  3. +Policy: add the optimized placement policy from the offline solver.

The paper reports:

Variant Bamboo-7B speedup Falcon-40B speedup
+PO 1.87x 3.32x
+Engine 2.60x 7.80x
+Policy 3.62x 11.69x

The large jump from +PO to +Engine shows that neuron sparsity alone is not enough. The runtime must split work inside a layer so the GPU and CPU are both useful. The final jump from +Engine to +Policy shows that random neuron placement wastes GPU memory and creates bad communication patterns.

Predictor Overhead And Accuracy

Prediction is not free, but it is small enough in the measured setting.

Figure 17 shows predictor overhead on PC-Low. The paper reports that online predictor execution is less than 10% of total inference time on average. This matters because a perfect sparsity plan would be useless if the predictor cost were comparable to the skipped MLP work.

The paper also evaluates model accuracy after using predictors. The short version is that the reported benchmark averages remain close to the original models. This does not mean misprediction is harmless. It means the missed neurons tend to have small contribution in the evaluated tasks, and the predictors were sized to keep perplexity close to baseline.

RTX 4090 Versus A100

The headline comparison is not “4090 beats A100.” It is more careful: PowerInfer narrows the gap between a local consumer GPU setup and a server GPU that can hold the whole model.

The paper compares PowerInfer on RTX 4090 with vLLM on an 80 GB A100 for OPT-30B and Falcon-40B. With input length 1, llama.cpp on 4090 is 93% and 92% slower than vLLM on A100, while PowerInfer reduces the gap to 18% and 23%. With input length 64, PowerInfer reduces the gap to 28% and 29%.

This result is the strongest systems message in the paper. The 4090 does not magically become an A100. The CPU still becomes a bottleneck in some cases. But neuron-level locality makes the consumer-GPU setup much closer than layer offloading can.

What I Would Check In A Reproduction

For a real reproduction, I would measure these items separately:

Measurement Why it matters
Per-layer activation sparsity Decides whether PowerInfer is applicable
Hot-neuron overlap across tasks Tests whether offline placement generalizes
Predictor false negatives Missed active neurons can hurt accuracy
Predictor runtime and memory Predictor overhead can consume the saved budget
GPU/CPU neuron load split Shows whether the GPU is actually doing the common work
PCIe transfer volume Verifies that the system is not secretly transfer-bound
Prefill versus decode latency Sparsity is much cleaner during token-by-token generation
Batch size sweep Finds where joint activation destroys sparsity

The most important test is distribution shift. If a new workload activates a different hot set, an offline policy from Wikipedia may be less effective. The paper’s task-overlap result is encouraging, but a deployment should still profile on representative prompts.

Limitations

PowerInfer has clear boundaries:

  • It works best when MLP activation sparsity is high. ReLU-family models are the best fit.
  • Larger batches reduce the advantage because the union of active neurons grows.
  • Long prefill is less sparse than single-token decode, so the generation phase carries most of the win.
  • The system needs an offline profiling, predictor training, and placement step per model.
  • Predictor errors are acceptable only if missed neurons have low output impact.
  • CPU execution can become the bottleneck when the GPU cannot host enough hot neurons.
  • The design is more complex than quantization or simple layer offloading.

The paper is therefore not a universal serving recipe. It is a strong design for one important corner: large-model, low-latency, small-batch inference on a local machine with limited GPU memory and enough CPU memory.

Takeaway

PowerInfer reframes local LLM serving as a locality problem. Instead of asking only “how do I make the model smaller?”, it asks:

Which parts of the model are usually needed for the next token, and where should those parts live?

That makes the paper complementary to quantization, KV-cache paging, and speculative decoding. PowerInfer’s useful lesson is that activation sparsity is not only an arithmetic shortcut. When the hot set is stable, it becomes a memory-placement primitive.

entry.title: Primer: Searching Transformer Primitives
entry.content:
So D R, Mańke W, Liu H, Dai Z, Shazeer N, Le Q V. Primer: Searching for Efficient Transformers for Language Modeling.

Paper

Primer is a useful AutoML paper because its output is not an opaque architecture that only works inside one search codebase. The search finds two small Transformer block changes that are easy to reimplement: squared ReLU in the feed-forward network and depthwise convolution in the attention projections.

That makes the paper more interesting than a normal “NAS beats baseline” result. The search acts as an idea generator, and the real contribution is the evidence that the discovered primitives transfer across codebases, datasets, hardware, and larger model sizes.

All figures and tables below are cropped from the original paper PDF.

Search Over Programs

Primer searches over decoder-block programs written from TensorFlow-style primitives. A candidate architecture is represented as a DNA. The DNA contains subprograms, each subprogram contains instructions, and those instructions are translated into TensorFlow code.

This is a lower-level search space than most NAS work. Instead of choosing only a layer type or a macro cell topology, the search can compose primitive operations inside the Transformer block. That is why the final result can look like a small local edit rather than a brand-new model family.

The search objective is still pragmatic: evaluate candidates on an auto-regressive language modeling proxy task, then keep the architectural ideas that improve compute efficiency without requiring a new optimizer recipe.

The Two Useful Changes

The paper names the simpler, easy-to-adopt variant Primer-EZ. It keeps the two changes that explain most of the gains:

  1. Replace feed-forward ReLU with squared ReLU.
  2. Add spatial depthwise convolution after the Q, K, and V projections in multi-head attention.

The left diagram is Multi-DConv-Head Attention, or MDHA. After each per-head Q, K, and V projection, Primer applies a causal 3x1 depthwise convolution along the sequence dimension. This injects a small amount of local mixing before attention. It does not remove attention, and it does not change the global attention path.

The middle diagram is the feed-forward change. The ordinary activation is replaced with . The shape is simple, but it changes the activation’s asymptotic behavior and overlaps with some of the benefits that gated linear unit variants try to capture.

The right plot in this figure is the part I would pay attention to. In the paper’s C4 language-modeling comparison, squared ReLU is better than ReLU, GELU, Swish, ReGLU, and SwiGLU under the reported setup. That does not mean squared ReLU dominates everywhere, but it explains why the authors considered it a reusable primitive instead of a search artifact.

Search-Task Evidence

The first empirical check is the LM1B proxy task with roughly 35M-parameter models. The paper compares vanilla Transformer, Transformer+GELU, Transformer++, Primer, and Primer-EZ across Tensor2Tensor, T5, TPUv2, and V100 settings.

Speedup here means compute needed to reach the same quality as the vanilla Transformer baseline trained for the full budget. On the search task, Primer and Primer-EZ are consistently above 1.7x.

Some exact rows from the table:

  • Tensor2Tensor on TPUv2: vanilla Transformer reaches 35.44 PPLX, Primer reaches 33.77, and Primer-EZ reaches 33.53 with a 2.34x speedup.
  • Tensor2Tensor on V100: vanilla Transformer reaches 37.19 PPLX, Primer reaches 35.06, and Primer-EZ reaches 35.16 with a 2.03x speedup.
  • T5 on TPUv2: vanilla Transformer reaches 23.30 PPLX, Primer reaches 22.71, and Primer-EZ reaches 22.62 with a 1.75x speedup.

Two details matter. First, Primer-EZ is not slower because of the extra depthwise convolution; its step rate is slightly lower in some rows, but the quality gain more than pays for it. Second, the result transfers from Tensor2Tensor to T5. That is a stronger signal than a single-codebase search win.

Scaling-Law View

The authors then ask whether the gain survives when model size and training compute vary. They sweep layer count, model width, feed-forward projection ratio, and training budget, then plot validation loss versus TPUv2 hours.

The key visual claim is that the lines remain roughly parallel in log-log space. Primer is not just better at one point; it shifts the loss-compute curve. When curves are parallel, a vertical improvement can be interpreted as a compute reduction at a fixed target quality.

This is also where the paper’s argument becomes more deployment-relevant. A fixed final perplexity target is common in real training decisions: if a model variant reaches that target earlier, it saves accelerator time even if each step is not dramatically faster.

Transfer Beyond The Proxy

Proxy-task NAS results often fail when moved to larger data, larger budgets, or different implementation stacks. Primer spends a lot of the paper showing the opposite direction: the same primitives continue to help on C4, PG19, Switch Transformer, and Synthesizer variants.

The C4 and PG19 bars are the cleanest transfer result. Primer and Primer-EZ remain more efficient than the baselines after moving from the small LM1B search setup to larger datasets and longer training. The Switch and Synthesizer cases are also useful because they show the primitives are not only compatible with vanilla dense Transformers.

The larger T5-scale comparison is especially direct. The paper copies the original T5 auto-regressive language-modeling setup at 537M parameters and compares the compute needed to hit target perplexities.

Target PPLX Model Steps TPUv3 hours
13.25 Original T5 1M 15.7K
13.25 T5++ 251K 4.6K
13.25 Primer 207K 3.8K
12.69 T5++ 1M 16.5K
12.69 Primer 480K 8.3K
12.35 Primer 1M 17.3K

At the original T5 quality target, Primer reaches parity with about 3.8K TPUv3 hours instead of 15.7K. The paper reports this as roughly 4.2x less compute than the original T5 architecture.

The compute-saving curve is worth reading carefully. The saving factor grows as training continues because the Primer and T5 perplexity curves separate asymptotically. This also means the reported saving depends on the target quality. The higher the quality target, the more important the shape of the whole training curve becomes.

One-Shot Transfer At Larger Scale

The last main experiment moves to 1.9B parameters and one-shot downstream evaluation, following the style of GPT-3-style pretraining evaluation. This is not a direct GPT-3 comparison; it is a controlled comparison between Transformer+GELU and Primer under the paper’s setup.

Primer with 24K TPUv4 hours roughly matches Transformer+GELU with 72K TPUv4 hours on the averaged pretraining and one-shot bars. With the same 72K-hour budget, Primer is ahead.

The per-task grid is noisier than the averaged figure, as expected. The useful conclusion is not that Primer wins every task. The useful conclusion is that the training-efficiency gain is not limited to validation perplexity; it mostly carries into downstream one-shot task scores.

Which Pieces Actually Matter?

One reason I like this paper is that it does not stop at “the searched model is better.” It runs insertion and ablation studies to see which modifications are robust.

In the insertion study, each modification is added to a vanilla Transformer. In the ablation study, each modification is removed from Primer. Positive values mean the modification is beneficial under the paper’s normalization.

The result separates “found by search” from “worth recommending.” A larger 12x feed-forward projection helps at this small scale, but the paper does not recommend it as the simple transferable recipe. The two robust and easy pieces are MDHA and squared ReLU, which become Primer-EZ.

Full Program View

The appendix expands the full Transformer and Primer programs into primitive operations. This figure is dense, but it is a useful reminder of what the search actually changed.

The orange nodes are Primer’s differences. Some of them are more complicated than the two Primer-EZ edits. That is the reason Primer-EZ matters: it turns a searched program into a small recipe a practitioner can implement without importing the whole search system.

Engineering Notes And Limits

Primer is strongest as evidence for primitive-level architecture search, not as a universal Transformer replacement.

  • The search task is small: about 35M parameters, LM1B, and short sequences. The paper does run larger transfer experiments, but the discovered primitives still come from a proxy setting.
  • The main focus is decoder-only auto-regressive language modeling. The paper’s appendix discusses masked language modeling, but the authors explicitly treat encoder or encoder-decoder search as future work.
  • Depthwise convolution inside attention projections is not free. Whether MDHA helps wall-clock latency depends on the runtime kernel, sequence length, batch size, and hardware. The paper reports training compute savings, but an inference system still needs direct measurement.
  • Squared ReLU is simple enough to try almost anywhere, but activation changes can interact with initialization, normalization, optimizer settings, and mixed precision.

The broader lesson is that NAS can be most useful when it returns simple hypotheses. Primer’s search found candidates, but the paper’s value comes from the follow-up: transfer tests, ablations, scaling curves, and a simplified recipe.

Takeaway

Primer is not important because it discovered a mysterious architecture. It is important because it shows that searching at the primitive level can surface small Transformer edits that humans can understand, ablate, and reuse.

The practical recipe is Primer-EZ: use squared ReLU in the feed-forward block and add causal depthwise convolution after Q, K, and V projections. The practical caution is that the recipe should be benchmarked in the target codebase. The paper makes a strong case that it transfers, but the real unit of evidence is still measured compute, not architectural elegance.

entry.title: Q8BERT: 8-bit Quantization-Aware Training for BERT
entry.content:
Paper: Q8BERT: Quantized 8Bit BERT

Code: NLP Architect

Q8BERT is a compact paper, but it is a useful baseline for reading later BERT quantization work. The main question is practical:

If we are allowed to run quantization-aware fine-tuning, can BERT’s dominant matrix multiplications and embedding tables be moved to INT8 with small task accuracy loss?

The answer is mostly yes. Q8BERT quantizes the weights of BERT’s embedding and fully connected layers to 8-bit integers, simulates the quantized path during fine-tuning, and keeps higher-risk nonlinear operators such as Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32.

That makes Q8BERT different from I-BERT:

  • Q8BERT is an 8-bit quantization-aware training baseline for the GEMM-heavy parts of BERT.
  • I-BERT later asks for integer-only inference and replaces Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm with integer approximations.
  • BinaryBERT later goes to the opposite extreme: 1-bit weight compression with distillation and special initialization.

All crops below are taken from the original 2019 PDF.

The Problem

BERT-Base has about 110M parameters. BERT-Large has about 334M parameters. In FP32, that means large memory footprint, high bandwidth demand, and expensive feed-forward computation during inference. For latency-sensitive NLP services, this is not just a training cost problem; it is a production deployment problem.

Q8BERT’s target is conservative: stay at 8 bits, keep the original BERT architecture, and use quantization-aware training during downstream fine-tuning.

The abstract already states the scope: compress BERT by 4x with minimal accuracy loss and make the resulting model suitable for hardware with optimized 8-bit integer arithmetic.

The 4x number is straightforward. Moving most model weights from FP32 to INT8 reduces storage from 4 bytes per parameter to 1 byte per parameter. Since the paper quantizes all fully connected and embedding weights, which account for more than 99% of the model weights, the total model footprint approaches this 4x reduction.

What Is Quantized

The implementation goal is narrow and clear:

Component Q8BERT treatment
Embedding layer weights Quantized to INT8
Fully connected layer weights Quantized to INT8
FC input activations Fake-quantized during training; INT8 path for inference
GEMM accumulation INT32 accumulation
Bias Quantized to INT32
Softmax Kept in FP32
LayerNorm Kept in FP32
GELU Kept in FP32

This is why I read Q8BERT as a practical partial-integer inference paper, not an integer-only inference paper. It attacks the dominant memory and GEMM cost, but it does not eliminate floating-point islands from the Transformer block.

The implementation section is explicit: quantized embedding and FC layers replace the original layers, while Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU remain FP32 because they require higher precision.

Why 8-bit GEMM Is The Main Target

BERT inference is dominated by dense matrix multiplications:

  • Q/K/V projections in self-attention;
  • output projection after attention;
  • the two feed-forward network linear layers;
  • embedding lookup storage and movement.

INT8 helps in two ways:

  1. Weight memory shrinks, reducing model footprint and memory bandwidth.
  2. Matrix multiplication can use integer hardware paths, such as VNNI-style instructions or other accelerator INT8 kernels.

The paper cites prior transformer INT8 GEMM work reporting 3.7x speedup over FP32 matrix multiplication on Intel Xeon Cascade Lake VNNI. Q8BERT does not prove a universal end-to-end 3.7x BERT speedup; it uses that hardware fact to justify targeting the GEMM-heavy parts of BERT.

This distinction matters. End-to-end latency depends on operator coverage, layout conversion, dequantization/requantization boundaries, memory movement, batch size, and backend implementation. Q8BERT’s accuracy result is strong evidence that BERT tolerates this INT8 GEMM path under QAT, but deployment speed still depends on the runtime.

Symmetric Linear Quantization

Q8BERT uses symmetric linear quantization for weights and activations. The paper writes the integer quantizer as:

with:

For 8-bit signed quantization, . The paper’s is a multiplicative scaling factor from real value to integer value. This is the reciprocal convention of the common “real = scale * integer” notation.

The weight scale is computed from the max absolute weight:

The activation scale is based on values observed during training:

The symmetric choice removes the zero-point term. This simplifies integer GEMM because the quantized value is centered around zero:

In an asymmetric formulation, matrix multiplication may need correction terms involving zero points. Q8BERT intentionally uses the symmetric case to simplify the inference path.

QAT During Fine-tuning

The central training choice is to insert fake quantization into the fine-tuning graph. Forward propagation sees quantized values, but the underlying trainable parameters remain floating point.

Fake quantization creates the same rounding/clipping noise that the model will see at inference. During backpropagation, Q8BERT uses the straight-through estimator:

This is the standard QAT compromise. Rounding is not differentiable, but if the backward pass treats it as identity, the model can adapt its FP32 latent weights to produce quantization-friendly forward activations.

The practical pipeline is:

  1. Start from a pre-trained BERT checkpoint.
  2. Replace embedding and FC layers with quantized versions.
  3. During fine-tuning, run fake quantization for weights and activations.
  4. Keep latent weights in FP32 for optimization.
  5. Export INT8 weights and INT8 activation scales for inference.
  6. Run quantized embedding/FC/GEMM while keeping Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32.

QAT is done during downstream fine-tuning, not during the original large-scale pre-training. This is why the paper is practical: it does not require pre-training BERT again.

Dynamic Quantization Baseline

The paper compares QAT with a dynamic quantization baseline. In this baseline, activations are quantized during inference, and the activation scale is computed from each incoming activation tensor using a max-absolute rule, similar to the weight scale.

The distinction is:

Method Scale source Why it behaves differently
DQ Current tensor max abs at inference The task fine-tuning stage never sees quantization noise
QAT EMA statistics from training Fine-tuning adapts to rounding and clipping noise

The authors find that dynamic quantization is consistently worse. This is not surprising: BERT is fine-tuned for a downstream task, and the quantized model needs that fine-tuning stage to see the same perturbations it will face at inference.

Main Results

The paper evaluates on GLUE tasks and SQuAD v1.1. It reports the mean and standard deviation over five runs. Most experiments use BERT-Base, with selected BERT-Large rows marked as Large.

The important pattern is that QAT stays close to FP32 while DQ often drops more:

Task FP32 baseline QAT INT8 DQ INT8
CoLA 58.48 58.48 56.74
MRPC F1 90.00 89.56 87.88
QNLI 90.30 90.62 89.34
QQP F1 87.84 87.96 84.98
RTE 69.70 68.78 63.32
SST-2 92.36 92.24 91.04
STS-B 89.62 89.04 87.66
SQuAD v1.1 F1 88.46 87.74 80.02

QAT sometimes slightly exceeds the baseline due to run variance, for example QNLI and QQP in the table. I would not over-interpret those small gains. The main claim is that QAT preserves accuracy, not that INT8 improves BERT.

Relative Error

Table 2 is a cleaner way to read the result because it reports the relative accuracy drop from quantization.

QAT has less than 1% relative error on every listed task except RTE:

Method Typical behavior
DQ Often multiple percent relative drop; 9.13% on RTE and 9.54% on SQuAD
QAT Usually below 1% relative drop; 1.32% on RTE and 0.81% on SQuAD

RTE is a small dataset and tends to have higher variance. The QAT row still improves substantially over DQ, but the relative drop is larger than the other GLUE tasks.

What The Paper Does Not Claim

Q8BERT is easy to overstate. The paper does not claim:

  • post-training quantization is enough for BERT;
  • every Transformer operator runs in INT8;
  • Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU are solved in integer arithmetic;
  • end-to-end latency must improve by the same ratio as INT8 GEMM;
  • 4-bit or 2-bit BERT is covered by the same recipe.

The actual claim is narrower and more defensible:

With quantization-aware downstream fine-tuning, the GEMM-heavy embedding and fully connected layers of BERT can be quantized to INT8 while preserving most task accuracy.

This is why Q8BERT is still useful. It establishes a strong simple baseline for 8-bit QAT. Any more complex BERT quantization paper should explain what extra constraint it solves: lower bit-width, no task fine-tuning, integer-only nonlinear ops, better latency, or smaller memory.

Relationship To I-BERT

I-BERT directly addresses Q8BERT’s main limitation. Q8BERT leaves Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32. I-BERT replaces them with integer-friendly approximations and keeps the whole inference path in integer arithmetic.

The comparison:

Aspect Q8BERT I-BERT
Main goal 8-bit BERT with QAT Integer-only BERT inference
Linear layers INT8 GEMM INT8 GEMM
Embeddings INT8 INT8
GELU FP32 Integer polynomial approximation
Softmax FP32 Integer exponential approximation
LayerNorm FP32 Integer sqrt and normalization
Practical message 8-bit QAT is enough for accuracy Operator coverage matters for integer-only deployment

So Q8BERT is not obsolete; it is a different operating point. If the backend already handles mixed INT8/FP32 efficiently, Q8BERT is a simple baseline. If the target hardware prefers integer-only execution, I-BERT’s stricter graph coverage becomes necessary.

Implementation Notes

A faithful reproduction should pay attention to quantization boundaries. It is not enough to say “BERT is INT8.” The questions are:

  1. Are embedding tables stored and returned as INT8?
  2. Are Q/K/V, attention output, and FFN matrix multiplications using INT8 inputs and weights?
  3. Are accumulators INT32?
  4. How are bias tensors quantized?
  5. Where does the graph dequantize before Softmax, LayerNorm, or GELU?
  6. Are activation scales static from training EMA, dynamic per batch, or calibrated post-training?
  7. Does the exported graph run on an actual INT8 backend, or only evaluate fake quantization?

The last point is important. Fake-quantized evaluation measures numerical robustness. It does not by itself measure speed. Speed requires an execution backend that maps the quantized FC layers to optimized INT8 kernels.

Reproduction Checklist

For a clean reproduction, I would separate accuracy, model size, and runtime:

Check What to measure
Accuracy GLUE/SQuAD metrics for FP32, DQ, and QAT over multiple seeds
Model size Serialized parameter footprint before and after INT8 export
Operator coverage Which layers run INT8, INT32, or FP32
GEMM speed Isolated FC/GEMM latency on the target hardware
End-to-end latency Full BERT request latency with tokenization excluded and included
Dequant overhead Cast/requant time around Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU

The expected result is not just “the model is 4x smaller.” A deployment-oriented reproduction should show whether the model is also faster under the intended batch size and hardware backend.

Takeaway

Q8BERT is the clean 8-bit QAT baseline for BERT. It shows that if downstream fine-tuning is available, BERT’s embedding and fully connected layers can tolerate INT8 quantization with small accuracy loss across GLUE and SQuAD.

The most important caveat is operator coverage. Q8BERT quantizes the parts that dominate parameters and GEMM compute, but it keeps Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32. That makes it practical and accurate, but not integer-only. Later papers like I-BERT should be read as tightening this exact gap.

entry.title: Q-BERT: Hessian Based Ultra Low Precision Quantization of BERT
QLoRA: 4-bit LLM Fine-Tuning
entry.content:
Paper: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
Code: artidoro/qlora , bitsandbytes

QLoRA is one of those papers that looks simple after it becomes infrastructure. The headline is “fine-tune a 65B model on one 48GB GPU”, but the useful idea is more specific: keep the pretrained base model frozen in a 4-bit storage format, dequantize it only when it participates in BF16 computation, and train LoRA adapters through that frozen quantized model.

That makes QLoRA a training-memory paper more than an inference-speed paper. It does not say that every serving stack should run NF4 directly. It says that the expensive part of adapting a large language model can be moved from full-precision optimizer state over all weights to low-rank adapter updates plus a carefully quantized frozen backbone.

Figure 1 from the paper. Full fine-tuning stores and updates the whole model; LoRA freezes the base model but still keeps it in 16-bit; QLoRA freezes a 4-bit base model and trains adapters through it.

Why QLoRA mattered

Before QLoRA, the common memory story was already clear:

  • Full fine-tuning is high quality but expensive because model weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers all have to fit.
  • LoRA reduces trainable parameters by inserting low-rank adapter matrices, but the frozen base model still consumes 16-bit memory.
  • Post-training quantization can reduce inference memory, but earlier low-bit training attempts often lost quality or became unstable at large LLM scale.

QLoRA connects those pieces. It keeps the large base model in a 4-bit representation, but it does not update those base weights. Gradients flow through the dequantized base computation into LoRA adapters, and only the adapters receive optimizer updates.

The paper gives the strongest motivation number in the introduction: regular 16-bit fine-tuning of LLaMA-65B requires more than 780GB of GPU memory, while QLoRA brings the 65B fine-tuning footprint below 48GB without observed degradation against the 16-bit fine-tuning baselines they can compare to. That is not a minor engineering tweak; it changes the class of experiments a small lab can run.

The memory account

The model weight reduction is the obvious part, but QLoRA is careful about the full training footprint. The important buckets are:

  • Base model weights: frozen, stored in NF4, dequantized to BF16 for compute.
  • LoRA adapters: trainable BF16 parameters, small compared with the base model.
  • Adapter gradients: still need memory, but far smaller than full-model gradients.
  • Optimizer states: only for the adapters, with paged allocation to survive spikes.
  • Activations and temporary buffers: managed with checkpointing and paged optimizer behavior.

The appendix memory breakdown is useful because it prevents a common misunderstanding: LoRA parameters are not the only memory that matters. Even in parameter-efficient fine-tuning, gradients and activations can dominate specific steps, and the 4-bit base model is still the largest persistent object.

Figure 6 from the appendix. The paper reports QLoRA training footprints of about 6.9GB, 11.3GB, 24.7GB, and 45.0GB for 7B, 13B, 33B, and 65B LLaMA models under the stated setup.

The practical reading is:

  • 7B and 13B fine-tuning become routine on single consumer GPUs.
  • 33B is close to a 24GB boundary, so transient memory spikes matter.
  • 65B fits the single professional-GPU story, but only because the paper attacks weight storage, scale metadata, and optimizer spikes together.

The QLoRA layer

For one linear layer, standard LoRA starts from a frozen projection:

where is the frozen base weight, and are low-rank trainable matrices, and is the LoRA scaling factor.

QLoRA changes the storage path for . The base weight is stored as NF4 plus quantization constants; when used, it is double-dequantized into the BF16 compute type. Let be the dequantized base weight:

Then the QLoRA layer is:

The key distinction is storage type versus compute type:

  • Storage type: usually 4-bit NF4 for the frozen base weight.
  • Compute type: usually BF16 for the matrix multiplication and backward pass.
  • Trainable type: LoRA adapters are trained in BF16.

This is why QLoRA is not “training a 4-bit model” in the naive sense of updating 4-bit weights. It is training adapter weights through a frozen quantized model.

NF4: 4-bit storage for normally distributed weights

The first technical contribution is NormalFloat4, or NF4. The motivation is that pretrained neural network weights are usually roughly zero-centered and normal-looking after blockwise scaling. If that assumption is good enough, then a uniform int4 grid is not the most efficient way to spend 16 representable values.

NF4 uses quantile-based levels for a standard normal distribution, then normalizes the values into a fixed range. In other words, it puts more representational resolution where normal weights are likely to appear. The paper also forces an exact zero representation, which matters for padding and exact zero values.

The exact NF4 codebook in the appendix is:

That list is a useful reminder that NF4 is not the same thing as ordinary signed int4. It is a small floating-style codebook specialized for zero-centered normal weights.

Table 2 from the paper. On Pile Common Crawl perplexity across OPT, BLOOM, LLaMA, and Pythia models, NF4 plus double quantization has the best mean perplexity among the tested 4-bit formats.

The table is small but important. The reported mean perplexities are:

  • Int4: 34.34
  • Float4 (E2M1): 31.07
  • Float4 (E3M0): 29.48
  • NFloat4 + DQ: 27.41

Lower perplexity is better, and NF4 wins before any downstream instruction tuning story is added.

Figure 3 from the paper. For LLaMA models, NF4 gives better bit-for-bit zero-shot accuracy than the tested FP4 baseline, while double quantization keeps the memory budget tighter.

The reason this result matters for training is simple: LoRA has to learn through the frozen base model. If quantization destroys too much signal, the adapter update has less useful information to work with. NF4 reduces that damage enough that the later LoRA stage can recover 16-bit behavior in the tested setups.

Double quantization: quantize the scales too

Blockwise low-bit quantization needs scale constants. With a small block size, those constants are not free.

In the paper’s main setup:

  • The base weight block size is 64.
  • A 32-bit scale per 64 parameters costs bits per parameter.
  • Double quantization stores those scale constants in an 8-bit second quantization with block size 256.
  • The amortized scale cost becomes bits per parameter.
  • The saving is bits per parameter, about 3GB for a 65B model.

This is an easy detail to skip, but it is one of the reasons the method actually fits large models. At 65B scale, metadata is no longer bookkeeping noise.

The dequantization path is two-level:

The base weights stay in NF4 storage, the first-level quantization constants are themselves quantized, and the final matrix multiplication uses BF16 values after dequantization.

Paged optimizers: protect against spikes

The third contribution is less mathematical but very practical. Paged optimizers use NVIDIA unified memory to let optimizer state move between CPU and GPU memory when a training step has an unusual memory spike.

This is not advertised as a speed optimization. The paper says paging is critical for 33B and 65B QLoRA tuning on single 24GB and 48GB GPUs, but also notes that paging happens only when memory pressure appears. In their 65B analysis with batch size 16, paged optimizers had the same training speed as regular optimizers.

The right mental model is:

  • NF4 lowers persistent model memory.
  • Double quantization lowers quantization metadata memory.
  • LoRA lowers trainable parameter and optimizer memory.
  • Paged optimizers make the remaining spikes survivable.

If a method fits on average but crashes on long examples, it is not useful. QLoRA treats peak memory as the real constraint.

LoRA placement matters more than rank

A subtle but important result is that “use LoRA” is not enough. The paper finds that the default practice of adding LoRA only to query and value projection matrices does not match full fine-tuning for larger base models.

Figure 2 from the paper. Applying LoRA broadly across transformer layers is necessary to match the stronger 16-bit baseline on Alpaca.

The practical conclusion is that adapter coverage matters. Because the LoRA parameter memory is small compared with the frozen base model and activation-related costs, QLoRA can afford to place adapters on all linear layers rather than only on a narrow subset.

The rank ablation is also useful:

Figure 4 from the appendix. Once LoRA is applied broadly, the tested LoRA rank values are not strongly predictive of final performance.

The paper’s default large-scale instruction tuning setup uses:

  • LoRA rank
  • LoRA alpha
  • LoRA modules on all linear layers
  • NF4 storage with double quantization
  • BF16 computation
  • paged optimizers

This is the part that many reproductions get wrong: rank alone is not the main knob if adapter placement is too sparse.

Does 4-bit fine-tuning recover 16-bit quality?

The strongest scientific question is not whether QLoRA saves memory. It obviously does. The important question is whether training through the quantized backbone loses quality.

The paper checks this in two stages:

  1. Smaller established benchmark setups where full 16-bit fine-tuning is feasible.
  2. Larger LLaMA instruction-tuning experiments where 16-bit LoRA is used as the comparison.

Table 3 from the paper. On GLUE and Super-NaturalInstructions, 4-bit QLoRA variants replicate the 16-bit LoRA and full fine-tuning baselines.

The main observation from Table 3 is not that NF4 wins every cell by a large amount. It is that the 4-bit adapter-tuning path stays in the same performance band as 16-bit fine-tuning and LoRA. That is the result QLoRA needs: the memory savings should not force a visible quality tax.

Table 4 from the paper. On LLaMA 7B to 65B models fine-tuned on Alpaca and FLAN v2, NF4 plus double quantization matches the BFloat16 LoRA mean MMLU score.

The MMLU dtype comparison is concise:

  • BFloat16 mean: 53.0
  • Float4 mean: 52.2
  • NFloat4 + DQ mean: 53.1

This supports two separate claims:

  • 4-bit QLoRA can match 16-bit LoRA in the tested instruction-tuning setup.
  • NF4 is a better 4-bit storage format than the tested FP4 alternative.

Guanaco: QLoRA as an instruction-tuning tool

The paper then uses QLoRA to train a family of chat models called Guanaco. These are not just quantization benchmarks; they are instruction-tuned models trained across model sizes and datasets.

The dataset result is worth reading carefully because it separates “MMLU is high” from “chatbot is good”.

Table 5 from the paper. Different instruction datasets move MMLU differently across model sizes. FLAN v2 is strong on MMLU, while OASST1/Guanaco is the stronger chatbot direction later in the paper.

The important lesson is that benchmark similarity and data quality matter. FLAN v2 performs well on MMLU, but it is not the best chat dataset in the Vicuna-style evaluation. OASST1 is much smaller but better aligned with multi-turn assistant behavior.

This is one reason the paper’s conclusion is stronger than “4-bit works”. QLoRA made it cheap enough to run more than 1,000 fine-tuning experiments, and that scale exposed data effects that would have been difficult to study with full fine-tuning.

Vicuna benchmark results

The headline Guanaco result comes from the Vicuna benchmark. GPT-4 scores model responses relative to ChatGPT, and the paper reports both prompt orders because GPT-4 has an ordering bias.

Table 6 from the paper. Guanaco 65B reaches 99.3% of ChatGPT’s Vicuna benchmark score while using 4-bit model weights and 41GB of memory.

Key numbers from Table 6:

  • Guanaco 65B: 41GB, 99.3% mean score relative to ChatGPT.
  • Guanaco 33B: 21GB, 97.8%.
  • Vicuna 13B: 26GB, 94.9%.
  • Guanaco 13B: 10GB, 90.4%.
  • Guanaco 7B: 5GB, 87.0%.

The comparison with Vicuna 13B is especially interesting. Guanaco 33B uses more parameters but lower precision, so its memory footprint is 21GB compared with Vicuna 13B at 26GB, while scoring higher in this evaluation.

That points to a broader scaling tradeoff: given a fixed memory budget, it can be better to use a larger lower-precision base model than a smaller higher-precision one, as long as the quantization error is controlled.

Elo ranking and evaluation caveats

The authors do not rely only on absolute GPT-4 scores. They also run pairwise tournaments and aggregate Elo ratings from human or GPT-4 judgments.

Table 7 from the paper. Guanaco 65B and 33B are near the top of the tournament rankings, but the judge and benchmark choice still matter.

The table makes Guanaco look very strong, but the caveats are part of the result:

  • GPT-4 is ranked first overall.
  • Guanaco 65B has median rank 2.
  • Guanaco 33B has median rank 4.
  • ChatGPT-3.5 Turbo has median rank 5.
  • The OpenAssistant benchmark favors ChatGPT more than the smaller Vicuna prompt set.

The paper reports only moderate agreement between GPT-4 and humans on the Vicuna benchmark: system-level Kendall tau is 0.43, Spearman rank correlation is 0.55, and example-level agreement with human majority vote has Fleiss kappa 0.25.

That means the chatbot claim should be read as “very competitive under these evaluation protocols”, not as a universal proof of model quality.

Table 13 from the appendix. Pairwise GPT-4 judgments induce an ordering where Guanaco 65B and 33B rank ahead of Vicuna, ChatGPT-3.5 Turbo, Bard, and smaller Guanaco variants.

The evaluation section is also useful as a warning for later LLM papers. When the judge is another model, prompt order and self-preference can move scores. Averaging both orders and supplementing with human ratings is not optional polish; it changes how much the result can be trusted.

Training recipe details

The appendix gives enough training detail to make the method concrete.

Table 9 from the appendix. QLoRA training hyperparameters across model sizes and datasets.

The core setup is:

  • NF4 with double quantization.
  • BF16 computation.
  • LoRA , alpha .
  • LoRA on all linear layers.
  • Adam beta2 .
  • max grad norm .
  • constant learning rate schedule.
  • group-by-length batching.
  • dropout 0.1 up to 13B, dropout 0.05 for 33B and 65B.

Learning rate and batch size change with scale:

  • 7B and 13B use learning rate , usually batch size 16.
  • 33B and 65B use learning rate , with larger batch sizes for some datasets.
  • OASST1 keeps batch size 16 and 1,875 steps across model sizes.

A compact reproduction checklist would look like this:

The most important reproduction trap is adapter coverage. If LoRA is only attached to the query and value projections, the result is not the paper’s main QLoRA recipe.

Target-only training and data quality

For instruction tuning, the paper studies whether to train on both source and target text or only on the target response.

Table 10 from the appendix. Training only on the target response improves mean MMLU in this ablation.

The target-only result is modest but consistent in the reported setup:

  • Train on source and target: mean 37.5.
  • Train on target: mean 38.6.

That matches a common supervised fine-tuning practice: do not spend loss on reproducing the user instruction when the goal is to improve assistant response behavior.

The data-size ablation is more important:

Table 11 from the appendix. Increasing dataset size and epochs helps less than choosing a better-suited dataset.

The authors report that increasing dataset size or epochs only marginally improves MMLU, while differences between datasets are much larger. This explains why a small high-quality chat dataset can beat a much larger but less suitable instruction mixture on chatbot evaluations.

For practical work, this is one of the strongest takeaways from the paper:

  • Use QLoRA to make iteration cheap.
  • Spend the saved budget on dataset selection, cleaning, and evaluation.
  • Do not assume that more instruction data is automatically better.

What QLoRA is not

QLoRA is sometimes casually described as “4-bit fine-tuning”, but a few boundaries matter.

First, the base weights are frozen. QLoRA is not doing full 4-bit weight updates. If the task requires changing the whole model distribution in ways LoRA cannot express, QLoRA may not match full fine-tuning.

Second, NF4 is primarily a training-memory storage format. The paper dequantizes to BF16 for computation. For production inference, the fastest representation may be INT4, FP8, AWQ/GPTQ-style layouts, or a custom kernel format depending on the serving stack.

Third, the paper does not fully prove 33B and 65B equality to full 16-bit fine-tuning. The resource cost of those baselines is too high, so the large-scale comparison is mostly against 16-bit LoRA and task evaluations.

Fourth, chatbot evaluation is noisy. The Guanaco results are strong, but GPT-4-as-judge is not a perfect measurement instrument.

My reading

The clean technical contribution is the combination, not any single isolated trick:

  • NF4 preserves enough information in the frozen model.
  • Double quantization makes the 4-bit representation honest at large scale by accounting for metadata.
  • Paged optimizers address peak memory instead of average memory.
  • Broad LoRA placement recovers quality because adapter memory is cheap compared with the base model.

QLoRA became popular because it matched the way people actually work: download a strong base model, adapt it to a dataset, and do not buy a cluster for every experiment. The method also made a useful empirical point: for many adaptation tasks, the base model capacity is more valuable than keeping every base weight in 16-bit precision.

If I were reproducing the paper today, I would track three numbers for every run:

  • Peak GPU memory, not just steady-state memory.
  • Evaluation quality on the target behavior, not just MMLU or perplexity.
  • Adapter target modules, because a “LoRA” run with sparse targets is not comparable to the paper’s all-linear-layer recipe.

Takeaway

QLoRA is best understood as a practical memory system for supervised adaptation of large language models. It does not make low-bit training magically free, and it does not remove the need for good data or careful evaluation. What it does is move 33B and 65B fine-tuning from “cluster-only” into the range of single-GPU experiments, while preserving 16-bit quality in the paper’s tested settings.

That change is why this paper matters: it turned quantization from a deployment-only trick into a core part of the fine-tuning workflow.

SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
entry.content:
Paper: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs

Code: sgl-project/sglang

SGLang is easy to under-read if it is described as “a prompting language” or “a prefix cache.” My reading is different:

SGLang is a paper about making LLM application structure visible to the serving runtime.

That visibility is the real contribution. A normal OpenAI-style completion API receives strings. It does not know that several calls are branches of the same program, that the same few-shot prefix is reused by all options, that a tree-search branch inherits a search history, or that a JSON literal has only one valid continuation for the next several tokens. SGLang’s frontend exposes those relationships through a small Python-embedded DSL. Its backend then turns them into concrete runtime optimizations: KV-cache reuse through RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, parallel execution inside one program, compressed finite-state-machine decoding, and speculative execution for black-box APIs.

The important lesson is not only “use a radix tree for prefix caching.” The stronger lesson is:

If the serving runtime sees a workload as unrelated strings, it can only optimize generic batching. If it sees the workload as a structured program, it can optimize the graph of shared prefixes, forks, joins, and constraints.

All figures below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF.

The System In One Figure

Figure 1. SGLang has a frontend language and a backend runtime. The runtime optimizations are not bolted on after the fact; they depend on the frontend exposing program structure.

The frontend contains language primitives for prompt state, generation, selection, multimodal input, and parallelism. The backend runtime includes three main optimizations:

  • RadixAttention for automatic KV-cache reuse across calls and program instances.
  • Compressed FSM decoding for faster structured output generation, such as JSON under a regex constraint.
  • API speculative execution for API-only models where the runtime cannot modify the model backend.

The paper reports up to 6.4x higher throughput and up to 3.7x lower latency compared with the evaluated systems across workloads such as MMLU, ReAct agents, tree-of-thought, skeleton-of-thought, LLM-as-judge, HellaSwag, JSON decoding, multi-turn chat, and DSPy RAG.

I would summarize the paper as a three-layer system:

Layer What it sees What it can optimize
String API independent prompt strings batching and generic model execution
SGLang frontend prompt state, gen, select, fork, join, constraints dependency order, intra-program parallelism, frontend hints
SGLang runtime token prefixes, KV pages, FSM states, batch queues prefix reuse, eviction, scheduling, constrained decoding

The last two rows are inseparable. The runtime optimization works because the frontend gives the runtime a better shape of the computation.

What Is A Language Model Program?

The paper uses “language model program” for applications that are no longer a single prompt and a single completion. Examples include:

  • an agent loop that repeatedly calls an LLM and a tool;
  • a few-shot benchmark where all questions share the same demonstrations;
  • self-consistency sampling where several generations branch from the same prompt;
  • tree-of-thought search where nodes share search history;
  • an LLM judge that evaluates several dimensions in parallel and then merges them;
  • a RAG pipeline where many queries share retrieved context or examples;
  • a JSON decoder that must obey a schema.

The two common properties are:

  • Multiple dependent LLM calls: there is control flow, branching, and synchronization.
  • Structured inputs or outputs: multimodal inputs, schemas, choices, tool results, or downstream parsers.

If these calls are submitted as independent strings, the backend cannot exploit the application structure. It can still do continuous batching, but it misses two categories of reuse:

  • Prefix reuse: repeated prompt tokens should reuse the same KV cache.
  • Program-level parallelism: independent branches should execute concurrently rather than serially through Python glue code.

This is why SGLang belongs in the serving-system family. It is not only a nicer syntax for writing prompts. It changes what information the runtime can use.

The KV-Cache Cost Model

For one request with cached tokens, a rough KV-cache memory estimate is:

Here:

  • is for key and value tensors.
  • is the number of transformer layers.
  • is the number of KV heads.
  • is the head dimension.
  • is the number of cached tokens.
  • is bytes per element.

The linear dependence on is why prefix reuse matters. If a long system prompt, few-shot prefix, retrieved document, chat history, or tree-search context is recomputed many times, the cost is paid in both prefill compute and KV-cache memory.

For a set of requests , let be the prompt-token sequence for request . Without reuse, the prefill token work is roughly:

If those prompts form a prefix tree, and each edge represents a token span that needs to be computed once, the lower bound for reusable prefix computation is:

The gap between and the tree cost is exactly the redundant prefill work. SGLang’s RadixAttention tries to make the runtime approach that tree cost online, under memory pressure and continuous batching.

This mental model also explains why this paper is not identical to PagedAttention. PagedAttention is mainly about representing live KV memory efficiently inside a serving runtime. RadixAttention is about retaining and matching KV prefixes across calls and program instances. The two are compatible, but they answer different questions.

Programming Model

Figure 2. The running example is a multi-dimensional essay judge. The red primitives are SGLang operations that expose generation, selection, constraints, and parallel branches.

The frontend is a Python-embedded DSL. The core object is a prompt state, usually named s. Strings and primitives are appended to it. The primitives that matter most are:

  • gen: generate text and store it under a variable name.
  • select: choose the highest-probability option from a list.
  • += or extend: append text to the prompt state.
  • s["name"]: fetch a generated variable and synchronize if needed.
  • fork: create parallel copies of the prompt state.
  • join: merge prompt states.
  • image and video: add multimodal inputs.
  • regex: constrain gen output to match a regular expression.

A simplified shape of the example is:

The code is not the full contribution. The runtime consequences are:

  • The fork call tells the runtime that several branches share the same prefix.
  • The generated judgments can run in parallel.
  • Fetching f["judgment"] is a synchronization point.
  • The final regex tells the backend that constrained decoding is possible.
  • The image input can be hashed and reused if the same image appears again.

This is a useful programming model because it does not hide the prompt from the user. SGLang is closer to LMQL and Guidance than to high-level agent frameworks such as LangChain or DSPy. The user still controls the low-level prompt state, but the runtime sees more structure than a raw completion server would see.

Table 1. Compared with LMQL and Guidance, the paper emphasizes SGLang’s Python syntax, multimodal primitives, fork and join, and the dedicated SGLang Runtime backend.

My reading of this comparison: SGLang is not trying to be the most abstract programming layer. It is trying to be low-level enough that runtime optimization remains possible.

RadixAttention

SGLang’s most important backend idea is RadixAttention.

The observation is simple:

The KV cache for a token prefix depends only on that exact prefix.

If two token sequences share the prefix , then their KV tensors for those first positions can be reused. The catch is that this is exact prefix reuse, not semantic similarity. “Same text after a different earlier context” is not the same KV state, because self-attention conditions on all previous tokens.

RadixAttention stores reusable KV cache in a radix tree keyed by token prefixes. A radix tree is a compressed trie: edges can contain token spans rather than one token per edge. This is a good fit because prompts often share long segments such as:

  • a system message;
  • few-shot demonstrations;
  • a retrieved document;
  • earlier chat turns;
  • a tree-search path;
  • a common schema or instruction block.

Figure 3. RadixAttention maintains a radix tree under an LRU eviction policy. It handles chat history, few-shot sharing, branching, splitting, insertion, and eviction.

The runtime operations are:

  1. Prefix match: find the longest cached prefix for an incoming token sequence.
  2. Reuse: load/use the cached KV prefix and prefill only the unmatched suffix.
  3. Reference counting: protect nodes used by currently running requests.
  4. Insertion: after a request finishes, insert its prompt and generated continuation into the tree.
  5. Edge splitting: if two prompts share only part of an edge, split the edge so the shared prefix becomes reusable.
  6. Eviction: when memory is needed, evict least-recently-used leaves first.

The leaf-first eviction detail matters. If a leaf is removed, common ancestors remain cached and can still be reused. If the runtime evicted internal shared nodes first, it would destroy reuse for many descendants.

The paper defines cache hit rate as:

This is a prefill-centric metric. A higher hit rate means fewer prompt tokens must be recomputed. It can also reduce memory pressure because shared KV cache allows a larger effective batch.

One implementation detail I like: cached tokens and currently running requests share the same memory pool. There is no fixed cache quota. When the waiting batch needs memory, cached tokens can be evicted in favor of active execution. That is the right serving tradeoff. A cache is useful only if it helps throughput or latency; it should not block new work indefinitely.

Frontend Hints

The paper notes a subtle but important frontend-runtime interaction. During fork, the frontend can send the shared prefix first as a hint, then send the remaining branch prompts. This helps ensure the shared prefix is inserted correctly and gives the runtime a cleaner scheduling/matching structure.

This is the “co-designed” part of the system. The backend can do prefix matching on full strings by itself, but the frontend can make the relationship explicit earlier. That matters when execution is asynchronous and when multiple branches arrive around the same time.

My interpretation: frontend hints are not an implementation convenience. They are the mechanism by which the programming model becomes scheduling information.

Cache-Aware Scheduling

Prefix caching is not enough if the scheduler destroys locality. Suppose the waiting queue contains many requests from several prefix groups. A first-come, first-served schedule may keep switching groups and evict useful prefixes before all related requests are processed.

SGLang schedules requests by matched prefix length. Requests with longer cached prefixes are prioritized, approximating a depth-first traversal of the implicit request tree.

Algorithm 1. The scheduler matches waiting requests against the radix tree, sorts by prefix length, selects requests that fit available memory, protects prefix nodes with reference counters, evicts if needed, runs the batch, and inserts finished requests back into the tree.

The paper proves an offline result:

For a batch of requests, if cache size is at least the maximum request length, visiting the request radix tree in depth-first order achieves the optimal cache hit rate. Longest-shared-prefix-first is equivalent to a DFS order.

The proof’s lower bound is:

DFS achieves equality because when an edge is computed, the scheduler then processes the whole subtree under that edge while the shared prefix remains hot:

The resulting hit rate can be written as:

This is the cleanest theoretical part of the paper. It says the optimal offline schedule is not mysterious: keep walking the tree so the active prefix stays hot.

The online setting is messier:

  • requests arrive over time;
  • decode lengths are unknown;
  • active requests cannot have their referenced nodes evicted;
  • memory pressure changes with current batches;
  • latency-sensitive serving cannot reorder requests arbitrarily.

The paper acknowledges a fairness issue: greedy cache-aware scheduling can cause starvation. That is a real production concern. A scheduler that always favors hot prefixes may delay cold-prefix requests too long. In a real service, I would want a combined policy:

Here p(r) is matched prefix length, w(r) is waiting time, and m(r) is memory risk. The paper does not present this exact formula; this is my mental model for how I would extend it. Prefix locality is valuable, but it should be balanced against fairness and memory risk.

What Patterns Does RadixAttention Cover?

Figure 9. The appendix shows common KV sharing structures: few-shot learning, self-consistency, multi-turn chat, and tree-of-thought.

The four examples are worth reading separately.

Few-shot learning: all questions share the same demonstrations. If the demonstrations are long, caching them once saves a large amount of prefill.

Self-consistency: several answers are sampled from the same prompt. The prompt KV cache is shared, while generated answers diverge.

Multi-turn chat: later turns share earlier chat history. This is a natural prefix reuse pattern, but the reusable prefix grows over time.

Tree-of-thought: branches share search history. This is the irregular case where a simple one-level prefix cache is not enough. A tree is the natural representation.

This is why a radix tree is a better abstraction than a flat hash table. A table can cache full prompts, but it does not naturally represent multi-level partial sharing or subtree locality.

Compressed FSM For Structured Outputs

SGLang’s second runtime optimization targets constrained decoding.

When a model must output JSON or another structured format, a common method is:

  1. Convert the regex or grammar into a finite state machine.
  2. Track the current FSM state.
  3. At each decode step, mask out invalid next tokens.
  4. Generate one token.
  5. Update the FSM state and repeat.

This is correct but slow when the next several characters or tokens are deterministic. For example, after the model begins a JSON object, the literal prefix {"summary": " may have only one valid continuation for many positions. A normal FSM still steps token by token.

Figure 4. A compressed FSM merges deterministic chains, allowing the runtime to jump forward through forced text instead of decoding one token at a time.

Formally, view a regex-derived FSM as:

where is the set of states, is the character or string alphabet, is the transition function, is the initial state, and is the set of final states.

At decoding state , the normal constrained decoder can define an allowed-token set:

Then it masks all other vocabulary tokens:

The compressed-FSM idea is to find singular transition chains. If a state has only one legal outgoing transition and that next state also has only one legal continuation, those edges can be merged into one compressed edge. The runtime can then perform a jump-forward step through the deterministic string.

Figure 10. The appendix gives the background: regex is converted into an FSM, and the FSM guides decoding by masking invalid continuations.

Figure 11. Compressed FSM can jump through deterministic substrings, while normal FSM decoding spends a forward pass on every small step.

The paper reports that compressed FSM increases JSON-decoding throughput by 1.6x. It also notes an important engineering detail: FSM preprocessing should be reused across a batch. Redoing the preprocessing for every request makes throughput 2.4x lower.

There are two caveats I would keep in mind.

First, regex is character/string-level, while LLM decoding is token-level. The runtime must retokenize carefully so the jump-forward text aligns with the tokenizer’s behavior. Bad partitioning can create invalid token boundaries.

Second, compressed choices can distort probabilities. If a broad textual choice maps onto several tokenizations, comparing choices is not always equivalent to comparing one next-token probability. The paper mentions this as future work. For schema enforcement, compressed FSM is very practical; for exact probability accounting over choices, I would be more cautious.

API Speculative Execution

SGLang also supports API-only models, where the runtime cannot modify the backend or access KV cache. The paper proposes API speculative execution for multi-call templates.

The example pattern is:

Naively, the two gen calls require separate API calls and repeat the input context. SGLang can let the first call continue a few extra tokens past the stop condition, cache the extra generated text, and match it against later primitives. If the model follows the template correctly, later calls can reuse the speculative output.

The input-token cost difference can be approximated as:

while speculative execution tries to move toward:

where is the shared context, are per-field prompt fragments, and extra is the additional speculative continuation. The paper reports about a threefold input-token cost reduction in a GPT-3.5 field-extraction example.

This optimization is more fragile than RadixAttention because it depends on the model following a predictable template. I would treat it as a useful API-cost trick, not as a correctness-preserving compiler transformation in every program.

End-To-End Evaluation

The evaluation covers:

  • Models: Llama-2 7B/70B, Mixtral-8x7B, LLaVA image/video models, and GPT-3.5 for API experiments.
  • Hardware: mainly AWS G5 instances with A10G 24GB GPUs, plus A100G 80GB for some larger experiments.
  • Baselines: Guidance, vLLM, and LMQL.
  • Workloads: MMLU, HellaSwag, ReAct agents, generative agents, tree-of-thought, skeleton-of-thought, LLM judge, JSON decoding, multi-turn chat, and DSPy RAG.
  • Metrics: maximum throughput in programs per second, and average single-program latency.

Figure 5. Normalized throughput on Llama-7B. SGLang is normalized to 1.0, so smaller bars indicate slower baselines.

Figure 6. Normalized latency on Llama-7B. Lower is better. SGLang has the smallest latency on most workloads in this figure.

The results should be interpreted by workload type:

  • MMLU benefits because the 5-shot examples are shared.
  • HellaSwag benefits from both few-shot reuse and common question-prefix reuse across choices.
  • ReAct and generative agents reuse agent templates and previous calls.
  • Tree-of-thought and skeleton-of-thought benefit from parallel branches and shared search/skeleton prefixes.
  • JSON decoding benefits mainly from compressed FSM.
  • Multi-turn chat short outputs benefit because prefill reuse matters more when decode is short.
  • Multi-turn chat long outputs benefits less because decode dominates and different sessions have less sharing.
  • DSPy RAG benefits from shared context examples.

This breakdown is more useful than the headline speedup. SGLang is strongest when the workload has visible structure: shared prefixes, branches, short outputs, constrained literals, or repeated context. It is less special when requests are independent and decode dominates.
