Figure 7. Normalized throughput on Mixtral-8x7B with tensor parallelism. The same trend largely holds on a larger MoE model.

Figures 12 and 13. Appendix results for Llama-2-70B throughput and achieved versus optimal cache hit rate.

The appendix cache-hit figure is important. The paper reports cache hit rates from 50% to 99% across workloads, and says cache-aware scheduling reaches about 96% of the optimal hit rate on average. That is strong evidence that the scheduler is doing more than opportunistic prefix matching.

Multimodal Results And Production Deployment

Table 2. SGLang improves throughput on LLaVA image and video workloads, using image/video primitives and cache reuse for repeated visual inputs.

For multimodal models, the paper hashes image inputs and uses that hash as part of the radix-tree key, allowing reuse of image-token KV cache when the same image appears across questions. This is a practical detail. Multimodal prompts often contain expensive visual tokens, and repeated questions about the same image are common in evaluation and applications.

The production deployment note is also useful. In Chatbot Arena, after one month, the paper reports:

  • 52.4% RadixAttention cache hit rate for LLaVA-Next-34B.
  • 74.1% cache hit rate for Vicuna-33B.
  • 1.7x average first-token latency reduction for Vicuna-33B.

I like this result because it grounds the paper in real traffic. Cache hits came from common system messages, reused example images, and multi-turn chat histories. Those are exactly the repeated prefixes one would expect in a serving product.

Ablation Study

Figure 8. Higher cache hit rate improves batch size, throughput, total latency, and first-token latency. The component ablation shows that cache, tree structure, scheduling, frontend parallelism, and frontend hints all matter.

Figure 8 is the best evidence for the system design.

The left two plots show that as cache hit rate increases:

  • batch size increases;
  • throughput increases;
  • total latency decreases;
  • first-token latency decreases.

That aligns with the cost model: fewer prefill tokens mean less compute and memory pressure, which allows larger batches.

The right plot is more interesting. Disabling different components hurts different workloads:

  • No cache removes the main prefill reuse benefit.
  • No tree structure weakens multi-level sharing.
  • FCFS or random scheduling loses locality and cache-hit rate.
  • No frontend parallelism loses parallel branches inside one program.
  • No frontend hint makes runtime matching and scheduling less effective.

This ablation supports the paper’s central claim: the frontend and runtime must be designed together. A backend-only prefix cache helps, but it does not recover the full effect.

The overhead result is also important. On a ShareGPT benchmark without KV-cache reuse opportunities, the paper reports 74.3 seconds for 100 requests, with only 0.2 seconds spent managing RadixAttention data structures. That is less than 0.3% overhead. This justifies turning RadixAttention on by default, at least for the evaluated implementation.

Compiler Mode

The main paper uses interpreter mode, but the appendix also discusses compiler mode. SGLang can trace a program into an intermediate representation with streams, nodes, and dependencies.

Figure 14. An SGLang program and its corresponding dataflow graph. The graph exposes streams, constants, generated values, and synchronization dependencies.

This is conceptually important even if the paper’s main results are interpreter-based. Once the program becomes an IR graph, the system can apply compiler-like transformations:

  • reduce interpreter overhead;
  • serialize programs;
  • schedule streams more aggressively;
  • move code to increase prefix sharing;
  • plan memory and execution statically.

The paper’s code-movement case study is deliberately aggressive. It asks GPT-4 to reorder natural-language prompt components to increase the constant prefix length. On 15 test templates, GPT-4 successfully rewrote 12 without changing semantics by manual inspection, increasing shareable prefix length by 60 tokens on average.

I would treat this as a research direction, not a production-safe transformation. Natural-language code motion can silently change meaning. But the idea is valuable: once prompts are represented as a graph, prompt layout becomes an optimization target.

How SGLang Fits With vLLM, FlashInfer, And Mooncake

I would place these systems at different levels of the serving stack:

System Main abstraction What it optimizes
vLLM / PagedAttention KV blocks inside a worker memory fragmentation, continuous batching, copy-on-write
SGLang / RadixAttention structured LM programs and prefix trees prefix reuse across calls, branch parallelism, constrained decoding
FlashInfer serving attention kernels irregular KV layouts, dynamic scheduling, JIT variants
Mooncake distributed KV-cache lifecycle prefill/decode disaggregation, KV movement, SLO-aware scheduling

SGLang is closest to vLLM in implementation space, but its conceptual level is higher. It asks: what if the runtime sees program structure before it sees token tensors?

The systems are complementary:

  • SGLang can use paged KV memory layouts.
  • FlashInfer can accelerate the irregular attention shapes produced by SGLang.
  • Mooncake can extend KV-cache-aware thinking to cluster-level placement and transfer.

The throughline is that KV cache has become a first-class serving object. PagedAttention manages it as pages, SGLang manages it as a reusable prefix tree, FlashInfer consumes it through layout-aware kernels, and Mooncake schedules it as distributed state.

What I Would Measure In A Reproduction

A normal tokens-per-second benchmark is not enough for this paper. I would reproduce SGLang with metrics that separate the mechanisms:

  1. Prefix cache hit rate: measured in prompt tokens, not request count.
  2. Saved prefill tokens: compare naive prompt tokens with actually computed prompt suffix tokens.
  3. First-token latency: should improve when prefill is saved.
  4. Inter-token latency: should not regress from extra cache management.
  5. Effective batch size: cache reuse should allow larger batches under the same memory budget.
  6. KV memory occupancy: split active-request KV and cached reusable KV.
  7. Eviction rate: high hit rate with excessive eviction may still create instability.
  8. Tree operation overhead: CPU-side match, split, insert, ref-count, and eviction time.
  9. Fairness and tail latency: cache-aware scheduling can starve cold-prefix requests.
  10. Frontend contribution: compare full SGLang, no frontend parallelism, no frontend hints, and backend-only prefix caching.
  11. Constrained-decoding speed: separate FSM preprocessing cost from per-token decode cost.
  12. Correctness under regex: verify tokenization edge cases and probability behavior.

The workload suite should include both high-reuse and low-reuse cases. Otherwise the benchmark only proves that prefix caching helps when prefixes repeat, which is true but incomplete. The more interesting question is whether the runtime can detect reuse, exploit it without harming unrelated traffic, and keep overhead low when reuse is absent.

Limitations

SGLang is strong, but its assumptions matter.

First, RadixAttention helps most when prompts share exact prefixes. It does not help semantically similar prompts unless the token prefix is identical. The paper mentions fuzzy semantic matching as future work, but that would be a different correctness/performance tradeoff.

Second, cache-aware scheduling can conflict with fairness. A hot prefix group may keep getting priority, while cold-prefix requests wait. This is not a small issue in user-facing services. A production scheduler needs aging, SLO constraints, or admission control around the prefix-locality objective.

Third, memory pressure can erase cache benefits. Cached tokens and active requests share the pool. Under high load, cached prefixes may be evicted to admit larger active batches. That is the right behavior, but it means the speedup depends on workload shape and memory headroom.

Fourth, compressed FSM decoding is not free from modeling caveats. Regex constraints live at a string level; LLMs decode tokens. Retokenization and probability distortion are real edge cases.

Fifth, API speculative execution is heuristic. It can reduce API cost when templates are predictable, but if the model deviates from the assumed structure, the system must fall back or validate carefully.

Sixth, compiler-mode prompt rewriting is risky. Moving natural-language text can change semantics in ways a traditional compiler would not allow. The paper frames it as a case study, and I think that is the right level of confidence.

Finally, distributed prefix caching opens consistency and placement questions. The appendix discusses a weakly consistent meta-tree for data parallelism, but the full production design space includes replication, eviction propagation, worker failure, privacy isolation, and cross-node KV movement.

Takeaway

SGLang’s core contribution is the connection between a structured frontend and an optimized runtime. The frontend primitives expose where a program branches, synchronizes, reuses context, and constrains outputs. The backend uses that information to reuse KV cache, schedule for prefix locality, run branches in parallel, and skip deterministic constrained-decoding steps.

The paper’s practical message is:

  • do not submit structured LLM workflows as unrelated strings if you want the serving stack to optimize them;
  • exact prefix reuse is a runtime resource, not just an application convenience;
  • a tree-structured cache is a better fit than a flat cache for agents, self-consistency, multi-turn chat, and tree search;
  • constrained decoding should exploit deterministic spans, not only mask one token at a time;
  • frontend/runtime co-design can matter as much as a faster kernel.

For me, SGLang is the missing middle layer between prompt programming and serving infrastructure. It is above PagedAttention-style memory management and below high-level agent frameworks. That is exactly where many real LLM applications now live: not one prompt, not a full distributed service by itself, but a structured program whose execution shape is rich enough to optimize.

entry.title: Single-Path NAS: Designing Hardware-Efficient ConvNets in Less Than 4 Hours
SmoothQuant: W8A8 LLM Quantization
SNAS: Stochastic Neural Architecture Search
SpQR: Sparse-Quantized LLM Weight Compression
SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization
Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
TE-NAS: Training-Free Architecture Search
TernaryBERT: Distillation-aware Ultra-low Bit BERT
TransNAS-Bench-101: Cross-Task NAS Benchmarking
entry.content:
Duan Y, Chen X, Xu H, et al. TransNAS-Bench-101: Improving Transferability and Generalizability of Cross-Task Neural Architecture Search. 2021.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.11871.pdf
  • Dataset: MindSpore TransNAS-Bench-101
  • VEGA docs: TransNAS-Bench-101

TransNAS-Bench-101 is a NAS benchmark for a question that older tabular benchmarks only partially answer: if an architecture is good on one vision task, does that tell us anything about another task?

NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 are useful because they make architecture search queryable, repeatable, and cheap. But both are still classification-centered. TransNAS-Bench-101 shifts the benchmark target from “find a good cell for classification” to “understand how architecture choices behave across tasks.”

The benchmark evaluates 7,352 backbones on seven vision tasks. That means 51,464 trained models, plus per-epoch metrics, inference time, FLOPs, parameter counts, and training time. The paper says the full generation cost was 193,760 V100 GPU hours, about 22.12 years on one V100. The point is not that everyone should reproduce this cost. The point is that the cost has already been paid once, so transfer-NAS algorithms can be tested without training tens of thousands of networks again.

What It Adds

The main contribution is not simply a larger table. It is a benchmark design that makes task transfer explicit.

There are two search spaces:

  • Cell-level search space: 4,096 DAG cells following the NAS-Bench-201 style, with four operation candidates: zeroize, skip connection, 1x1 convolution, and 3x3 convolution.
  • Macro-level search space: 3,256 residual-block skeletons where depth, downsampling locations, and channel-doubling locations vary.

This distinction matters. A lot of early NAS work searches cells while keeping the macro skeleton fixed. TransNAS-Bench-101 asks whether that is enough when the target task changes. Dense prediction, image reconstruction, and layout regression may care more about where resolution is lost, how channels expand, and how much capacity is allocated at each stage.

Seven Tasks

The benchmark uses Taskonomy-style indoor images and constructs seven tasks from the same visual source distribution.

The tasks cover several types of supervision:

  • Classification: object classification and scene classification.
  • Point regression: room layout.
  • Self-supervised learning: jigsaw puzzle and autoencoding.
  • Pixel-level prediction: surface normal and semantic segmentation.

This choice is deliberate. If every task came from unrelated datasets, transfer failure could be blamed on dataset shift. Here, the images share a common source, so architecture-task interaction becomes easier to isolate.

The paper uses 24 buildings from Taskonomy, about 120K images, split into 80K train, 20K validation, and 20K test. Every architecture is trained on every task.

Task-Specific Heads

The benchmark searches the backbone and plugs it into task-specific decoders.

Classification-like tasks use global average pooling plus a linear head. Pixel-level prediction tasks use convolution and deconvolution decoders. Losses and metrics also differ by task: accuracy for classification and jigsaw, SSIM for autoencoding and surface normal, mIoU for semantic segmentation, and L2 loss for room layout.

This is important for reading the results. The benchmark is not forcing all tasks into a classification interface. The backbone is the common object being searched, but the task head and metric remain task-specific.

Compared With NAS-Bench-101 And NAS-Bench-201

The paper includes a short benchmark comparison.

TransNAS-Bench-101 is smaller than NAS-Bench-101 in raw search-space size, but broader in task coverage:

  • NAS-Bench-101: one dataset, one task domain, cell search.
  • NAS-Bench-201: three datasets, one task domain, cell search.
  • TransNAS-Bench-101: one image source, seven task domains, cell and macro search.

That is the right tradeoff for cross-task NAS. Exhaustively evaluating hundreds of millions of architectures across seven tasks would be impractical. A smaller but fully trained benchmark is more useful for diagnosing transfer behavior.

Search-Space Statistics

The aggregate statistics already show that the macro and cell spaces are not interchangeable.

The macro-level space reports better average performance on all seven tasks in the table. It also tends to cost more, especially for dense output tasks such as autoencoding, surface normal, and semantic segmentation.

A few numbers are useful anchors:

  • Object classification average accuracy: 39.71 for cell-level vs 44.24 for macro-level.
  • Scene classification average accuracy: 45.23 for cell-level vs 52.92 for macro-level.
  • Semantic segmentation average mIoU: 19.95 for cell-level vs 24.47 for macro-level.
  • Jigsaw average accuracy: 76.57 for cell-level vs 93.43 for macro-level.

This does not mean macro search is always the final answer. It means that benchmark conclusions can change when the search space changes. A transfer-NAS method that only works on a cell grammar may not be robust enough.

Architecture Landscape

Figure 3 plots average task ranking against FLOPs and parameter count.

The macro space has a smoother spread of architectures across compute. The cell space is more clustered because the macro skeleton is fixed and only the cell operation choices vary. This makes the macro search space more expressive for compute allocation, but also creates a wider range of training costs.

The paper observes that more FLOPs and longer training time often correlate with better average ranking, but only within a reasonable range. The largest networks are not automatically the best. This is exactly why the benchmark records compute information: an algorithm should not be rewarded only for discovering expensive architectures.

Cross-Task Correlation

The most useful part of the paper is the cross-task rank-correlation analysis.

The all-network correlations can look encouraging. Many task pairs have positive rank correlation, especially in the cell-level search space. But the top-half correlations shrink quickly. This is the hard NAS regime: after weak architectures are filtered out, the remaining candidates are all plausible, and task transfer becomes much less reliable.

The paper gives a concrete example in the macro search space.

Scene classification and semantic segmentation have a high correlation in the macro-level space. Room layout and autoencoding are much weaker. This is not obvious from the task names alone. Both room layout and autoencoding use the same image source, but architecture ranking still behaves differently.

The autoencoding example is even more revealing:

  • In the macro space, autoencoding has moderate correlation with semantic segmentation and surface normal.
  • In the cell space, autoencoding has almost no correlation with semantic segmentation and only weak correlation with surface normal.

So transferability is not only a property of source and target tasks. It also depends on the search space. That is the core lesson of this benchmark.

Cross-Task Performance Structure

The appendix gives a more detailed pairwise view of task performance.

The cell-level plots show more fragmented behavior. Some cell choices produce very poor networks on particular tasks, which creates larger gaps. The macro-level plots look smoother because changing downsampling and channel schedules affects the backbone more globally.

This is useful when designing a transfer method. If the target task enters a part of the architecture space where source-task ranking is unstable, direct transfer can become negative transfer.

Transfer Baselines

The paper evaluates five transfer/search schemes:

  • Random search.
  • Direct transfer of top architectures.
  • Regularized evolution trained from scratch.
  • Regularized evolution with transferred population initialization.
  • PPO-style policy transfer and CATCH-style contextual policy transfer.

The REA curves are a good baseline because evolution is simple and robust.

REA-transfer gives small but stable improvements. It does not magically solve transfer, but it is less brittle than directly reusing the best architecture from another task. The transferred population gives the target-task search a better starting point while still allowing mutation to adapt.

The policy-transfer result is more cautionary.

Plain PPO transfer can underperform PPO trained from scratch. That is classic negative transfer: the policy overfits to the source task and starts the target task with the wrong bias. CATCH helps by adding task context and an evaluator, and it can work very well on some settings such as macro-space object classification. But the paper is careful not to present policy transfer as universally solved.

Overall Transfer Results

The full result table makes the baseline story concrete.

A few takeaways from the table:

  • Direct transfer is weak. Its percentile is 77.17 in the cell space and 83.59 in the macro space, far below random search.
  • Random search is already strong: 97.91 percentile in the cell space and 98.18 in the macro space.
  • REA-transfer is near the top: 99.02 percentile in the cell space and 99.11 in the macro space.
  • PPO-transfer is fragile: it drops to 94.94 percentile in the cell space, below PPO trained from scratch.
  • CATCH improves policy transfer in some cases, but it is not uniformly best.

This is a good benchmark behavior. It does not let a paper win by beating a weak baseline once. Random search is strong, direct transfer can fail, and the algorithm has to be robust across task families and search spaces.

Ranking Convergence

The appendix also checks whether per-epoch rankings stabilize.

Most tasks trend upward: later-epoch rankings become more consistent with previous-epoch rankings. Some tasks stabilize quickly, while room layout and semantic segmentation are noisier. This matters if a NAS algorithm wants to use early training curves. Early signals may be useful, but the benchmark warns against treating early rank as exact final rank.

How I Would Use It

TransNAS-Bench-101 is most useful as a diagnostic benchmark, not as a final claim that an architecture will transfer to all real systems.

I would use it to answer questions like:

  • Does my search method beat random search consistently?
  • Does it still work when the target task is dense prediction instead of classification?
  • Does it depend on cell search, or can it handle macro skeleton choices?
  • Does transfer help after the method is allowed to adapt, or is it just direct reuse?
  • Does the method avoid negative transfer when the source and target task rankings disagree?

Those questions are closer to real NAS deployment than “did it win on one small classification dataset?”

Limitations

The benchmark is still controlled.

  • All tasks come from an indoor-scene image source.
  • The search spaces are finite and handcrafted.
  • The cell space has only four operation choices.
  • The macro space searches a residual-block skeleton, not arbitrary modern backbones.
  • Hardware measurements are tied to the benchmark setup.
  • Querying the benchmark is much cheaper than real training, so algorithms can accidentally overfit to the tabular benchmark if evaluation protocol is loose.

The value is that these constraints are explicit. They make controlled transfer experiments possible.

Takeaway

TransNAS-Bench-101 is a good reminder that NAS transfer is not a free byproduct of finding a strong architecture on one task. Architecture rankings can change across tasks, and the amount of transfer depends heavily on the search space. A convincing NAS method should beat strong simple baselines, adapt after transfer, and survive both cell-level and macro-level search spaces.

entry.title: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context
entry.content:
Paper: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context

Code: kimiyoung/transformer-xl

Transformer-XL is an early long-context Transformer paper that is still worth reading carefully. The idea is not simply “make the context longer.” The paper identifies two concrete failures in fixed-length Transformer language models:

  • context fragmentation: training cuts a long corpus into short independent segments, so information cannot flow across segment boundaries;
  • evaluation recomputation: a vanilla Transformer can use a sliding window at inference, but each shifted window has to be recomputed from scratch.

Transformer-XL fixes both with a recurrence over segment hidden states. The model caches hidden states from previous segments, reuses them as memory for the next segment, and changes positional encoding from absolute positions to relative distances so the cached states remain positionally meaningful.

All crops below are taken from the original 2019 PDF.

Fixed-Length Transformer LM

A vanilla Transformer language model can only attend inside the segment it is currently processing. If the segment length is , the largest direct dependency visible to the model is bounded by , even if the original article is thousands of tokens long.

Figure 1. Vanilla Transformer LM training and evaluation with segment length 4. Training sees independent segments. Evaluation can slide the segment one token at a time, but that recomputes the whole segment repeatedly.

This has two different costs.

First, training loses cross-segment context. The first tokens of each segment are predicted with little left context even if the previous segment contained exactly the information needed. This is what the paper calls context fragmentation.

Second, evaluation is expensive. To give each prediction the longest context seen during training, a vanilla model evaluates a full length- segment, predicts only the last position, shifts the window by one token, and evaluates another full segment. That procedure uses context, but it throws away almost all computation from the previous step.

For a decoder-only model this is an unnatural use of self-attention. The hidden states for old tokens do not change when the next token arrives. Transformer-XL turns that observation into a recurrent state.

Segment-Level Recurrence

Transformer-XL processes a stream as consecutive segments, but it does not discard the previous segment’s hidden states. For each layer, it stores the hidden state sequence from previous segments as a memory and concatenates that memory with the current segment when forming keys and values.

Figure 2. Transformer-XL reuses previous hidden states as fixed memory. During training the memory is stop-gradient. During evaluation the same mechanism gives an extended context without recomputing old segments.

Let and be two consecutive segments of length . Let be the hidden state sequence of layer for segment . Transformer-XL builds an extended layer input for segment :

where means stop-gradient and is concatenation along the sequence dimension. Queries come only from the current segment, while keys and values come from the concatenated memory plus current segment:

The key detail is the layer index. Layer in the current segment attends to cached states from layer of the previous segment. Therefore, dependency across segments shifts one layer downward each time it crosses a segment boundary. With layers and segment length , the maximum dependency path grows on the order of rather than just .

This is similar in spirit to truncated BPTT for RNNs, but the stored state is different:

Model family Reused state What is truncated
RNN-LM with truncated BPTT Usually the last hidden state Gradient through time
Transformer-XL A sequence of hidden states per layer Gradient across segments
Modern KV-cache decoding Projected keys and values per layer Usually no training gradient, inference only

Transformer-XL is not exactly the same abstraction as the modern KV cache. The paper describes caching hidden states and then using them to form keys and values for the next segment. But conceptually it is one of the clean ancestors of state reuse in decoder-only Transformers: do not recompute old token representations when the new segment only needs to attend to them.

Training And Evaluation Behavior

During training, the previous memory is fixed. Gradients do not propagate into old segments:

The stop-gradient choice is a practical compromise. It keeps training close to ordinary segment training in memory cost, while letting each segment condition on previous segments in the forward pass.

During evaluation, the memory can be longer than one previous segment. The paper uses a memory length and a segment length , so each segment can attend over positions. The old representations are reused instead of recomputed. This is where the large evaluation speedup comes from: the model still attends to history, but it does not run all layers again for every shifted window.

The causal mask has to cover two regions:

  • memory positions are always in the past, so current tokens may attend to them;
  • inside the current segment, token may attend only to positions up to .

That mask is what makes chunked stream processing equivalent to autoregressive modeling rather than leaking future tokens.

Why Absolute Position Breaks Memory Reuse

Caching hidden states alone is not enough. If a Transformer uses absolute positional embeddings, then each segment reuses the same position indices . Token in the previous segment and token in the current segment both carry the same absolute position even though their relative distance to the query is different.

For recurrence, the model needs to know where a memory token is relative to the current query, not where that token sat inside its original segment.

The paper makes this precise by decomposing the absolute-position attention score:

The four terms can be read as:

Term Role in absolute attention
content-to-content addressing
content query to absolute key position
absolute query position to key content
absolute query position to absolute key position

Those and terms are tied to positions inside a segment. They do not survive state reuse cleanly.

Relative Positional Encoding

Transformer-XL replaces absolute positional dependence with relative distance dependence. The new attention score is:

Here is a sinusoidal relative positional encoding for the distance between the query position and the key position . The learned vectors and replace the absolute query-position terms with global content and position biases.

The four relative terms have a useful interpretation:

Term Meaning
(a) content-based addressing Which token content should this query attend to?
(b) content-dependent positional bias Given this query content, which relative distances are useful?
(c) global content bias Which key contents are generally important?
(d) global positional bias Which relative distances are generally important?

The comparison to Shaw et al. (2018) is important. Shaw-style relative attention mainly keeps terms (a) and (b), and it uses learned relative embeddings. Transformer-XL keeps two additional bias terms and uses sinusoidal relative encodings. The paper argues that the sinusoidal structure helps the model generalize to longer memory at evaluation time than it saw during training.

There is also an implementation issue. Naively computing for every pair would be quadratic in the number of pairwise distances. Appendix B shows the usual efficient trick: compute the relative logits as a matrix product over all possible distances, then shift rows so each query sees the correct relative offset. In later codebases this family of operations is often called a relative shift.

What The Architecture Actually Buys

It is useful to separate the two proposed pieces:

Piece Main purpose Without it
Segment-level recurrence Reuse past hidden states and extend context beyond one segment Context is fragmented and evaluation recomputes old segments
Relative positional encoding Make cached states positionally coherent Memory states carry stale absolute positions

The recurrence solves the systems and context problem. The relative position scheme makes the recurrence mathematically usable.

This is why the method is stronger than simply increasing segment length. A larger segment helps, but it increases attention cost and still imposes a hard boundary. Transformer-XL keeps the training segment manageable and adds a rolling memory that can be longer during evaluation.

Main Results

The headline numbers are strong for the 2019 language modeling setting. Transformer-XL reports state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art results on word-level and character-level benchmarks.

Table 1. On WikiText-103, the large Transformer-XL reaches 18.3 perplexity, improving over the contemporary adaptive-input result of 20.5.

WikiText-103 is the benchmark that most directly matches the paper’s motivation. The articles are long enough that cross-segment dependencies matter. The paper uses attention length 384 during training and 1600 during evaluation for the standard word-level setting.

Table 2. On enwik8, the 24-layer Transformer-XL reaches 0.99 bits per character. The 12-layer 41M-parameter model already matches the 64-layer vanilla Transformer result from Al-Rfou et al. (2018).

Table 3. On text8, the 24-layer Transformer-XL reaches 1.08 bits per character.

The character-level results show that the architecture is not only improving a word-level softmax setup. On enwik8, the paper trains with attention length 784 and evaluates with attention length 3800. That train/eval mismatch is exactly where relative positional encoding matters.

Table 4. On One Billion Word, the large Transformer-XL reports 21.8 perplexity.

One Billion Word is shuffled at the sentence level, so it does not preserve long document dependencies. The improvement there is therefore not mainly about modeling thousand-token discourse. The paper uses it as evidence that recurrence also reduces context fragmentation for short sequences.

Table 5. On Penn Treebank, Transformer-XL reaches 54.52 perplexity without two-step finetuning, close to the best finetuned MoS result.

Penn Treebank is much smaller, so this result is less central to the long-context argument. It is still useful because it shows the method does not only work when the dataset is large.

Ablation: Recurrence And Position Encoding

The ablation table is the most important evidence in the paper. It asks whether the performance comes from recurrence, from the new positional encoding, or from both.

Table 6. WikiText-103 ablation. Recurrence plus the Transformer-XL relative position scheme gives the best result and can benefit from longer evaluation attention length.

The pattern is clear:

  • using recurrence with the paper’s relative positional encoding gives the best perplexity;
  • replacing it with Shaw et al. relative encoding is worse;
  • removing recurrence is worse;
  • absolute encodings do not generalize cleanly to longer attention length;
  • increasing evaluation attention length helps only when the positional scheme can handle reused states.

The 151M setting is especially useful to read. The model is trained with a finite backpropagation length, but perplexity improves when the evaluation attention length is increased. That is the intended behavior: train on manageable segments, then reuse a longer memory at inference.

One Billion Word And Evaluation Speed

The paper also isolates context fragmentation using One Billion Word. Since the dataset is shuffled and lacks document-level long dependencies, an improvement from recurrence is harder to attribute to long-range discourse. It is more likely to come from not starting every segment cold.

Tables 7 and 9. On One Billion Word, recurrence improves perplexity even without document-level long dependency. The same state reuse gives very large evaluation speedups over the vanilla sliding-window Transformer.

The table reports:

Variant One Billion Word PPL
Transformer-XL 25.2
With Shaw et al. encoding 25.7
Without recurrence 27.1

For evaluation speed, the paper compares against a vanilla Transformer that repeatedly evaluates shifted windows. The largest reported slowdown of the vanilla baseline is 1,874x relative to Transformer-XL. This number is not a claim that attention itself becomes 1,874x cheaper. It is a consequence of avoiding massive repeated full-window recomputation.

Effective Context Length

The paper introduces Relative Effective Context Length (RECL) because ordinary effective context length is hard to compare across models with different base perplexities. RECL asks whether increasing context still gives a relative improvement over a shared short-context baseline.

Table 8. Transformer-XL has longer RECL than QRNN, LSTM, and the vanilla Transformer baseline. The strongest 151M Transformer-XL reaches 900 words at .

The table is compact but important:

Model RECL at RECL at RECL at
Transformer-XL 151M 900 800 700
QRNN 500 400 300
LSTM 400 300 200
Transformer-XL 128M 700 600 500
Transformer-XL 128M with Shaw encoding 400 400 300
Transformer-XL 128M without recurrence 300 300 300
Vanilla Transformer 128 128 128

The authors summarize this as Transformer-XL modeling dependencies 80% longer than RNNs and 450% longer than the vanilla Transformer under their RECL comparison.

The supporting plots make the same point visually.

Figure 3. Relative perplexity gains remain useful over longer context spans for Transformer-XL than for the recurrent and Transformer baselines.

Figure 4. Perplexity keeps improving as context length grows, especially for Transformer-XL with recurrence and the proposed relative positional encoding.

This is the strongest part of the paper for me. The benchmark tables show that the model is good, but the context-length analysis shows why it is good. The model is not just a larger Transformer with a better softmax; it is extracting measurable value from longer history.

Attention Visualization

The appendix visualizes attention behavior for the WikiText-103 model with 16 layers, 10 heads per layer, and memory length 640.

Figure 5. Average attention over the previous 640 tokens. Most heads prefer nearby tokens, but some heads spread attention over much longer ranges.

The average heatmap is unsurprising at first: nearby context gets more attention. The useful detail is that a few heads maintain broad attention over the memory span. Those heads are the mechanism by which the model can keep long-range information accessible instead of collapsing entirely into local n-gram behavior.

Figure 6. Three wide-range heads selected from different layers. The low-level head is broad, while later heads become sparse and more token-specific.

The paper interprets the three selected heads as different long-range behaviors:

  • an early-layer head scans broadly across memory;
  • a middle-layer head picks sparse positions across the full range;
  • a final-layer head gives each target token a distinct sparse focus.

That pattern is plausible: early layers gather candidate information, deeper layers decide which pieces matter for the current prediction.

Figure 7. The attention score decomposition shows different behavior for content addressing, content-dependent positional bias, and global positional bias.

The score-term visualization is a useful sanity check for the relative attention formula. Term (a), the pure content-based term, is comparatively broad. Term (b), the content-dependent positional bias, resembles the final attention distribution more strongly. Term (d), the global positional bias, also favors nearby positions but is flatter. This supports the paper’s claim that the four-term decomposition is not just algebraic decoration; the terms learn different roles.

Implementation Notes

If I were implementing Transformer-XL from scratch, these are the pieces I would treat as bug-prone:

  1. Memory shape. Each layer needs its own memory tensor. The memory length can differ between training and evaluation.
  2. Stop-gradient. The memory used during training must be detached, otherwise the graph grows across segments.
  3. Causal mask. Current tokens can attend to all memory positions and to previous current-segment positions, but never to future current-segment positions.
  4. Relative shift. Relative attention logits need the correct distance alignment. An off-by-one error can silently preserve tensor shapes while corrupting position semantics.
  5. Position scheme. Absolute positional embeddings are not a drop-in choice when hidden states are reused across segments.
  6. Memory update. After each segment, append the new hidden states and keep only the latest states.
  7. Train/eval mismatch. If evaluation memory is longer than training memory, the relative position encoding must be able to represent those longer distances.

A minimal memory update looks like this:

The real implementation has to do this for each layer and keep the hidden state list aligned with the layer stack.

Relation To Later LLM Systems

Transformer-XL sits before the current LLM serving vocabulary, so it is easy to read it through later ideas:

  • XLNet directly builds on Transformer-XL’s recurrence and relative positions.
  • Modern decoder inference uses KV cache rather than recomputing previous tokens; Transformer-XL is an earlier training-and-evaluation version of the same state-reuse instinct.
  • T5-style relative bias, RoPE, and ALiBi are not the same method, but they belong to the same broader move away from fixed absolute position embeddings.
  • Sliding-window and recurrent-memory Transformers keep revisiting the same tradeoff: finite memory is cheap enough to use, but it is still finite.

The limitation is equally important. Transformer-XL does not make arbitrary full-context attention cheap. For a segment length and memory length , attention still scales like per layer. The method avoids recomputing old segments and extends usable context, but it does not remove attention’s dependence on the visible memory size.

The stop-gradient boundary is another limitation. The model can attend to old hidden states in the forward pass, but learning signals do not backpropagate through all historical tokens. That is the price paid to keep training feasible.

Takeaway

The core lesson of Transformer-XL is that long-context modeling needs both a state mechanism and a position mechanism. Caching hidden states solves the fixed-window systems problem, but it only works if the model interprets cached states by relative distance rather than stale absolute indices.

The paper’s strongest evidence is not just the perplexity table. It is the combination of:

  • better language modeling results on WikiText-103, enwik8, text8, One Billion Word, and PTB;
  • ablations showing recurrence and the proposed relative encoding both matter;
  • RECL analysis showing longer usable context;
  • evaluation speedups from avoiding sliding-window recomputation;
  • attention visualizations showing that some heads actually use long memory.

That combination is why Transformer-XL is still a useful reference point. It is not the final answer to long-context attention, but it is one of the cleanest demonstrations that Transformer language models need memory reuse and position handling to move beyond fixed-length segments.

entry.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
ViTAS: Vision Transformer Architecture Search
entry.content:
Paper: ViTAS: Vision Transformer Architecture Search

Su X, You S, Xie J, Zheng M, Wang F, Qian C, Zhang C, Wang X, Xu C. ViTAS: Vision Transformer Architecture Search. ECCV 2022.

ViTAS is a Vision Transformer NAS paper, but the useful part is not only that it searches a better ViT backbone. The deeper point is about whether a one-shot Transformer supernet can rank candidate architectures fairly.

The paper’s diagnosis is sharp:

  • one-shot NAS trains a large supernet and lets candidate architectures inherit weights from it;
  • in width/dimension search, common ordinal sharing gives small dimensions the first channels;
  • those early channels are trained more often than later channels;
  • for ViTs, where token embeddings and FC projections dominate the block, this channel imbalance makes inherited accuracy a biased estimator;
  • if inherited accuracy is biased, the search loop can select architectures that merely received better shared weights.

ViTAS attacks this with cyclic weight sharing for token embedding dimensions, then adds identity shifting and a weak superformer training recipe to stabilize search.

All crops below are taken from the original PDF.

Why ViT NAS Is Not Just CNN NAS

Vision Transformers expose several architecture dimensions at once:

  • patch size or local/global attention granularity;
  • number of attention heads;
  • attention projection width;
  • MLP hidden width;
  • operation type in each layer;
  • stage depth through identity operations.

In a one-shot setting, a superformer must contain many candidates and give each candidate a meaningful inherited evaluation. This is already hard for CNNs. It becomes more fragile for ViTs because changing token embedding dimension changes the FC projections used by attention and MLP blocks.

The paper uses two search spaces:

Table 1. Twins-based ViTAS space. It searches patch size/head choices, attention dimensions, MLP dimensions, and depth through TBS layers.

For the Twins-small based space, the paper reports a search-space size around 1.1e54, with FLOPs ranging from 0.02G to 11.2G and parameters from 0.16M to 86.1M.

Table 2. DeiT-based ViTAS space. It searches patch size, head number, attention/MLP dimensions, and depth through vanilla ViT block vs identity choices.

For the DeiT-small based space, the paper reports around 5.4e34 candidates, with FLOPs ranging from 0.1G to 20.0G and parameters from 0.5M to 97.5M.

The search problem is roughly:

The weak link is step 2. If the superformer trains some channels more than others, inherited validation accuracy is not a clean architecture score.

The Channel Fairness Problem

The core figure compares three ways to share channels when searching width.

Figure 1. Ordinal sharing over-trains early channels. Bilateral sharing reduces part of the imbalance but doubles the cost. Cyclic sharing aims to balance training time and channel influence with single-pass cost.

In ordinal sharing, a candidate of width uses the first channels:

If the maximum width is , channel 1 appears in every sampled width, while channel appears only when the widest candidate is sampled. The paper writes the training count for channel as C_A(i) = l - i + 1. That is the bias.

This is dangerous in a supernet:

  • narrow candidates inherit heavily trained early channels;
  • wide candidates inherit a mix of heavily trained and under-trained channels;
  • the search algorithm may confuse weight quality with architecture quality.

BCNet-style bilateral sharing improves the picture by training from both sides, but it needs double training cost and still does not fully equalize the influence of each channel. ViTAS proposes cyclic sharing as a single-pass mapping.

Cyclic Weight Sharing

ViTAS designs an indicator matrix for channel use. In plain notation:

The mapping is chosen under two goals.

Goal Meaning
Training fairness Each channel should be selected about the same number of times.
Influence uniformity Each channel should contribute similar total gradient influence across the dimensions that use it.

The second condition is the more interesting one. In an FC layer, a dimension with more input channels distributes gradient contribution across more channels. The paper approximates the influence of a channel in a width- layer as proportional to 1 / j. Therefore, equal training count alone is not enough; the method also tries to equalize weighted influence.

The final mapping is solved as a small quadratically constrained quadratic program over the binary assignment matrix. This sounds heavy, but it is not in the training loop. Once the mapping is selected, cyclic sharing is just an index mapping for channel slices.

The appendix visualizes cyclic maps for different group counts:

Figure 10. Cyclic channel maps for group counts from 5 to 10. Red channels rotate across layer-width choices rather than staying fixed at the left side.

For the blog-level takeaway, I read cyclic sharing as a fairness patch for width-search supernets:

This matters because ViTAS is not trying to search from a randomly initialized subnetwork each time. It relies on inherited weights. Any systematic imbalance in inherited weights directly biases the search.

Private Class Token

Pure ViT and DeiT-style models use a class token. If patch size is searched, the number of patch tokens changes, and the class token interacts with different token layouts.

ViTAS uses a private class token per patch-size setting.

Figure 2. Different patch sizes get private class tokens, avoiding interference between paths with different token counts.

The point is small but practical. The class token has very few parameters, so privatizing it barely changes memory or compute. But it avoids forcing architectures with different token grids to share one class-token parameter.

Identity Shifting

Depth search is implemented with identity operations. A layer can be a real operation or an identity, so the effective depth changes.

The problem is that the same final architecture can be represented by multiple paths through the superformer. If identity operations are allowed anywhere, several path layouts can collapse to the same sequence of real operations. Those paths may train differently, which makes architecture evaluation noisy.

Figure 3. The original search space can map several superformer paths to the same architecture. ViTAS shifts identity operations deeper so each architecture has a cleaner path representation.

ViTAS resolves this by arranging identity choices at deeper layers inside a stage. With three operation choices and twelve searched layers, the paper says this reduces the operation search space from 3^12 path layouts to 2^13 - 1 effective choices.

The important part is not the exact count. The useful idea is that depth search should avoid many-to-one path encodings. Otherwise the superformer is asked to rank paths even when the final architecture is identical.

Superformer Training Recipe

The authors found that a strong augmentation and regularization recipe can destabilize superformer training. That is slightly counterintuitive because strong recipes are usually helpful for final ViT training.

For search, the superformer is not the final model. It is a ranking proxy. The paper therefore uses a weak recipe:

Table 4. Weakening augmentation and regularization improves the searched/retrained model. The best searched Twins 1.4G model reaches 79.4% after retraining.

The selected superformer search recipe is simple:

Item Setting
Epochs 300
Batch size 1024
Optimizer AdamW
Learning rate 0.001
LR decay cosine
Warmup 5 epochs

The appendix clarifies that superformers for DeiT- and Twins-based spaces use the same search recipe. The final searched architectures are then retrained with the corresponding DeiT or Twins recipe.

This separation is important:

  • superformer training should make ranking stable;
  • final retraining should make the chosen architecture strong.

Treating those as the same objective can make the search proxy worse.

Training Stability Evidence

The loss curves are one of the most useful figures in the paper.

Figure 4. Cyclic sharing is slower in the first few epochs but reaches lower superformer loss later. Identity shifting also converges to a lower loss than the original path encoding.

The paper’s interpretation:

  • ordinal sharing can look better early because a subset of channels gets trained heavily;
  • after enough epochs, that imbalance hurts the superformer as a whole;
  • cyclic sharing trains more evenly and ends with lower loss;
  • identity shifting removes redundant path encodings and also improves convergence.

The text reports final training losses around 2.4 for the original identity setting and 1.5 with identity shifting on ImageNet-100. It also reports that searched architectures from the shifted setting reach 90.4%, compared with 88.3% from the original setting in that experiment.

The ranking-correlation experiment is even closer to the NAS objective.

Figure 5. Cyclic sharing gives higher Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation over sampled paths than ordinal or bilateral sharing.

This is the evidence I care about most. A superformer can have a nice validation loss and still rank candidates poorly. ViTAS explicitly checks correlation over 2000 sampled paths across FLOPs groups, which directly tests whether inherited evaluation is a better search signal.

ImageNet Results: Twins Space

ViTAS first searches in a Twins-based hierarchical transformer space.

Table 3. Searched Twins-based ViTAS models on ImageNet-1k under different FLOPs budgets.

Key rows:

Model FLOPs Params Top-1
Twins-T reimplementation 1.4G 11.5M 77.8%
ViTAS-Twins-T 1.4G 13.8M 79.4%
Twins-SVT-S reimplementation 2.9G 24.0M 81.6%
ViTAS-Twins-S 3.0G 30.5M 82.0%
Twins-SVT-B reimplementation 8.6G 56.0M 83.2%
ViTAS-Twins-B 8.8G 66.0M 83.5%
ViTAS-Twins-L 16.1G 124.8M 84.0%

The tiny result is the cleanest gain: ViTAS-Twins-T improves the reimplemented Twins-T by 1.6 percentage points at roughly the same FLOPs. At larger scales the gains are smaller but still positive.

There is a tradeoff: ViTAS-Twins models often use more parameters and lower throughput than the nearest baseline. The paper reports FLOPs, parameters, and throughput together, which is good. The result should not be read as “searched is always faster.” It is more accurate to say that ViTAS finds stronger accuracy/compute points inside the chosen transformer space.

ImageNet Results: DeiT Space

ViTAS also searches a pure DeiT-style space, without the hierarchical/local attention biases of Twins.

Table 6. DeiT-based ViTAS results on ImageNet-1k.

The small-budget case:

Model FLOPs Top-1
DeiT-T reimplementation 1.3G 72.3%
AutoFormer-T reimplementation 1.3G 74.7%
ViTAS-DeiT-A 1.4G 75.6%

The larger case:

Model FLOPs Top-1
DeiT-S reimplementation 4.6G 79.9%
AutoFormer-S reimplementation 5.1G 79.8%
ViTAS-DeiT-B 4.9G 80.2%

The result is useful because it separates ViTAS from Twins-specific priors. Cyclic sharing and the stabilized superformer recipe still help in a DeiT-style space.

Transfer To Detection And Segmentation

Searched ImageNet classifiers can fail to transfer. ViTAS evaluates the searched Twins backbones on COCO2017 and ADE20K.

Table 7. COCO2017 object detection and instance segmentation transfer with Mask R-CNN and RetinaNet.

Representative Mask R-CNN box AP:

Backbone Mask R-CNN box AP Mask AP
Twins-SVT-S reimplementation 43.5 40.1
ViTAS-Twins-S 45.9 41.5
Twins-SVT-B reimplementation 45.5 41.4
ViTAS-Twins-B 47.6 42.9
Twins-SVT-L reimplementation 45.9 41.6
ViTAS-Twins-L 48.2 43.3

The RetinaNet side shows the same pattern: ViTAS backbones improve over the reimplemented Twins baselines across S/B/L sizes.

Table 8. ADE20K semantic segmentation transfer with Semantic FPN and UperNet.

Representative mIoU:

Backbone Semantic FPN mIoU UperNet mIoU
Twins-SVT-S reimplementation 43.6 45.9
ViTAS-Twins-S 46.6 47.9
Twins-SVT-B reimplementation 45.5 47.7
ViTAS-Twins-B 49.5 50.2
Twins-SVT-L reimplementation 46.9 49.2
ViTAS-Twins-L 50.4 51.3

The transfer results matter because they weaken a common NAS criticism: maybe the architecture only fits ImageNet classification. Here the searched backbones remain strong for dense prediction.

The appendix plots the same comparison as curves:

Figure 9. ViTAS transfer curves on ADE20K and COCO2017. Under similar FLOPs budgets, the searched backbones stay above the baseline curves.

Ablation: What Actually Matters

The compact ablation table is the best summary of ViTAS as a method.

Table 9. Cyclic sharing improves over ordinal and bilateral sharing, and weak augmentation adds another large gain.

The table can be read in two blocks.

Without weak augmentation:

Sharing Top-1
Ordinal 77.2%
Bilateral 77.6%
Cyclic 77.9%

With weak augmentation:

Sharing Top-1
Ordinal + weak aug 78.1%
Bilateral + weak aug 78.5%
Cyclic + weak aug 79.4%

This says two things:

  1. cyclic sharing is better than the two channel-sharing baselines under the same augmentation regime;
  2. the superformer training recipe is not a side detail, because weak augmentation contributes a large part of the final gain.

So I would not summarize ViTAS as only “cyclic weight sharing.” The method is a package: cyclic sharing, identity shifting, private class token for DeiT-style patch search, and a search-specific weak training recipe.

Comparison With AutoFormer

AutoFormer and ViTAS are close in time and motivation. Both are one-shot NAS methods for Vision Transformers. The difference is where they focus:

Paper Main issue Mechanism
AutoFormer Make inherited subnet evaluation reliable in a ViT supernet weight entanglement
ViTAS Make dimension/channel sharing fair in a ViT superformer cyclic channel sharing

The appendix compares the searched DeiT-T style architectures.

Figure 8. ViTAS and AutoFormer choose different DeiT-T width/head patterns. ViTAS keeps smaller dimensions in early layers and allocates more dimension/head budget later.

The authors point out several patterns:

  • ViTAS keeps smaller dimensions in earlier layers and more dimensions later.
  • Early layers tend to use smaller attention dimensions than MLP output dimensions.
  • Attention dimensions become larger in later layers.
  • ViTAS uses fewer blocks under the tight 1.4G budget, while AutoFormer stays closer to DeiT-T’s layer count.

This is not a universal design law, but it is a useful search result. Under a tight compute budget, the method prefers to save early-layer width and spend more capacity in later attention/head choices.

Searched Architecture Visualization

The appendix visualizes searched Twins architectures.

Figure 11. Visualization of searched ViTAS-Twins architectures and dimension percentages.

The figure is dense, but it gives an intuition for why NAS can still be useful even after strong manual ViT designs. The searched models do not simply scale every stage uniformly. They vary local/global choices, depth, and layer dimensions stage by stage.

The paper’s appendix makes three practical observations from the searched architectures:

  • in the last stage, local blocks can behave similarly to global blocks because the feature size is already small;
  • dimension changes are more obvious in Twins-based architectures than in DeiT-based architectures;
  • MLP and attention dimensions are not uniformly scaled together.

Again, these are clues, not laws. But they are the kind of clues that make a NAS paper more useful than just a leaderboard entry.

Implementation Notes

If I were reproducing ViTAS, I would validate the proxy before trusting the final searched model.

  1. Implement the search space and make sure every sampled path has valid head/dimension divisibility.
  2. Build ordinal sharing first as a baseline; measure whether early channels receive more updates.
  3. Add cyclic channel mapping and verify training-count fairness across channel groups.
  4. Approximate influence balance for FC layers; check that cyclic reduces the channel influence gap.
  5. Add identity shifting for depth search; confirm that multiple superformer paths no longer collapse to the same final architecture.
  6. For DeiT-style patch-size search, keep private class tokens per patch size.
  7. Train a small superformer and compare inherited ranking against a small set of retrained candidates.
  8. Only then scale to ImageNet and evolutionary search.

The paper uses evolutionary search under FLOPs constraints after superformer training. The appendix says it partitions dimensions into 10 groups, samples 50 architectures per budget range, and trains/retrains according to the reported recipes. The search details matter less than the estimator quality: if inherited accuracy is biased, a better evolutionary solver will still optimize the wrong signal.

Limitations

ViTAS is a strong paper, but the boundaries are clear.

  • The search space is still manually designed around DeiT and Twins. It does not discover entirely new attention operators or macro backbones.
  • Cyclic sharing is designed for dimension search. It does not automatically solve every kind of operation-sharing bias.
  • The influence calculation is a useful approximation for FC-heavy layers, not a full theory of supernet training dynamics.
  • The compute budget is substantial: superformer training uses 300 ImageNet epochs, and the final architectures are retrained.
  • Final results depend on the retraining recipe. The paper is careful to reimplement baselines under its recipe, but recipe sensitivity is always a concern in ViT comparisons.
  • Throughput is not always better. Several ViTAS models trade more parameters or lower image/s for higher accuracy.

Takeaway

ViTAS is worth remembering for one sentence:

In Transformer NAS, inherited accuracy is only useful if the superformer trains dimensions fairly.

The paper’s main contribution is not just a searched ViT model. It is the argument that ordinal channel sharing makes the superformer itself biased, and that cyclic channel sharing gives a more reliable ranking signal for token embedding dimensions.

The strongest evidence is the combination of:

  • Figure 1, which makes the channel imbalance visible;
  • Figure 5, which tests ranking correlation directly;
  • Table 9, which isolates cyclic sharing and weak augmentation;
  • ImageNet results in both Twins and DeiT spaces;
  • COCO/ADE transfer results showing the searched backbones are not ImageNet-only artifacts.

That makes ViTAS a useful bridge between AutoFormer and later ViT search-space work such as S3. AutoFormer makes weight sharing more structured; ViTAS makes dimension sharing fairer; S3 later asks how to evolve the search space itself. All three are really about the same hidden problem: the supernet is the measurement instrument, and if the instrument is biased, NAS optimizes noise.

entry.title: XLNet: Generalized Autoregressive Pretraining for Language Understanding
Zen-NAS: A Zero-Shot NAS for High-Performance Deep Image Recognition
Zero-Cost Proxies for Lightweight NAS
ZeroQ: Data-Free Post-Training Quantization
ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable PTQ for Large Transformers
entry.content:
Paper: ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers

Code: microsoft/DeepSpeed

ZeroQuant is an important paper because it treats quantization as a modeling problem and a serving-system problem at the same time. The paper is not just saying “large Transformers can use INT8.” It asks a more practical question:

Can post-training quantization serve BERT-size and GPT-style models without full quantization-aware training, while still producing real GPU latency gains?

The answer is a system recipe:

  • use group-wise quantization for weights, because a single matrix scale wastes range on rows with small magnitude;
  • use token-wise quantization for activations, because different tokens can have very different ranges;
  • use layer-by-layer knowledge distillation when INT4 weights are involved;
  • fuse quantization and dequantization around INT8 GEMM, otherwise fine-grained quantization can lose its latency benefit to memory traffic.

All crops below are taken from the original PDF.

Why ZeroQuant Matters

Before ZeroQuant, there were already useful Transformer quantization papers. Q8BERT showed that BERT can tolerate 8-bit quantization with quantization-aware fine-tuning. Q-BERT pushed BERT weight precision down with Hessian information. But two gaps remained:

  1. Full QAT or hidden-state distillation becomes expensive when the model has hundreds of millions or billions of parameters.
  2. Accuracy-only quantization results do not prove that the method is useful for serving, because token-wise scales and low-bit formats can introduce extra quantize/dequantize kernels and memory movement.

ZeroQuant sits exactly at that boundary. It tries to keep the user-facing behavior close to FP16, while making the quantization process cheap enough for large models.

The paper evaluates:

Model family Examples in the paper Main benchmark
Encoder-only BERT-Base, BERT-Large GLUE development sets
Decoder-only GPT-3-style 350M and 1.3B 20 zero-shot tasks plus Wikitext-2
Larger open-source GPT models GPT-J 6B, GPT-NeoX 20B generation and zero-shot evaluation

The notation is WxAy: x bits for weights and y bits for activations. The paper also uses W4/8 for a mixed setting where multi-head self-attention weights stay INT8 and feed-forward weights are pushed to INT4. This is a sensible compromise because the feed-forward connection is a large fraction of Transformer parameters.

The Failure Mode Of Naive PTQ

Post-training quantization is attractive because it does not retrain the model. A common PTQ flow is:

That is cheap, but it assumes that a small number of scales can represent the distributions well enough. ZeroQuant shows why this is fragile for Transformers.

Figure 1. GPT-3 350M has large variation across token activation ranges and across rows of the attention output matrix. A single coarse scale either clips large values or wastes representational levels on smaller values.

The left plot is the activation problem. Token hidden states in the same layer can have very different max-absolute ranges. If all tokens share one activation scale, the largest token range determines the scale, and small-range tokens get a coarse quantization grid.

The right plot is the weight problem. Rows in the attention output matrix do not share the same magnitude. A matrix-wide scale is again inefficient: rows with small ranges are represented by too few integer values, and this becomes much worse when weights are pushed to INT4.

The first PTQ table makes the diagnosis concrete.

Table 1. Naive PTQ on GPT-3 350M. Activation quantization hurts more than INT8 weight quantization, and mixed INT4/INT8 weights can destroy generation quality.

The useful read is not only the average score:

  • W8A16 is close to the FP16 baseline on the shown tasks. Weight-only INT8 is not the main problem here.
  • W16A8 has a larger drop. Wikitext-2 perplexity moves from 21.5 to 24.6, so activation quantization is already painful.
  • W8A8 is worse again on Wikitext-2, with perplexity 26.2.
  • W4/8A16 collapses generation. Wikitext-2 becomes 1.76e5, which is effectively unusable.

This is why ZeroQuant is not a pure rounding paper. The method has to address the numerical range mismatch in both weights and activations.

Fine-Grained Quantization

ZeroQuant uses uniform symmetric scalar quantization. In plain notation:

Here S is the scale. The important part is not the scalar quantizer itself; it is how the scale is chosen.

Group-Wise Weight Quantization

For a weight matrix W, ZeroQuant partitions the matrix into groups and quantizes each group separately. This gives each group its own scale. Compared with matrix-wise quantization, group-wise quantization reduces the penalty from rows or blocks with small magnitude.

The group size is not arbitrary. The paper explicitly considers hardware constraints on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, where Tensor Core throughput depends on WMMA tile shapes. This is the system-aware part of the design: very fine groups might improve accuracy, but if they do not map well to GPU kernels, the final model may not be faster.

The appendix gives the concrete settings used in the experiments:

Model Group count used for weight quantization
BERT-Base 48 groups
BERT-Large 64 groups
GPT-3 350M 64 groups
GPT-3 1.3B 128 groups

I read this as a core ZeroQuant principle: choose quantization granularity where the model distribution needs it, but keep the layout friendly to the backend.

Token-Wise Activation Quantization

The activation side is different because activations are dynamic. A static calibration range can be too conservative for many tokens and too small for outlier tokens.

ZeroQuant instead uses token-wise activation quantization. Each token has its own activation range during inference, so the quantizer can adapt to token-level variation.

The benefit is accuracy. The cost is that dynamic token-wise quantization can introduce extra operations:

If those steps are implemented as separate kernels, the extra memory traffic can eat the speedup. That is why the method and the kernel design have to be read together.

Layer-By-Layer Knowledge Distillation

W8A8 is the moderate target. For the more aggressive W4/8 settings, ZeroQuant adds layer-by-layer knowledge distillation, abbreviated as LKD.

The usual full-model distillation setup is expensive for large models:

  • it may need both teacher and student models in memory;
  • optimizer states are kept for many student parameters;
  • training is end-to-end, so memory and compute scale with the whole model;
  • original training data may not be available.

ZeroQuant’s LKD makes the optimization local. For layer L_k, it compares the original FP layer with the quantized copy of the same layer. Only that layer is optimized.

This has three practical consequences.

First, it does not need a separate full teacher model. The original layer acts as the teacher for the quantized layer.

Second, optimizer memory is small because only one layer is being updated.

Third, labels are not required. The objective is local feature reconstruction, not task supervision. This makes it possible to use alternative text data when the original pretraining corpus is unavailable.

This local nature is also the limitation. LKD reconstructs one layer at a time. It can miss error accumulation across layers, and it is weaker than a fully tuned end-to-end student. But it is cheap enough to be practical, which is the whole point of the paper.

Quantization-Optimized Kernels

The kernel section is easy to skip, but it is essential. Token-wise activation quantization and group-wise weight quantization add scale handling around GEMM. A naive implementation can perform extra reads, writes, and kernel launches.

Figure 2. The normal path pays separate quantize and dequantize costs. ZeroQuant fuses activation quantization with the preceding operator and fuses dequantization into the GEMM epilogue.

The paper’s backend uses CUTLASS INT8 GEMM and fusion:

  • activation quantization is fused with preceding operations such as LayerNorm, GELU, or bias-add;
  • INT32 GEMM accumulation is dequantized in the GEMM epilogue using activation and weight scales;
  • the output is written back as FP16 when the next operator is still FP16;
  • CUDA Graph support is used to reduce CPU launch overhead for small models such as BERT-Base.

This explains why ZeroQuant can claim both accuracy and speed. Without these fusions, token-wise activation quantization would be a nice accuracy trick but a questionable serving method.

BERT Results

BERT is the cleanest place to see the difference between naive PTQ, ZeroQuant, and QAT.

Table 2. BERT-Base GLUE results. ZeroQuant recovers most of the W8A8 PTQ loss without QAT, and LKD helps the mixed INT4/INT8 settings.

The headline numbers:

Setting Average score Average quantization time
FP16 baseline W16A16 83.95 N/A
W8A8 PTQ 77.41 6 seconds
W8A8 QAT 83.37 2900 seconds
W8A8 ZeroQuant 83.75 0 seconds
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant 81.55 0 seconds
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant-LKD 82.71 31 seconds

For W8A8, ZeroQuant is almost at the FP16 average and slightly above the internal QAT row in this table, with no activation calibration cost. I would not over-read the small difference between 83.75 and 83.37; the important point is that ZeroQuant is in the same accuracy band as QAT without QAT’s retraining cost.

For W4/8, naive PTQ is not usable. W4/8A16 PTQ averages 33.11, close to random behavior on several tasks. ZeroQuant raises it to 81.65, and LKD raises it again to 82.35. The same pattern holds for W4/8A8: ZeroQuant gives 81.55, and LKD improves it to 82.71.

The BERT-Large table in the paper follows the same broad pattern:

  • W8A8 PTQ average drops to 73.54;
  • W8A8 ZeroQuant reaches 84.81 against an FP16 baseline of 85.03;
  • W4/8A8 ZeroQuant-LKD reaches 81.62;
  • LKD costs about 550 seconds per task on one A100, far below the reported QAT cost.

The main caveat is RTE. Both QAT and ZeroQuant struggle more on RTE, which is a small dataset and often has high variance. This is a reminder that average GLUE scores can hide task-specific fragility.

GPT-3-Style Results

Decoder-only generation makes the quantization problem sharper. A classification task can sometimes tolerate small hidden-state perturbations, but autoregressive generation exposes accumulated errors token by token.

Table 4. GPT-3 350M results. ZeroQuant fixes most of the W8A8 PTQ damage, while LKD is needed for usable mixed INT4/INT8 generation.

For GPT-3 350M, the W8A8 result is the strongest moderate-precision claim:

Setting Average over 19 accuracy tasks Wikitext-2 PPL
W16A16 38.9 21.5
W8A8 PTQ 37.8 26.2
W8A8 ZeroQuant 38.7 21.7

ZeroQuant nearly removes the generation penalty: Wikitext-2 moves from PTQ’s 26.2 back to 21.7, close to the FP16 baseline 21.5.

The low-bit setting is more revealing:

Setting Average over 19 accuracy tasks Wikitext-2 PPL
W4/8A16 ZeroQuant 33.5 88.6
W4/8A16 ZeroQuant-LKD 37.0 30.6
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant 33.4 92.1
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant-LKD 36.6 31.1

LKD does not fully restore FP16 generation, but it changes the result from badly degraded to meaningfully usable. The paper reports that this LKD pass costs about 1.1 hours on one A100 for GPT-3 350M, which is tiny compared with pretraining.

The GPT-3 1.3B table shows the same direction. W8A8 ZeroQuant gets Wikitext-2 PPL 15.7, close to FP16 15.3 and better than PTQ 18.9. For W4/8, LKD again improves both average accuracy and generation perplexity.

Latency

Accuracy preservation is only half the story. ZeroQuant also reports end-to-end latency with the fused INT8 path.

Table 6. BERT latency on one A100. The W8A8 path gives roughly 2.27x to 5.19x speedup on BERT-Base and 2.47x to 5.01x on BERT-Large depending on sequence length and batch size.

The speedup is larger at higher batch sizes because the integer GEMM path is better utilized and the fixed overhead is amortized. But the table also shows speedups at batch size 1, which matters for online serving.

The paper also reports decoder-side speedups:

Model Quantized setting Reported latency result
GPT-3 350M W8A8 4.16x speedup over FP16
GPT-3 1.3B W8A8 4.06x speedup over FP16
GPT-J 6B W8A8 29.13 ms to 7.94 ms for first-50-token generation, 3.67x
GPT-NeoX 20B W8A8/16 2 x 65 ms on two A100s to 1 x 25 ms on one A100, reported as 5.2x better efficiency

The GPT-NeoX 20B result has an important qualification. The paper could not quantize all activation inputs to self-attention in pure W8A8 without accuracy loss, so it uses A8/16: FP16 activation for self-attention calculation and INT8 elsewhere. This is a practical result, but it also shows that extra-large decoder models can still have sensitive activation paths.

Ablation: Which Component Matters?

The ablation table is one of the most useful parts of the paper because it separates the three pieces: group-wise weight quantization, token-wise activation quantization, and LKD.

Table 9. BERT-Large ablation under W4/8A8. Group-wise weight quantization prevents collapse; token-wise activation quantization gives the largest additional gain; LKD adds a smaller but consistent improvement.

The average score progression is clear:

Components Average score
no GQ, no TQ, no LKD 35.85
GQ only 66.52
GQ + TQ 81.06
GQ + TQ + LKD 81.62

My read:

  • group-wise weight quantization is the first gate. Without it, mixed INT4/INT8 weights are too destructive;
  • token-wise activation quantization is the biggest BERT-Large jump in this ablation, from 66.52 to 81.06;
  • LKD’s average gain is small on this BERT-Large table, but it matters more for GPT generation under W4/8.

So I would not summarize ZeroQuant as “LKD solves PTQ.” The stronger summary is: fine-grained quantization solves most of the W8A8 and W4/8A8 representation issue, and LKD repairs the remaining low-bit damage when the quantized layer needs local reconstruction.

Distillation Without Original Data

Because LKD uses layer outputs rather than labels, it can use data from outside the original training set.

Table 10. GPT-3 350M W4/8A8 LKD with different data sources. Wikipedia data is close to original training data, and even random token data improves over no LKD.

This table is interesting for deployment teams. The original pretraining data may be private, unavailable, or too large to reconstruct. ZeroQuant shows:

  • no LKD: Wikitext-2 PPL 92.1;
  • random data LKD: PPL improves to 40.6;
  • Wikipedia data LKD: PPL improves to 30.4;
  • original data LKD: PPL 31.1.

The random-data result should not be overstated. It does not mean random data is as good as real text. But it does support the paper’s local-reconstruction argument: even random token sequences can provide enough layer input variation for the quantized layer to learn a better approximation of the FP layer.

The Wikipedia result is more practically useful. A clean public text dataset can be enough for LKD when original data is not available.

Relationship To Later LLM Quantization

ZeroQuant is not the final word on LLM quantization. Later methods became more specialized:

Method Main idea Difference from ZeroQuant
LLM.int8() Keep outlier channels in higher precision Explicitly isolates activation outliers instead of relying mainly on token-wise quantization
SmoothQuant Move activation outlier difficulty into weights through equivalent scaling Cleaner W8A8 transform for serving large LLMs
GPTQ Weight-only second-order reconstruction Stronger local solver for low-bit weights, usually without activation quantization
AWQ Activation-aware weight quantization Protects salient weight channels based on activation statistics
ZeroQuant Fine-grained W8A8/W4/8A8 plus LKD and fused kernels Broader system recipe across BERT and GPT-style models

This is why ZeroQuant still matters. It makes the serving constraint explicit: a quantizer is not successful unless the backend can run it efficiently. It also shows that activation quantization is not a minor detail for generation models. W8A8 needs a real activation strategy, not just weight rounding.

Reproduction Notes

If I were reproducing ZeroQuant, I would start smaller than the full paper:

  1. Pick one Transformer block and implement symmetric quantization for its linear layers.
  2. Compare matrix-wise weight quantization with group-wise weight quantization using layer-output error.
  3. Compare static activation calibration with token-wise dynamic activation quantization.
  4. Evaluate both classification accuracy and generation perplexity. Perplexity is more sensitive to accumulated quantization error.
  5. Add LKD for one quantized layer and verify that the local MSE objective reduces output error.
  6. Stack quantized layers progressively and check where error accumulation becomes visible.
  7. Only after the numerical path works, optimize the kernels. Otherwise it is hard to tell whether failures come from quantization math or backend layout.

The kernel checks I would add:

Check Why it matters
Scale layout matches GEMM tiling Bad scale reads can erase Tensor Core gains
Quantization fused with LayerNorm/GELU/bias-add Separate kernels add memory traffic
Dequantization in GEMM epilogue Avoids writing and rereading INT32 outputs
Batch/sequence-specific schedules Small batch serving and large batch throughput have different bottlenecks
CUDA Graph path for small models Kernel launch overhead can dominate BERT-Base latency

The most important experiment is not only “does W8A8 match FP16?” It is:

Without that, a quantization paper can look good in accuracy tables and still fail as a deployment method.

Limitations

ZeroQuant has several clear limitations.

First, W4/8 generation still needs LKD and remains worse than FP16. The paper makes the low-bit setting practical, but it does not make it free.
