Second, the local LKD objective does not directly optimize final task loss or long-range generation behavior. Layer-wise reconstruction can reduce local error while still allowing small errors to accumulate through the network.

Third, the best results depend on custom kernels. Token-wise activation quantization is not automatically fast in a generic framework. The method assumes a backend that can fuse quantization and dequantization with GEMM-adjacent operators.

Fourth, the GPT-NeoX 20B result uses W8A8/16, not pure W8A8 for every activation path. That is a useful engineering compromise, but it shows that some self-attention activations remain sensitive at larger scales.

Finally, this paper predates the modern 4-bit LLM deployment stack. If the target is weight-only 4-bit serving for very large decoder-only models, GPTQ/AWQ-style methods may be closer baselines. If the target is true W8A8 serving with integer GEMM, ZeroQuant and SmoothQuant are more directly relevant.

Takeaway

ZeroQuant’s main contribution is the combination:

The paper is worth reading because it does not separate algorithm and system concerns. Token-wise activation quantization fixes a real numerical problem, but it only becomes deployable after fusion. Group-wise weight quantization fixes a real representation problem, but the group layout has to respect GPU kernels. LKD helps low-bit weights, but it is designed around the memory constraints of large models.

That is the enduring lesson: for large Transformer quantization, accuracy tables, calibration cost, memory layout, and kernel fusion are one problem.

entry.title: BlockQNN: Efficient Block-wise Neural Network Architecture Generation
[CUDA]element-wise
[CUDA]reduce
entry.content:
Reference

  • https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-best-practices-guide/index.html
  • https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html
  • https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/426978026

Basic Concepts

Reduction problems are a common category of questions encountered in interviews. Compared to elementwise problems, where each thread independently performs tasks, reduction problems become more complex due to the involvement of synchronization and communication between threads. Additionally, these problems can leverage the previously introduced optimization techniques for vectorized memory access, which adds a layer of complexity in terms of thought process.
The reductions.cu file primarily implements the following three kernel functions for reduction summation:

  1. The most basic atomic_reduction(), which extensively utilizes the atomicAdd() function.
  2. The sweep style reduction sum reduction_a(), which calls atomicAdd once at the end.
  3. The warp shuffle reduction reduction_ws(), which also calls atomicAdd once at the end.

Theory: The atomic_reduction() is the slowest because it heavily relies on the atomicAdd() function. Compared to reduction_a, reduction_ws tends to perform better due to its minimal use of shared memory.

Observed Phenomena:

  1. As the data size increases, the performance advantage of reduce_ws over reduction_a diminishes.
  2. The use of the atomicAdd function affects the Memory utilization rate, and this impact does not vary with the scale of the data.

Regarding the first point: Both reduce_ws and reduction_a require loading data within a grid-stride loop initially. As the data size grows, the time taken to load the data becomes the dominant factor in the overall time consumption. At this juncture, the specific method of performing reduction matters less, hence the time difference narrows with increasing data sizes. In theory, warp shuffle should offer better performance than the classic reduction sum, but in practice, it still depends on the specific data scale of the problem at hand and requires a detailed analysis.

Regarding the second point: The impact of the atomicAdd function on performance is significant because it can reduce the Memory utilization rate to a very low level, and this is difficult to improve by simply changing the data scale.

Usefull basic reduction functions

Here is a collection of some fundamental reduction kernel functions:

warp reduce sum

warp reduce max

block reduce sum

block reduce max

All reduce sum

All reduce sum float4

Complex scenario

dot product

dot product float4

softmax

safe softmax

layernorm

layernorm float4

rmsnorm

rmsnorm float4

entry.content:
Reference

  • https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-best-practices-guide/index.html
  • https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html
  • https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/494144694

Basic concepts

The General Matrix-Vector Multiplication (GEMV) is a specialized form of General Matrix-Matrix Multiplication (GEMM), tailored for operations involving a matrix and a vector. This operation differs from GEMM in that it is optimized for scenarios where one of the operands is a vector, as opposed to another matrix. On Nvidia GPUs, the optimization methods for GEMV can be distinct from those used for GEMM. For instance, Cublas provides specific Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) such as cublasSgemv and cublasDgemv for the computation of single-precision (FP32) and double-precision (FP64) GEMV operations, respectively. However, the performance of these APIs is not always optimal. In some cases, custom implementations of GEMV can outperform the built-in Cublas functions due to the unique requirements and opportunities for optimization presented by the GEMV operation. It is often beneficial to experiment with both the provided Cublas APIs and custom implementations to determine which yields the best performance for a particular use case or hardware configuration.

k = 32/64/96

In this scenario, each block is set to have 128 threads, organized into 4 warps, with each warp responsible for the computation of a row of elements. During the computation, data must be read from global memory, followed by an internal reduce operation for summation within the warp. The code is as follows:

k = 16

At this point, if a warp is still tasked with computing a single row of elements, then half of the threads within the warp would be idling. Therefore, it is more efficient to assign a warp to compute multiple rows of elements, ensuring that all 32 threads are actively engaged. The code is as follows:

k > 128

Similar to the case when k equals 32, where a warp is responsible for the computation of a single row of elements, the current approach takes advantage of the fact that there are now 128 elements per row. entry.title: DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search
Real-time Federated Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Paper : Real-time Federated Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search.

I will call the method FedEvo below. The interesting part of this paper is not that it uses evolutionary NAS again, but that it tries to make NAS happen inside the normal communication loop of federated learning. A conventional evolutionary NAS setup evaluates many candidate networks after training them, while federated learning already pays a high price for every communication round. If we naively combine the two, each client would have to download, train, and upload too many models.

The paper’s answer is simple: keep one shared master model, sample sub-models from it, train those sub-models on sampled clients, and use NSGA-II to select architectures under both accuracy and FLOPs constraints.

Motivation

Federated learning has two constraints that make centralized NAS awkward.

First, clients are usually small devices. Training a whole population of candidate networks on every client is unrealistic. Second, communication is the bottleneck. Sending a full model population, or retraining every offspring from scratch, quickly dominates the cost.

The paper also points out a less obvious issue: many NAS methods rely on transfer, proxy tasks, or centralized validation. In FL, data is distributed and often non-IID, so the architecture that looks good on one data split or one client group may not be stable globally.

So the target problem is:

Requirement Why it matters in FL
Search during training Avoid an expensive offline NAS stage.
Train only small sampled models Reduce local compute and upload size.
Reuse model weights Avoid reinitializing every offspring.
Optimize model size too Edge clients care about FLOPs, not only accuracy.

Contributions

The paper has three concrete contributions.

  1. Double sampling. For every evolutionary generation, the server samples both architectures and participating clients. A client trains only one sub-model in that generation instead of a full population.
  2. Sub-model aggregation. Uploaded sub-models are reconstructed back into the master-model parameter space. Trained branches use client updates; missing branches are filled from the previous master model before aggregation.
  3. Online multi-objective search. One generation of NSGA-II is aligned with one communication round. The objectives are test error and FLOPs (the paper reports FLOPs as MACs).

The high-level loop looks like this:

The key detail is that NAS is not a separate pre-processing step. In this design, architecture search and federated training share the same rounds.

Search Space

The master network is a small CNN for CIFAR-10. It starts with a convolution block, then uses 12 choice blocks grouped by channel width: 64, 128, 256, and 512. Each choice block has four candidate branches.

Each choice block chooses one of four candidates:

  • identity block
  • residual block
  • inverted residual block
  • depthwise separable block

Because each choice block has four options, it can be encoded with 2 bits. With 12 choice blocks, an architecture choice key has 24 bits. This is a small search space by modern NAS standards, but it is enough for the paper’s point: reduce federated compute and communication while still searching over meaningful CNN blocks.

Double Sampling

The double-sampling step has two levels.

First, the server samples one sub-model from the master model according to a choice key. Instead of sending the whole supernet, the client receives a concrete path through the choice blocks.

Second, the server samples clients. If there are total clients and the client participation ratio is , then the round samples clients. These clients are split over the evolutionary population of size , so one candidate is trained by roughly clients.

This matters because each client sees only one sub-model per generation. The local workload becomes bounded by a single sampled network, not by the population size.

Aggregation

Aggregation is the part I found most useful in this paper. A client only trains the branches that exist in its sampled sub-model, but the server still needs to update one master model.

The paper handles this by reconstructing a full master-shaped model for each upload:

  • branches selected by the client use the trained client weights;
  • branches not selected by that client are copied from the previous master model;
  • reconstructed models are averaged, weighted by client data size.

This is basically weight sharing plus federated averaging, but applied at the branch level. It avoids random reinitialization of offspring models, which is one reason the real-time version is more stable than the offline evolutionary baseline in the paper.

NSGA-II Objective

FedEvo uses NSGA-II to keep a Pareto set instead of choosing one scalar reward. The two objectives are:

Objective Meaning
Test error Lower is better. Used as the accuracy-side fitness.
FLOPs (MAC) Lower is better. Used as the efficiency-side fitness.

The paper then marks two representative solutions on the Pareto front:

  • High: the solution with the highest accuracy;
  • Knee: the solution near the knee point, usually a better accuracy/FLOPs tradeoff.

One small caveat: the paper writes “test error” as the fitness. In a production FL setup, I would expect this to be a validation metric or a server-side held-out evaluation, otherwise the test set becomes part of model selection.

Experiments

The experiments are on CIFAR-10 with 50,000 training images and 10,000 test images. The paper simulates 10, 20, and 50 clients under both IID and non-IID splits. For non-IID, each client has images from 5 classes.

Important settings:

Item Value
Dataset CIFAR-10
Clients 10, 20, 50
Local epoch 1
Train batch size 50
NSGA-II population 10
Generations / rounds 500
Baseline ResNet18 for CIFAR-10
Baseline FLOPs 0.5587G MAC

The Pareto fronts after 500 rounds are shown below. Lower-left is better: lower test error and lower FLOPs.

The table in the paper is worth reading directly because it shows the tradeoff clearly.

A few rows are enough to see the pattern:

Setting ResNet18 High solution Knee solution
10 clients, IID 81.14%, 0.5587G 86.68%, 0.2796G 83.36%, 0.031G
10 clients, non-IID 80.29%, 0.5587G 81.27%, 0.2272G 78.94%, 0.0302G
20 clients, IID 82.50%, 0.5587G 85.16%, 0.2012G 83.65%, 0.0398G
20 clients, non-IID 79.91%, 0.5587G 83.01%, 0.3936G 81.58%, 0.1098G
50 clients, IID 80.78%, 0.5587G 77.10%, 0.3360G 71.46%, 0.0547G
50 clients, non-IID 77.63%, 0.5587G 75.10%, 0.1719G 69.22%, 0.0635G

For 10 and 20 clients, the best evolved model usually beats ResNet18 while using fewer FLOPs. The knee solution is more aggressive: it gives up some accuracy but cuts computation heavily. The 50-client case is weaker. The paper explains this as a data-per-client issue: when total data is fixed, more clients means less local data per client, so it becomes harder to find a stable global model.

Real-time Behavior

The real-time curves for 20 clients are the most convincing part of the experiments.

At the beginning, ResNet18 is better. That is expected: the searched models are still being optimized while the master model is changing. After about 200 communication rounds, the selected high-accuracy and knee solutions catch up and pass ResNet18 in the reported 20-client settings.

The FLOPs curves also show the point of multi-objective search. The knee solution stays far below ResNet18 in compute, while the high-accuracy solution fluctuates more because it is chasing accuracy during the search.

The paper also compares against an offline evolutionary federated NAS baseline. In that baseline, the selected model is trained from scratch for 500 communication rounds. The reported runtime is about 16.1 hours/GPU for real-time NAS over 500 generations, versus about 6.55 hours/GPU for only 50 offline generations before retraining cost. The paper summarizes this as roughly a 5x speedup per search round for the real-time method.

Takeaways

I like this paper because it treats communication rounds as the unit of NAS cost. Many NAS papers hide the search cost behind a centralized proxy task; here, the search loop is forced to live inside FL.

What I would keep from this paper:

  • Represent architectures with compact choice keys.
  • Do not ask each client to train a population.
  • Aggregate partial sub-model updates back into a shared master model.
  • Optimize compute explicitly, not as an afterthought.

What feels limited:

  • The search space is small and CNN-specific.
  • The experiments are only on CIFAR-10.
  • The 50-client results show that the method is sensitive to data fragmentation.
  • Using “test error” as the search fitness is not ideal if interpreted literally.

Overall, FedEvo is a useful early design for federated NAS: it is not the most powerful NAS method, but it gives a concrete recipe for making evolutionary search compatible with FL communication constraints.

entry.title: Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search
entry.content:
Liu, Simonyan, Vinyals, Fernando, and Kavukcuoglu. Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search. ICLR 2018.

Paper

This paper is a useful counterweight to early NAS papers that made the controller or optimizer look like the main story. The central claim here is simpler: if the architecture representation is well structured, even simple search methods such as random search and tournament evolution become strong.

Instead of searching one flat graph of primitive operations, the paper builds networks from motifs. Low-level motifs combine primitive operations. Higher-level motifs combine lower-level motifs. A change to a lower motif can therefore propagate through many parts of the final architecture.

Representation

Figure 1 shows the key idea. The bottom level contains primitive operations. A level-2 motif is assembled from those primitives. A level-3 motif is assembled from level-2 motifs. The final network is therefore a recursively composed graph, not just a one-shot list of edge operations.

In plain notation:

The primitive set is intentionally small:

  • 1x1 convolution;
  • 3x3 depthwise convolution;
  • 3x3 separable convolution;
  • 3x3 max pooling;
  • 3x3 average pooling;
  • identity.

The paper also uses a none operation to represent missing edges. Larger receptive fields and wider computations are meant to emerge from composing these primitives rather than adding many hand-designed primitives.

Why Hierarchy Matters

The representation encodes a strong prior: good neural networks often reuse patterns. ResNet blocks, Inception modules, MobileNet inverted residuals, and Transformer layers are all examples of repeated structure. Hierarchical NAS makes that reuse part of the search space.

The tradeoff is bias. A hierarchical representation can make search efficient when the true solution has reusable substructure. It can also hide architectures that do not fit the recursive grammar.

Representation Search bias
Flat graph flexible, but harder to search and can grow parameter count quickly
Cell-based graph reusable normal/reduction cells with a fixed macro skeleton
Hierarchical motif reusable substructures at multiple levels

This is why I read the paper as a search-space paper more than an evolution paper.

Search Algorithm

The search algorithm is asynchronous tournament evolution. A controller maintains a queue of unevaluated genotypes and a memory table of evaluated genotypes. Workers repeatedly pop genotypes, assemble the architecture, train it from scratch, evaluate validation fitness, and write the result back.

There is no ENAS-style weight sharing and no inherited weights from parent to child. Every architecture evaluation trains a model from scratch for a fixed number of steps. That makes the fitness estimate cleaner than one-shot NAS, but it also means the method still spends serious compute.

The mutation operator changes one edge in one motif:

  1. sample a non-primitive level;
  2. sample a motif at that level;
  3. sample a successor node and predecessor node;
  4. replace the edge operation with another operation from the previous level, possibly none.

This single rule can add an edge, remove an edge, or change an existing edge. In the hierarchical case, changing a lower-level motif can affect all higher-level places where that motif is reused.

Model Evaluation Setup

The paper searches for a convolutional cell on CIFAR-10, then evaluates the found cell in larger CIFAR-10 and ImageNet models.

The experimental setup has three model sizes:

  • a small CIFAR-10 model used during architecture search;
  • a larger CIFAR-10 model used for final cell evaluation;
  • an ImageNet model that transfers the searched cell to a larger-scale task.

This is similar in spirit to NASNet: search a small reusable component, then scale it. The difference is that the searched component itself is hierarchical.

Search Curves

The authors run evolution for 7000 steps using 200 GPU workers. The first 200 steps are random initialization; after that, tournament selection and mutation start.

Figure 3 has an important nuance:

  • the flat representation can reach higher small-model fitness;
  • the flat representation also tends to create larger models;
  • when the flat representation is parameter-constrained, it becomes closer to the hierarchical representation.

So the hierarchy is not magic accuracy by itself. It is a way to bias the search toward reusable structures without letting the parameter count grow as freely.

The authors also check whether search progress on the small model transfers to the final larger model. The curve is not perfectly proportional, but improvement in the small fitness generally corresponds to improvement in the large model. That matters because NAS often fails when the proxy task ranking does not transfer.

Main Results

Table 1 is the most useful result in the paper. The best hierarchical evolution run reports:

Search method CIFAR-10 error ImageNet top-1/top-5 error
Hierarchical random architecture 4.21 +/- 0.11 21.5 / 5.8
Hierarchical random search, 200 samples 4.04 +/- 0.20 20.4 / 5.3
Hierarchical random search, 7000 samples 3.91 +/- 0.15 21.0 / 5.5
Hierarchical evolution, 7000 samples 3.75 +/- 0.12 20.3 / 5.2

Two points stand out.

First, random search is surprisingly strong. With 200 samples, it is only 0.29 percentage points worse than the best hierarchical evolution result on CIFAR-10 and only 0.1 top-1 error worse on ImageNet. Because 200 samples can be evaluated in parallel, the paper reports this random-search setting as about 1 hour with 200 P100 GPUs.

Second, evolution is still the best result in the table, but the paper’s own evidence says representation quality is doing a lot of the work.

Comparison To Prior Models

On CIFAR-10, the best hierarchical evolutionary architecture reaches 3.75 +/- 0.12% error with c0 = 64, and 3.63 +/- 0.10% with c0 = 128. In the paper’s 2018 context, this is competitive with early RL-based NAS results such as NAS v3, Block-QNN, and NASNet-A.

On ImageNet, the transferred hierarchical architecture reports 20.3% top-1 error and 5.2% top-5 error. That is behind NASNet-A in the table, but still competitive with strong manual convolutional baselines from that period. The paper notes that the ImageNet model has 64M parameters, which is larger than NASNet-A’s 22.6M.

Found Cell

The learned cell uses motifs as edges. The paper notes that only motifs 1, 3, 4, and 5 are used in the final cell, with motifs 3 and 5 dominating.

The motif visualization is a good reminder that hierarchical NAS does not just learn “which operation goes on this edge.” It learns small graphs that become operations for the next level. Several motifs contain direct skip-style paths, so the final cell inherits skip connections through the motif hierarchy.

Takeaway

The strongest lesson is that search-space design can dominate optimizer design. A well-built representation makes random search a serious baseline. This paper shows that with a hierarchical motif space, even 200 random samples are competitive with a much longer evolutionary run.

The limitations are clear:

  • the method still trains candidate models from scratch;
  • the reported search uses 200 P100 workers;
  • the ImageNet model is larger than NASNet-A;
  • the hierarchical grammar is a strong prior and may exclude useful flat architectures;
  • the final result is a convolutional cell search result, not a general architecture generator.

I would use this paper as a reminder before designing a new NAS optimizer: first ask whether the representation already makes good architectures easy to sample. If random search is strong, the optimizer needs to clear a much higher bar.

entry.title: Joint Neural Architecture Search and Quantization
Large-Scale Evolution of Image Classifiers
entry.content:
Real E, Moore S, Selle A, et al. Large-Scale Evolution of Image Classifiers. ICML 2017.

Paper

This paper is an early large-scale neural architecture search result, but it does not look like later RL-controller NAS or differentiable NAS. The algorithm keeps a population of trained CNNs, repeatedly mutates selected parents, trains the children, and uses validation accuracy as the selection signal.

The interesting part is how little algorithmic machinery is needed. The search is black-box, asynchronous, and almost embarrassingly parallel. The expensive part is that every child still has to be trained for real.

Result Positioning

The paper reports 94.6% CIFAR-10 accuracy for a single evolved model, 95.6% for an ensemble, and 77.0% on CIFAR-100. At the time, this was not just a toy architecture search demo.

Table 1 compares the evolved model with hand-designed CNNs. The evolved CIFAR-10 model is below the strongest Wide ResNet and DenseNet numbers, but it is competitive with a much less human-designed starting point. The “Reachable?” column also matters: some hand-designed baselines live outside the search space.

Table 2 is the more relevant comparison. Against other automatically discovered architectures, the evolutionary run reaches 94.6% on CIFAR-10, 77.0% on CIFAR-100, and 95.6% with an ensemble. The starting point is deliberately weak: a single layer with zero convolutions.

Search Loop

The evolutionary loop is pairwise tournament selection:

Fitness is validation accuracy. The population size in the main experiments is 1000, and the paper reports running experiments over 250 parallel workers. Each child is trained for 25,600 SGD steps with momentum 0.9, batch size 50, and weight decay 0.0001.

The search object is a full CNN graph plus training hyperparameters, not a neat repeated cell. Mutations can insert or remove convolutions, alter filter size, channel count, stride, learning rate, skip connections, and weight state. Some mutations preserve all weights, some preserve none, and many preserve only the compatible subset.

What Evolution Finds

Figure 1 shows a useful shape: many weak individuals appear early, then the population quickly moves into a high-accuracy band. The architecture sketches attached to lineage points are also instructive. The evolved networks are not clean human-designed templates; they contain stacked convolutions, skips, and repeated convolution-BN-ReLU patterns in places that a human probably would not draw first.

This is why I would not summarize the paper as “evolution invents ResNet.” It is closer to: given a mutation grammar and enough training budget, local search can build competent CNN programs from very weak initial conditions.

Controls

The controls are important. Random search is much worse in the reported wall-clock comparison. Evolution without weight inheritance is close early on but stays lower later. That does not prove evolutionary search is always better, but it does show the result is not only coming from repeatedly sampling random architectures.

The paper also makes a practical point about asynchronous search. Fast-training bad models can return early, enter the population, and get more chances to reproduce. That implicit bias is part of the system, so any reproduction should preserve the worker behavior instead of only copying the mutation list.

Meta-Parameters

The population-size and training-step sweeps explain why small NAS demos can be misleading. Larger populations explore more lineages, and longer child training gives the fitness estimate a better chance to reflect the architecture rather than just early optimization noise.

The downside is direct: the main result costs a huge amount of compute. The paper reports the best CIFAR-10 run at about 4 x 10^20 FLOPs, with the five-experiment average around 9 x 10^19 FLOPs. This is not a cheap recipe.

Local Optima

Figure 4 is a good reminder that evolutionary search is not magic. Populations can plateau. The authors tried increasing the mutation rate and resetting weights to help populations escape local optima. Both can work, but both are blunt tools.

The weight reset example is especially interesting. Weight inheritance helps make full-model evolution practical, but it can also make a mediocre architecture look good because it has accumulated more training. Resetting weights partially breaks that advantage and forces the population to re-evaluate architecture quality.

Takeaway

Large-Scale Evolution is rough by modern NAS benchmark standards. The search space is broad, the compute budget is large, and the results are not directly comparable to later cell-based search spaces or tabular NAS benchmarks.

The durable lesson is simpler: architecture search does not need a controller, relaxation, or differentiable proxy to be useful. If the evaluation loop is scalable and the mutation operators preserve enough structure, plain evolutionary pressure can discover strong trained models.

entry.title: Designing Neural Network Architectures using Reinforcement Learning
entry.content:
Paper / Project / Code

MetaQNN is one of the early reinforcement-learning based NAS papers. It is worth reading together with Zoph & Le’s controller-RNN NAS paper, because the search strategy is different: instead of training an RNN controller to emit architecture strings, MetaQNN uses tabular Q-learning over a hand-designed state-action graph.

The paper is not trying to discover arbitrary neural computation. The search space is deliberately limited to standard CNN components: convolution, pooling, fully connected layers, global average pooling, and softmax. That constraint is important. The interesting part of the paper is how the authors turn “choose a CNN architecture” into a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process that can be explored with a practical amount of computation.

Motivation

CNN design contains many coupled choices: layer type, ordering, filter size, number of channels, stride, pooling position, and termination point. Exhaustively enumerating this space is impossible even when every option is discretized.

Figure 1 summarizes the whole loop: sample a topology, train it, store its validation accuracy, and update the Q-values from replay memory.

The paper’s framing is direct:

  1. Let an agent build a CNN one layer at a time.
  2. Train the sampled CNN on the target dataset.
  3. Use validation accuracy as the reward.
  4. Update the agent so that future sampled architectures become better.

This is a clean formulation, but it only works if the architecture space is constrained enough. MetaQNN therefore spends a lot of effort on the state definition and action restrictions, not only on the reinforcement learning update.

Contribution

The useful contributions are:

  1. Formulate CNN architecture generation as a finite MDP, where a trajectory is a full network topology.
  2. Define a discrete state space for common CNN layers and use action constraints to avoid invalid or obviously degenerate networks.
  3. Use Q-learning with epsilon-greedy exploration and experience replay to search the architecture graph.
  4. Show that the discovered CNNs can outperform earlier networks that use only standard convolution, pooling, and fully connected layers.
  5. Release model definitions and code, although the original implementation is tied to an old Caffe/Python 2 stack.

The last point matters historically. MetaQNN is not only a conceptual NAS paper; it includes trained topologies, Caffe prototxt files, and a server-client training setup.

Methodology

State and Action Space

The MDP view is the core modeling choice. A path through this graph corresponds to one CNN, and the green path in the figure is one sampled architecture.

Each state represents the current layer choice plus enough metadata to decide what layer can come next. The notation used in the paper is:

  • C(d, f, l): convolution with d filters, receptive field size f, and stride l.
  • P(f, l): pooling with receptive field size f and stride l.
  • FC(d): fully connected layer with d neurons.
  • GAP / SM: global average pooling or softmax termination.

The experimental search space is small enough for tabular Q-learning but still large enough to contain useful CNNs:

Layer type Main choices
Convolution layer depth < 12, filter size {1, 3, 5}, stride 1, channels {64, 128, 256, 512}
Pooling layer depth < 12, (filter, stride) in {(5, 3), (3, 2), (2, 2)}
Fully connected layer depth < 12, at most two consecutive FC layers, neurons {512, 256, 128}
Termination global average pooling or softmax

The state also includes a binned representation size. This prevents the agent from repeatedly shrinking a feature map until later convolutions or pooling operations no longer make sense. For example, too many stride-2 pooling layers can reduce a 32 x 32 image to 1 x 1, so the action graph disallows transitions that would create invalid feature maps.

This is one of the most practical pieces of the paper: NAS needs a search space, but it also needs guardrails. Without them, much of the budget would be wasted on architectures that are legal as strings but useless as CNNs.

Q-learning Loop

MetaQNN uses the standard Q-learning update:

where s_i is the current state, u is the action, s_j is the next state, and the reward r is the validation accuracy of the completed CNN. The paper sets:

  • alpha = 0.01
  • gamma = 1
  • initial Q-values to 0.5
  • final policy to epsilon = 0.1, not 0, so the final sampler can still generate several high-quality variants for ensembling

The search loop is:

  1. Sample a CNN topology by walking through the state-action graph with epsilon-greedy exploration.
  2. Train the sampled topology with a short, aggressive schedule.
  3. Store the topology and validation accuracy in replay memory.
  4. Sample 100 previous models from memory and update Q-values backward along their trajectories.
  5. Anneal epsilon and repeat.

The epsilon schedule is deliberately exploration-heavy at the beginning:

Epsilon 1.0 0.9 0.8 0.7 0.6 0.5 0.4 0.3 0.2 0.1
Unique models trained 1500 100 100 100 150 150 150 150 150 150

So one full search run trains about 2700 unique models before the final fine-tuning stage. During exploration, each model is trained for only 20 epochs with Adam, batch size 128, initial learning rate 0.001, and dropout inserted after every two layers. The reported search cost is 8-10 days per dataset on 10 NVIDIA GPUs.

Why Replay Memory Helps Here

In a normal supervised training loop, one minibatch update is cheap. In NAS, one “environment step” can mean training a CNN. MetaQNN therefore cannot afford to learn only from the most recent sampled architecture.

The replay dictionary gives each trained architecture multiple chances to update the Q-table. If the same topology is sampled again, the paper does not retrain it; it reuses the stored validation accuracy. This is a simple engineering choice, but it matters because the expensive part is CNN training, not the Q-value update.

Results

Search Behavior

The Q-learning curves are the first sanity check. As epsilon decreases, the sampled models should become better on average. The paper reports that, for SVHN, mean model accuracy increases from 52.25% at epsilon = 1.0 to 88.02% at epsilon = 0.1.

This does not prove that the agent found a globally optimal architecture. It does show that the Q-table learned useful preferences inside the constrained search graph.

The learned preferences are also interpretable. In the appendix, the authors analyze Q-values by layer depth: convolution and pooling have higher Q-values early in the network, while fully connected and termination states become more likely deeper in the network. That matches the rough shape of hand-designed CNNs.

Benchmark Numbers

MetaQNN is strongest when compared with networks using similar layer types. The top CIFAR-10 model reaches 6.92% test error, better than the standard-layer baselines listed in the paper.

Method CIFAR-10 SVHN MNIST CIFAR-100
All-CNN 7.25 - - 33.71
MetaQNN ensemble 7.32 2.06 0.32 -
MetaQNN top model 6.92 2.28 0.44 27.14
ResNet-110 6.61 - - -
ELU network 6.55 - - 24.28
Tree+Max-Avg pooling 6.05 1.69 0.31 32.37

All numbers are test error percentages. The comparison against ResNet and more complex pooling methods is less flattering, but also less direct: those models use architectural ideas outside the MetaQNN search space. The more honest reading is that MetaQNN does well within a plain CNN search space, but the search space itself limits the ceiling.

Discovered Architectures

The top CIFAR-10 architecture reported in the appendix is:

It reaches 6.92% test error with 11.18M parameters. The top five CIFAR-10 models range from 11.18M down to 1.10M parameters, but the error varies from 6.92% to 11.63%. That spread is a useful reminder: validation-guided architecture search can find good candidates, but the top architectures are not all equally strong.

One design motif mentioned in the paper is the frequent use of 1 x 1 convolution near the input. The authors interpret it as a learned linear transformation of RGB channels, similar in spirit to preprocessing into another color space. I would treat that as an observation rather than a general rule, but it is a nice example of Q-value analysis producing inspectable architecture hints.

Transfer

The authors also test whether the best CIFAR-10 architecture transfers to other datasets. SOTA means the reference state-of-the-art number listed in the paper.

Target Scratch Fine-tune SOTA
CIFAR-100 27.14 34.93 24.28
SVHN 2.48 4.00 1.69
MNIST 0.80 0.81 0.31

The architecture transfers better than the weights. Fine-tuning from CIFAR-10 weights is worse than training from scratch in all three reported cases. That is not too surprising: the searched architecture can be reusable, but the learned filters from CIFAR-10 are not necessarily a good initialization for digit datasets or CIFAR-100.

Takeaway

MetaQNN is a good example of early NAS engineering. The paper’s main lesson is not that Q-learning is the final answer for architecture search. Later work moved toward controller RNNs, cell-based search, weight sharing, differentiable NAS, and hardware-aware search because training thousands of child models is too expensive.

The lasting idea is the decomposition:

  • Define a searchable but valid architecture graph.
  • Use a cheap policy representation over that graph.
  • Evaluate sampled architectures with a consistent reward.
  • Reuse expensive evaluations through replay or other performance-estimation tricks.

The limitation is equally clear. The method inherits the bias of its search space: only standard CNN layers, coarse discrete hyperparameters, and fixed training recipes. It can discover strong combinations inside that box, but it cannot invent residual blocks, depthwise separable convolutions, attention, or hardware-aware operators unless those choices are explicitly added to the state-action graph.

For me, MetaQNN is most useful as a baseline mental model for NAS: before thinking about supernets or differentiable relaxations, first ask what the states are, which actions are legal, how much one reward costs, and whether the search space itself is the real bottleneck.

entry.title: MONAS: Multi-Objective Neural Architecture Search
Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning
Progressive Neural Architecture Search
ProxylessNAS: Direct Neural Architecture Search on Target Task and Hardware
Random Search and Reproducibility for NAS
entry.content:
Li L, Talwalkar A. Random Search and Reproducibility for Neural Architecture Search. UAI 2020.

  • Paper
  • Code

This paper is useful because it attacks a boring but important question: when a NAS method looks good, how much of the gain comes from the search algorithm itself, and how much comes from the search space, the training recipe, the evaluation shortcut, or the final retraining protocol?

The answer is uncomfortable. In the DARTS-style PTB and CIFAR-10 spaces, carefully implemented random search is a hard baseline. Random search with early stopping already reaches competitive results, and random search with weight sharing can match or beat several specialized NAS methods under similar budgets.

NAS As Hyperparameter Optimization

The paper frames NAS as a special case of hyperparameter optimization. There are three moving parts:

  • the search space, such as a cell DAG or a macro architecture;
  • the search method, such as random search, RL, evolution, or gradient-based optimization;
  • the evaluation method, such as full training, partial training, or weight sharing.

This split is the main mental model of the paper. If a new algorithm is evaluated with a stronger training recipe or cheaper evaluation oracle than the baseline, it is not clear whether the algorithm did the work.

For NAS papers I think the minimum unit test should be:

Check What it catches
Same search space Avoids crediting a hand-designed space to the search method
Same evaluation budget Makes best-so-far comparisons meaningful
Same final training recipe Prevents retraining tricks from looking like search improvements
Multiple random seeds Measures variance instead of one lucky architecture
Released code and architecture Allows independent retraining and debugging

Reproducibility Audit

The authors first audit recent NAS papers. Their table checks whether a paper releases architecture-search code, model-evaluation code, random seeds, and hyperparameter-tuning details.

The important point is not that every paper is careless. NAS experiments are expensive, often multi-stage, and sensitive to implementation details. The problem is that missing seeds or missing hyperparameter logs make it impossible to separate an algorithmic contribution from a lucky or under-documented experimental setup.

The paper distinguishes two levels:

  • Exact reproducibility: rerun the same code with the same seed and get the same result.
  • Broad reproducibility: repeat the experiment with different seeds or equivalent code and get statistically similar conclusions.

Exact reproducibility is a low bar for a single-machine deterministic setup. Broad reproducibility is the bar that matters for judging whether a NAS method is robust.

Method: Random Search With Weight Sharing

The paper evaluates two random-search baselines:

  • Random search with early stopping. This uses ASHA to allocate more budget to promising architectures and stop poor ones early.
  • Random search with weight sharing. This samples architectures uniformly, trains one shared-weight supernet by activating one architecture per minibatch, then scores many sampled architectures using the shared weights.

The second baseline is the most interesting one. It removes the sophisticated controller from methods like ENAS and keeps the cheap evaluation mechanism. If that baseline works, then the search controller may not be the main contribution.

For PTB, the search space is a recurrent-cell DAG with (N=8) intermediate nodes. Each node selects a previous node as input and an operation from tanh, relu, sigmoid, or identity.

For CIFAR-10, the setup follows the DARTS normal-cell and reduction-cell space.

The search algorithm is simple, but the meta-hyperparameters are not. The result changes with the number of search epochs, batch size, network size, gradient clipping, number of sampled architectures, and final retraining length.

PTB Results

The PTB table is the cleanest evidence that random search is not a strawman.

Key rows from the table:

Method Test perplexity Total search cost Search method
ENAS, published 56.3 N/A RL
DARTS second order, published 55.7 2 GPU days gradient-based
DARTS second order, reproduced 55.9 2 GPU days gradient-based
ASHA baseline 56.4 2 GPU days random
Random search WS 55.5 1.25 GPU days random

Random search with weight sharing gets 55.5 test perplexity, better than the reproduced DARTS run and the ASHA baseline in this setup. This does not prove that random search is universally better. It proves that the NAS comparison is weak if it does not include this baseline.

The paper then digs into stage (2), where candidate architectures are retrained with a proxyless network for 300 epochs before choosing what to fully evaluate.

The table shows that the best Random (4) run has validation perplexity 63.8 after stage (2), close to the best published DARTS intermediate result. A second Random (4) run is worse, which is already a warning that a single search run is not enough.

The ranking table makes that warning more concrete.

At 300 epochs, several methods are close. By 3600 epochs, Random (4) Run 1 becomes best, while Random (4) Run 2 ends fourth. Intermediate validation rank is a noisy selection signal.

CIFAR-10 Results

The CIFAR-10 comparison is less one-sided, but it makes the same methodological point.

Key rows:

Method Best test error Average test error Total search cost Search method
ENAS, published 2.89 N/A N/A RL
DARTS second order, published N/A 2.76 +/- 0.09 5 GPU days gradient-based
DARTS second order, reproduced 2.62 2.78 +/- 0.12 10 GPU days gradient-based
ASHA baseline 2.85 3.03 +/- 0.13 9 GPU days random
Random search WS 2.71 2.85 +/- 0.08 9.7 GPU days random

Random search with weight sharing is competitive with the published DARTS/ENAS-style results, although the reproduced DARTS run still has the best average in this table. The important part is that the random baseline is in the same performance regime.

The authors also tune the random-search-with-weight-sharing setup. This table is a good reminder that even a “random” baseline has important engineering choices.

The large proxyless setting, lower gradient clipping, and more evaluated architectures improve the random-search baseline. Without reporting those tuning choices, it would be easy to compare against a weak version of the baseline.

Broad Reproducibility

The paper repeats CIFAR-10 random search with weight sharing across six independent runs.

The six-run average is 2.92 test error. Runs 1 to 3 are around 2.85 to 2.88, while Runs 4 to 6 degrade to 2.95, 2.98, and 3.00. This is still competitive, but the spread is large enough that reporting only the best discovered architecture would be misleading.

This is the most useful practical lesson for me: NAS results need distributions, not just a best architecture and a GPU-day number.

Cost Accounting

The computational-cost section is short but important. The paper compares cost per architecture under three evaluation styles:

Evaluation style PTB cost per architecture CIFAR-10 cost per architecture
Full training 0.5 GPU days 4 GPU hours
ASHA partial training 9 minutes 19 minutes
Random search WS, amortized 0.2 minutes 0.8 minutes

Weight sharing makes each architecture extremely cheap to score, but that number can hide the real total cost. If many supernet trials, seed sweeps, and final retraining runs are needed to get a stable result, the headline search cost is not the whole story.

Takeaways

Random search is not the conclusion of NAS. It is the control experiment.

My takeaways:

  • A NAS method should beat random search in the same search space and under the same final training recipe.
  • Early stopping and weight sharing are evaluation methods, not search algorithms by themselves.
  • Intermediate validation rankings can change after longer retraining, so short proxy evaluations need skepticism.
  • Reproducibility requires seeds, code, architecture definitions, and hyperparameter-tuning logs.
  • Best-run reporting is fragile. Average, variance, and rerun cost are part of the result.

The paper is a useful calibration point: before trusting a more complex NAS controller, first make the random baseline strong enough that beating it actually means something.

entry.title: SMASH: One-Shot Model Architecture Search through HyperNetworks
entry.content:
Brock A, Lim T, Ritchie J M, Weston N. SMASH: One-Shot Model Architecture Search through HyperNetworks. ICLR 2018.

  • Paper
  • Code

SMASH is an early one-shot NAS paper, but it is not the same kind of one-shot method as ENAS or DARTS. It does not keep one shared supernet and select subgraphs. Instead, it trains a HyperNetwork that maps an architecture encoding to a set of generated weights.

The core bet is:

where (c) is an architecture description, (H) is the HyperNetwork, and (W) is a subset of weights for the sampled CNN. If the validation error under (H(c)) correlates with the validation error after normal training, then architecture search becomes much cheaper: sample many architectures, score them with generated weights, keep the best, and train only the final architecture normally.

SMASH Loop

The algorithm is short enough to fit in one figure.

The first loop trains the HyperNetwork. Each step samples a minibatch and a random architecture (c), generates weights (H(c)), evaluates the sampled network (f_c(H(c), x_i)), and updates (H). The second loop samples architectures on a validation set and ranks them by their SMASH score. The selected architecture is then fixed and trained from scratch with freely learned weights.

This is important: generated weights are only a proxy. The final reported model is not deployed with HyperNetwork-generated weights.

Memory-Bank Search Space

The paper needs a way to describe variable CNN topologies in a tensor form that a HyperNetwork can consume. The proposed answer is a memory-bank view of feed-forward networks.

Instead of thinking of a CNN as a simple chain of layers, SMASH treats each operation as reading from and writing to memory banks. This makes several connectivity patterns expressible with the same machinery:

Pattern Memory-bank behavior
ResNet-like read a bank, transform it, add/write back
DenseNet-like read many previous banks, write to a fresh bank
FractalNet-like use a more complex branching read/write pattern

The sampled network uses a normal CNN skeleton: stem, block 1, transition, block 2, transition, block 3.

Inside a block, each op starts with a generated (1 \times 1) convolution over the memory banks, followed by up to two parallel paths of two convolutions each. The (1 \times 1) weights are generated by the HyperNetwork; the other convolution weights are normally learned and shared across ops within a block. This design keeps the dynamic part manageable while still making connectivity and width variable.

Architecture Encoding

The architecture (c) has to encode enough structure for (H(c)) to generate useful weights. SMASH encodes the read/write pattern, op choices, output units, dilation, and related settings into a tensor.

The paper uses a fully convolutional HyperNetwork so the output shape can change with the input architecture tensor. Conceptually, each spatial slice of the encoding corresponds to a slice of generated weights. The channel dimension stores one-hot architectural facts such as which memory banks are read, which banks are written, and what operation settings are active.

This is a clever trick, but it also explains why SMASH is not a universal graph-to-weights solution. The search space has to be engineered so that the encoding is regular enough for a convolutional generator.

Does The Proxy Rank Architectures?

The key experiment is not the final CIFAR number. The key experiment is whether the SMASH score is correlated with true performance.

For SMASHv1, the authors train a SMASH network on CIFAR-100 for 300 epochs, sample 250 random architectures, rank them by SMASH validation error, and fully train every fifth architecture for 30 epochs. Figure 4 shows 50 architectures. Lower is better on both axes, and the positive correlation is what makes the method plausible.

The authors are careful not to overclaim this. The correlation is one experimental condition, not a theorem. They then deliberately weaken the setup.

With a smaller “crippled” HyperNetwork, the relationship between generated-weight validation error and true validation error mostly breaks down. The rank plot also shows that scores from different HyperNetwork seeds have nontrivial spread.

This is the main limitation in practice: one-shot evaluation is only useful if the proxy ranking is reliable. A cheaper proxy that changes the ordering of architectures is not just noisy; it can actively select the wrong model.

Architectural Gradient By Proxy

SMASH also asks whether the architecture tensor itself can be optimized by gradient. Since (E = f(H(c), x)), one can in principle backpropagate to (c) and use (\frac{dE}{dc}) as a search signal.

The paper tests whether the HyperNetwork actually uses the encoding by corrupting (c), for example by shuffling dilation values. The correct encoding gives better validation performance, suggesting that (H) has learned a real architecture-to-weight mapping.

But the attempted gradient-descent-style update over discrete architecture choices did not beat random perturbations. This part reads more like a useful negative result than a complete algorithm.

Benchmark Results

SMASHv2 expands the search space with variable filter sizes, variable groups, and the full op structure from Figure 2. The best SMASHv2 models are then trained normally and compared with hand-designed and automatic methods.

Important rows from Table 1:

Method Params CIFAR-10+ error CIFAR-100+ error
Shake-Shake 26.2M 2.86 15.85
DenseNet-BC, k=40 25.6M 3.46 17.18
Neural Architecture Search with RL 32.0M 3.84 N/A
Large-Scale Evolution 5.4M / 40.4M 5.40 23.7
SMASHv1 4.6M 5.53 22.07
SMASHv2 16M 4.03 20.60

SMASHv2 is not state of the art against strong human-designed models. It is much closer to the automatic-design baselines of that period. The paper claims the discovered model is found with far less compute than Large-Scale Evolution, but the comparison is not perfectly symmetric: SMASH starts from a more structured search space and does not grow networks from trivial initial models.

Transfer Results

The paper also transfers the best CIFAR-100 SMASHv2 architecture to STL-10 and ImageNet32x32.

The STL-10 result is not great against Wide ResNet: SMASHv2 has 41.52 +/- 2.10 error, while WRN-40-4 reports 35.02 +/- 1.14. A smaller 3x3 SMASHv2 variant improves to 37.76 +/- 0.58. On ImageNet32x32, SMASHv2 gets 38.62 top-1 and 16.33 top-5 error, better than the listed WRN baselines in the table.

There is also an interesting earlier transfer observation in the text: the architecture found on CIFAR-100 beats the architecture found directly on STL-10 when both are trained on STL-10, suggesting that larger search datasets may produce architectures that generalize better.

What The Found Architecture Looks Like

The appendix visualization is messy, but that is part of the point. The discovered architecture is not a clean hand-designed motif.

This reinforces the engineering tradeoff in SMASH. The search space is flexible enough to produce long, irregular read/write graphs, but the method still depends on an encoding and HyperNetwork that can assign meaningful proxy weights to such graphs.

Takeaways

SMASH is historically useful because it separates two ideas that later get blended in one-shot NAS:

  • Cheap architecture evaluation can be learned and amortized.
  • The learned evaluator must be validated by ranking correlation, not only by final best accuracy.
  • A HyperNetwork evaluator is different from a shared-weight supernet.
  • Encoding design is part of the method; it constrains what the search can express.
  • Generated weights are a proxy, not the final model parameters.

My read is that SMASH is less a production NAS recipe and more a clean early experiment in amortized model evaluation. The paper’s best contribution is not “HyperNetworks solve NAS”; it is the explicit question: can a learned weight generator rank architectures well enough to make search cheap?
